synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Dr. Miles Wei, 31, lecturer in physics, holds office hours on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Shen Yu Jie, final-year student and the best mind in the department, comes on Wednesdays. Every Wednesday. With problems she has already solved.

He has one rule: nothing happens while she is a student in his department. He draws it on his chalkboard as a flat line. She adds an end date. 20 June, 16:00. Then she makes a calendar, two hundred and sixty-six squares long, and draws a physically inaccurate atom in every one.

Between them stand sticky-note physics jokes, a department that has started a betting pool, a supervisor who smokes on a balcony she isn’t allowed on, a mother who calls her daughter the Perfect Jewel in front of guests, a diplomat with a secret, and a grant nobody applied for.

Proof by Induction is a bright, slow-burn campus romance about waiting, about being taken seriously, and about a man who stopped laughing at seventeen and a woman who makes him start again.

The main story is told across four volumes and is complete. Side stories at the end can be read any time. Miles first appears as a side character in Every Flower in the Shop, but this book stands on its own.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers. Mature themes and heated love scenes.

This is a gentle book, but it has some hard moments:

• Emotional control and coercion by a parent, including being cut off financially and made to leave home (Volume Two and Volume Three)

• Online gossip and sexist rumours about a student (Rumours in the Department Kitchen)

• A character coming out to his family at a dinner table, and a parent walking out (The Perfect Jewel Says No)

• Illness with a high fever (Miles Gets Sick and Nobody Notices)

• A relationship between a lecturer and a student that stays strictly non-romantic until she has graduated, and is declared to the department

• Love scenes between the couple after graduation. They are sensual but not explicit (Yu Jie Gets a Job, The Night She Made Him Dance in the Empty Lab)

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Miles Wei walked into Every Flower in the Shop for one scene, dropped his clicker, asked Elowen if she was happy, and wouldn’t leave my head. This is his book.

I wanted a love story where the most romantic thing anyone does is take the other person’s mind seriously, and where waiting is not a delay but the point. The physics is real, kept at the level of a story: the harmonic oscillator, entropy as counting, strained graphene, and analogue black holes made in water tanks, which real laboratories build.

The jokes are, regrettably, also real. Thank you for reading.

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
Wednesday — The day Yu Jie comes to office hours, which are on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
The harmonic oscillator — The problem she brings on her first Wednesday. Its lowest energy, ½ħω, is never zero: nothing is ever completely at rest.
Lecture Theatre C — Where Miles teaches second-year Quantum Mechanics at ten, to a hundred and forty students.
The rule — Miles’s one rule: not while she is a student in his department.
The sticky notes — His physics jokes on the side of her tea. She catalogues every one, with a type, a rating out of ten and an annotation.
White Rabbit — The milk sweets Yu Jie keeps in her cardigan pocket. She writes on the wrappers.
The Perfect Jewel — What her mother calls her in front of guests.
Shen Holdings — Her family’s company. It owns half the harbour and a forty-storey building downtown.
Bell Street — The street by the old wall where the bakery called Fang’s stands.
Old Huang — The security guard at the blue door, eleven years on the night shift.
The red envelope — Twenty yuan from Tao Tao’s grandmother. Yu Jie never spends it.

chapters.title: The Girl Who Was Definitely Not Stuck on Quantum Mechanics
chapters.desc: Shen Yu Jie turns up on the wrong day with a problem she has already solved. Dr. Miles Wei solves it anyway, the long way, and keeps the pen she drops.
chapters.epigraph: “I have a question about the harmonic oscillator.” “It’s Wednesday.” “I know.”
chapters.content:
Office 412 had a sign on the door.

DR. MILES WEI Office hours: Tuesdays and Thursdays, 3–5 p.m. (Other times: please email. I will reply. Eventually.)

Under it, somebody had drawn a cat in a box. Green marker. Tiny. A question mark over its head. Miles hadn’t drawn it. He didn’t know who had. For three years he’d looked at it every morning with his key in the lock. Funny. Also wrong. Schrödinger’s cat was never in a superposition of confused.

He’d never rubbed it off, though.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second Wednesday of September, somebody knocked.

Miles was at his chalkboard. Not a whiteboard. Five years ago the department had put whiteboards in every office. That same weekend Miles bought two tins of chalkboard paint and did the whole back wall himself. Badly. Professor Zhou, head of department, came in on the Monday, stared at it and walked out without a word. Miles took that as a yes.

He was halfway through a line of algebra. He didn’t turn round.

“It’s open. Unless you’re from facilities about the radiator. Then I’m not here.”

The door opened.

“I’m not from facilities.” A girl’s voice. “Is it broken?”

“It makes a noise like a whale. Every forty minutes. I timed it.”

“What does it say?”

The chalk stopped.

He’d told the whale joke to four colleagues and the facilities man. Five polite laughs. Zero follow-up questions. He turned round.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was in the doorway with a notebook hugged to her chest. Twenty-two, maybe. Yellow sundress. White trainers that had cost a lot once and were now covered in biro. A grey cardigan big enough for two of her, sleeves shoved to the elbow. Her hair was piled up in a tortoiseshell claw clip that was losing the fight.

Four pens stuck in it. He counted. Four. Who needed four?

She was smiling like she’d just won something.

“Hello! Shen Yu Jie. Final year, Professor Gao’s group.” She held up the notebook. “I have a question about the harmonic oscillator.”

Miles looked at her. Then at the sign on the door. Then at the calendar on the wall.

“It’s Wednesday.”

“I know.”

“My office hours are Tuesdays and Thursdays.”

“I know that too.” She came in without being asked and sat down. The chair creaked like it had opinions. “But on Tuesdays and Thursdays there are fifteen second-years in here, and I didn’t want to queue behind a boy who thinks Planck’s constant is a type of sandwich.”

The chair creaked again when she shifted. She frowned down at it.

“Is it always like this?”

“Yes.”

“Do you have another one?”

“That’s the student chair.”

“I’m a student.”

“Then it’s your chair.”

Miles opened his mouth to say something else. Shut it.

Bai Tianyu. Last Thursday. Is Planck’s constant the same everywhere, or, like, regional? It had taken Miles twenty minutes to recover.

She was looking past him now. At the wall.

“Did you paint that?”

“Yes.”

“It’s crooked at the top.”

“It’s hand-finished.”

“It’s crooked.”

“…It’s slightly crooked.”

She looked delighted about that. Why was she delighted about that?

“Why paint it? The whiteboards are new.”

“Whiteboard pens squeak.”

“Chalk squeaks.”

“Chalk squeaks honestly.” He hadn’t meant to say that. It was true, though. “Whiteboard pens die halfway through a proof. Without warning. Chalk just gets shorter. You can see it coming.”

She stared at him. Then she wrote something in the margin of her notebook. He couldn’t see what.

He wanted to see what.

“You’re not in my course.”

“No. I took Quantum Two last year with Professor Lin. Top mark.” Flat. A weather report. She flipped the notebook round and pushed it at him. “But I’m stuck. Look. Really, really stuck.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He looked. The quantum harmonic oscillator. A particle in a bowl. A normal ball would roll to the bottom and stop. A quantum one can’t. Every physics student on the planet meets it in second year.

Three pages. Neat handwriting. She’d set it up and gone straight to the ladder operators. The elegant way. Most students only saw that at the end of the course.

Page three: a huge question mark. Underneath, small: ???? help Miles looked at the question mark. Then back at the three pages before it.

“You’re not stuck.”

Her smile didn’t move. Her eyes dropped, though.

“I am! Very. Page three. Question mark. Big one.”

“You’ve used the ladder operators.” He tapped page two. “You’ve normalised the ground state. That’s the hard bit. After that it’s one line.” He turned back to page one. There, in the margin, so small it was nearly hiding: (n + ½)ħω. The answer. Perfect. “You solved it before you started.”

The office went quiet. Then the radiator, right on schedule, let out a long, low moan across some imaginary ocean.

She glanced at it. Back at him.

“It says hello,” she said. “I think it’s lonely.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He should have sent her away.

He knew it even then. Student. His department. Wrong day, solved problem. A student only did that for one reason, and it wasn’t the harmonic oscillator. But under the smile there was a dare. And he’d shared this office with the whale for five years and a cactus for three.

He picked up the chalk.

“Fine. You’re stuck. Let me un-stick you.”

He solved it from scratch. The long way. The differential equation, the Hermite polynomials, no ladder operators at all. How they’d done it in 1926. He filled the whole wall. Twenty-five minutes. He didn’t look at her once.

“Wait. Are you doing Hermite polynomials?”

“Yes.”

“On purpose?”

“Yes.”

“Dr. Wei. It’s not 1926.”

“It is on this wall.”

She made a noise like a kettle. Then she stopped heckling. Around minute ten she went completely quiet, and he noticed, and he didn’t turn round.

“Uncertainty principle.” He kept writing. “If it sat still at the bottom, you’d know where it was and how fast it was going. Zero and zero. The universe won’t let you know both. So it keeps moving. A tiny bit. Forever. Even at absolute zero.” He drew a little wobble at the bottom of the bowl. “Zero-point energy. Nothing gets to be completely at rest.”

He stepped back. Chalk on his sleeve. Chalk on his hand. Probably his face. He turned round.

She wasn’t looking at the board. Chin in her hand, she was looking at him. The winning smile had gone. What was left looked surprised.

“That,” she said, “was the most boring way anyone has ever solved that problem.”

“Yes. On purpose. So you’d see you already know the interesting way.”

“You did the hard version… to prove I didn’t need help.”

“You don’t.” He put the chalk down. “You need a better excuse for Wednesdays.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went pink. Huh. He hadn’t expected that. She looked like someone who didn’t do pink.

She shot up. The chair complained. A purple pen slid out of her claw clip and rolled under his desk, and she didn’t notice.

“Okay! Right. Thank you, Dr. Wei! That was very helpful.”

“I didn’t help.”

“Still very helpful!” Notebook. Door. Then she stopped with one hand on the frame and turned round.

“What do you say back? To the whale?”

“Nothing. I don’t speak whale.”

“You should learn.” A real smile now. Crooked. Not winning anything. “It’s been calling for years. Somebody should answer.”

Then she was gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stood in the middle of his office, covered in chalk. Then he crouched and fished the pen out from under the desk.

Purple. A small plastic cat on the end, with a question mark painted on its head.

He looked at the pen. He looked at the door, where a green cat in a box had been staring back at him for three years. Question mark and all.

Oh. Oh, no.

He put the pen in his top drawer. Not the lost property box by the lift. Not the bin. The drawer. He told himself that was the efficient choice. She’d come back for it. Would she come back for it?

✦ ✦ ✦

At five he went down the corridor to the kitchen. Professor Lin was there, waiting for the kettle with a mug that said I’D RATHER BE IN A VACUUM.

“Lin. Quantum Two, last year. Shen Yu Jie?”

Lin’s whole face changed.

“Oh, her.”

“You remember her.”

“A HUNDRED, Wei. I’ve never given a hundred in my life.” He poured the water. “I cried a bit. Don’t tell anyone. Why?”

“She left a pen.”

“A pen.”

“Purple. There’s a cat on it.”

Lin looked at him over the top of the vacuum mug.

“You walked all the way down the corridor. About a pen.”

“It’s a nice pen.”

That was true. It wasn’t the reason. He didn’t say the reason, because he didn’t know it yet.

Lin dunked his teabag. “Give it to Gao. Gao’s terrifying. She’ll make sure the girl gets it back.”

“Yes. Good idea.”

He did not give it to Gao.

✦ ✦ ✦

He marked nothing until six. The whale called twice more. Both times he stopped writing to listen.

Was he waiting for it to say something? He was a physicist. It was a radiator. He listened anyway.

On Thursday, fifteen second-years crammed into 412 with their homework.

“Dr. Wei! Is it h-bar or h-slash?”

“Bar.”

“Because my roommate says slash.”

“Your roommate is wrong.”

“He does economics.”

“Then he’s wrong professionally.”

Bai Tianyu wrote that down. Miles had no idea why.

“Dr. Wei, are you waiting for someone?” A girl by the window. “You keep looking at the door.”

“It’s a very good door.”

Fifteen second-years turned and looked at the door. It was a door.

She didn’t come.

She came on Wednesday.

chapters.title: Office Hours Are Tuesdays and Thursdays
chapters.desc: She keeps coming on Wednesdays. He lies about the pen, buys a second mug, and starts leaving the door open.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s not small enough. You made it up. You decided it was small because it was easier.” — Yu Jie, to Dr. Miles Wei, on the wrong day
chapters.content:
Tao Tao was upside down again.

Head hanging off the end of Yu Jie’s bed. Feet up the wall. A packet of shrimp crisps balanced on her stomach. Biology student, roommate, and a person with opinions about everything.

“You went to his office.” Crunch. “On purpose. On the wrong day. With the harmonic oscillator.”

“I needed help.”

“You got a hundred in Quantum Two! Professor Lin cried, Jie Jie. You could teach the harmonic oscillator to the harmonic oscillator.”

Yu Jie was at her desk with her back to the room, drawing on a sticky note.

“He did it the long way.”

“What?”

“The whole wall. Hermite polynomials. Twenty-five minutes.” She put the pen down. “To prove I didn’t need him at all.”

Tao Tao stopped crunching.

“Okay. That’s either the most insulting thing a man has ever done to you or the most romantic. I genuinely can’t tell.”

Yu Jie stuck the note to the edge of her monitor. A tiny whale. A speech bubble: hello?

“Me neither. So I’m going back.”

“With what? You’ve solved everything.”

“I’ll find something.”

“You’ll un-solve something.”

“Perturbation theory.” Yu Jie spun her chair round. “Second order. I’ll put a question mark on it. A big one.”

Tao Tao gave her a long, judging look.

“You’re going to fake being stupid. For a man. You. Shen Yu Jie.”

“Not stupid! Stuck. It’s different.”

“Of course you are!” Tao Tao rolled the right way up and pointed a crisp at her. “What’s he like?”

“Tall. Glasses. His hair sticks up at the back. One bit.” Yu Jie showed her with a finger. “He has a chalkboard. He painted it. It’s crooked.”

“Is he HOT, though?”

“…He’s a physicist.”

“That’s not a no.”

“It’s not a no,” Yu Jie admitted, and put her whole face in her cardigan sleeve.

✦ ✦ ✦

Next Wednesday. Quarter to four. Perturbation theory.

She knocked. “It’s open,” he said, without turning round. Then he did turn round. He looked at her. At the calendar. At her again.

“It’s Wednesday.”

“It is.” She sat. The chair creaked hello.

“Did I leave a pen here last week? Purple. It’s got a cat on the end.”

His hand was on its way to the top drawer for fresh chalk. It changed direction.

“No.”

“Oh. Weird.” She shrugged. “Never mind. I’ve got nine.”

“Nine.”

“Pens are like socks. They just go somewhere.”

He took the chalk off the ledge instead. The drawer stayed shut.

He’d just lied to a student. About a pen. A pen with a cat on it.

He waited to feel bad about it. Any minute now.

No sending her away this time. No long way either. He read her three neat pages and the question mark at the end.

“What’s the real question?”

“That is the real question.”

“You’ve done first order. You’ve done second order. The question mark is at the bit you’ve already answered.” He pointed at the margin. There it was. Tiny. “You keep doing that. Hiding the answer in the margin.”

“Maybe I want someone to find it.”

He looked at her.

What was that face doing? It looked like it was thinking about four things at once. Three of them were probably equations. Was the fourth one her?

“Then here’s a real question.”

He wrote it in four lines. Not perturbation theory. A particle in a bowl that was almost a harmonic oscillator, but bent. Lopsided. Like someone had sat on it.

“Nobody’s solved that exactly.” He stepped back. “I don’t know the answer. I think it might be interesting.”

She stared at the board.

Then she got up, took the chalk out of his hand without asking, and started writing.

✦ ✦ ✦

They were still there at six.

The radiator called eight times. They stopped hearing it after four. The board filled up, got wiped, filled up again. Her handwriting and his, all tangled. Arrows. Crossings-out. A squashed bowl in the corner that she’d given a face. Somewhere along the way he’d ended up sitting on his own desk and she’d taken his chair. They were arguing. Loudly.

“It can’t go! Look. Throw that term away and the energy goes negative. Negative. That’s nonsense.”

“Not if the bend’s small enough.”

“Define small.”

“Small. Smaller than the other thing.”

“That’s not a definition, that’s a vibe.”

“I don’t know what that means and I disagree with it.”

“It’s not small enough! You made it up. You decided it was small because it was easier.”

He opened his mouth. Then he looked at the board. Properly.

“You’re right.”

She stopped.

Huh?

People didn’t say that to her. Her mother never had. Her father didn’t talk to her long enough. Her brother only said it when he wanted her to stop talking.

Dr. Wei said it like he was writing down a measurement.

“You’re right.” He slid off the desk and rubbed the term out with the side of his hand. Chalk all down his sleeve. “I was being lazy. It matters. That changes the whole thing.” He turned round, and his face was lit up like a kid’s. “You saw that in four seconds. I’ve been staring at it for a week.”

There was chalk on his face now. One white smear across the cheekbone.

She forgot her next sentence completely.

She stuffed her hands in her cardigan pockets. Where else were they supposed to go?

“You have chalk on your face.”

He touched his cheek. Made it worse.

“Other side.”

He did the other side. Now there were two smears. One per cheekbone. Perfectly matched. A very nervous tiger.

“Better?”

She kept her face straight. It nearly killed her.

“Much better. It’s symmetrical now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t tell him.

Not for the next hour of arguing. Not when she left. She made it to the third-floor landing before she cracked, and she laughed all the way down to the second.

He found out at nine that night, in the bathroom mirror.

Miles stood and looked at the tiger for some time.

He didn’t laugh. He came close, though. Something in his chest did a thing it hadn’t done in years. He told it to stop.

It didn’t stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday she passed him on the stairs. Perfectly clean face. He stopped two steps above her.

“You let me be a tiger,” he said. “For an hour.”

“Maybe.”

“I walked past the porter. He saluted me.”

“What did you say to him?”

“I said good evening.” He sounded wounded. “He said good evening, sir and he SALUTED.”

“You were a very good tiger, Dr. Wei.”

He looked at her for a second. Then he went on up the stairs, and she saw him check his reflection in the fire-door glass on the way. Both cheeks.

She bit the inside of her cheek until it hurt.

✦ ✦ ✦

After that, Wednesdays were hers.

Never Tuesdays. Never Thursdays. On those days 412 was packed with second-years. She’d walk past on her way to the lab and hear Bai Tianyu through the door.

“Dr. Wei, does the wave function, like, physically exist?”

“That’s actually a very old, very good question.”

Endless patience. She’d smile at nobody and keep walking.

On Wednesdays she brought a solved problem with a question mark and the answer in the margin. He always found it.

“You’ve already done this.”

“Have I?”

Then he’d sigh and write something real on the board. Something nobody knew the answer to.

And she noticed things.

Tea, not coffee. A mug that said WORLD’S OKAYEST SON in faded letters.

An egg sandwich every day, from the machine on the second floor. By noon the machine was out of everything else. He never seemed to mind.

“Do you ever eat anything else?”

“The machine has egg.”

“The machine has five things.”

“By noon it has egg.”

“So go before noon!”

“Before noon I’m teaching.” He took a bite, completely at peace. “Egg is fine. Egg is a complete protein.”

“That’s the saddest sentence I’ve ever heard.”

He considered this while he chewed. “Bai Tianyu once asked me if eggs have quantum states. That’s sadder.”

A cactus on the windowsill. Grey-green, a bit sad, in a small blue pot. A label in his handwriting: SCHRÖDINGER.

“Is it alive?”

“I don’t know. I’ve decided not to check. That way it’s both.”

She laughed so hard she had to put her head down on his desk.

He stood there holding the chalk, mildly alarmed. Like his beaker had started fizzing on its own.

“That was a joke. Wasn’t it? I made a joke.”

She nodded into her arms.

“Nobody usually laughs.” He put the chalk down like it might go off. “Should I write that down?”

“DON’T you dare write that down!”

He wrote it down. She saw him. Bottom of his notes, tiny: cactus — laughed.

She lifted her head. “Dr. Wei.”

“It’s data.”

“You’re keeping data on me?”

“On the joke.” He didn’t look up. “The joke is the variable.”

The joke was not the variable. They both knew the joke was not the variable.

✦ ✦ ✦

He knew her Tuesdays too. That was the embarrassing part.

Half past three, give or take a minute, she went past 412 on her way down to Gao’s lab. Ponytail on Tuesdays. Claw clip on Wednesdays. He could hear her trainers on the lino through the door, over fifteen second-years, over Bai Tianyu. Squeak, squeak, gone.

He’d started leaving a gap in his explanations around half past three. Just in case.

In case of what? He had no idea. It was a tiny gap.

On the Monday before the fourth Wednesday, he went to the shop by the east gate.

The auntie behind the counter had known him for five years. Egg sandwiches when the machine broke. Batteries. Chalk, once, in a crisis.

“Dr. Wei! Chalk again?”

“A mug.”

She pointed. There were three. One with a cartoon pig. One that said BOSS. One plain white.

“The white one.”

“For your girlfriend?”

“For a student.” He put it on the counter. “For tea. It’s a teaching mug.”

“A teaching mug.” The auntie looked at it. Looked at him. “Mm-hm.”

Then he stood at the tea shelf reading boxes. For an embarrassing amount of time. Jasmine. Jasmine with pearls. Jasmine superior. What was superior jasmine? Was regular jasmine an insult?

He bought the regular. She’d had the regular.

At the till there was a jar of White Rabbit sweets. He looked at it.

“Those too,” he heard himself say. “Please. A bag.”

“Teaching sweets?” said the auntie.

“Yes.”

“Mm-hm.”

The sweets went in his top drawer. Next to the purple pen with the cat on it. He didn’t give her any. He just liked knowing they were there.

✦ ✦ ✦

The night before the fourth Wednesday, Tao Tao watched her try on cardigans.

“That’s four.”

“It’s for tomorrow.”

“Tomorrow is Wednesday.” Tao Tao sat up on the bed. “Oh my god. You’re dressing up for office hours.”

“They’re not office hours. That’s the whole point.”

“You’re dressing up for not office hours.”

“I’m dressing for thermal reasons. His office has a radiator situation.”

“The whale.”

“The whale,” Yu Jie agreed, with dignity.

She put the grey one back on. The big one. The one he’d looked at twice last week when she pushed up the sleeves.

Not that she’d counted.

She’d counted.

Tao Tao’s voice went gentle. “Jie Jie. You’ve known him three weeks.”

“Three and a half.”

“Oh, that’s so much better!”

✦ ✦ ✦

Fourth Wednesday. Quarter to four. The door was open.

Not just open. Propped wide. A fat textbook on the floor holding it.

She stopped in the corridor.

He never propped it. Every other week she’d knocked, and he’d said “It’s open” without turning. This week there was nothing to knock on. Inside, he was at the board writing. And on the desk, in front of her chair, there was a second mug. Plain white. Teabag in. Steaming.

She walked in.

He didn’t turn round.

“Jasmine,” he said, writing. “The machine downstairs does jasmine or something that claims to be English Breakfast and isn’t. I guessed.”

She sat. Picked it up. Right temperature. She took a sip.

“I like jasmine.”

“Good.”

“You guessed?”

“I estimated.” The chalk squeaked. “Last week a teabag wrapper fell out of your cardigan when you took your pen out. Jasmine. Also three White Rabbit wrappers. I put them in the bin after you left.” A pause. “Educated guess. Most guesses in physics are.”

She looked at the back of his head. That one bit of hair. She held the warm mug in both hands.

He’d noticed her rubbish.

Who notices somebody’s rubbish?

She turned the mug over. Still a price sticker on the bottom. The shop by the east gate. New. Bought for this.

Twelve.

Her mother spent more than that on the flowers in the downstairs bathroom. Every day. Nobody at home had ever bought anything for her that cheap. It was always jade, or silk, or a car she hadn’t asked for, picked by an assistant.

She peeled the sticker off and put it in her pocket. He didn’t see.

He didn’t mention the door. She kept her questions about it to herself.

“Dr. Wei?”

“Mm.”

“The textbook. On the floor.”

“It’s holding the door.”

“It’s Principles of Quantum Mechanics.”

“It’s the heaviest one I own.” He finally glanced back at her. Then away again, fast. “Physics is load-bearing.”

She hid her face in the steam and drank her tea, and her ears were hot for the next two hours.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six she packed up. At the end of the corridor she looked back.

The door was still propped. Dr. Wei was still at his board. Not writing, though.

Looking at her chair.

Then he caught her looking. He dropped the chalk.

chapters.title: The Harmonic Oscillator Is Not a Metaphor
chapters.desc: In front of a hundred and forty second-years she asks if zero-point energy applies to people. He answers honestly, and the whole fourth floor knows by lunch.
chapters.epigraph: “Nothing is allowed to be completely at rest. Not even at absolute zero.” — Dr. Miles Wei, Quantum Mechanics, Lecture 7
chapters.content:
Lecture Theatre C. Tuesdays and Thursdays at ten. A hundred and forty second-years who mostly wanted to be in bed.

Miles didn’t blame them. Ten in the morning plus quantum mechanics was a lot to ask of anyone. So he drew pictures. He told them about the whale. He tried to make them see that the weirdness was the point. By eleven, some of them were awake. He counted that as a win.

Lecture seven was the harmonic oscillator. He’d given it five times. He knew it cold. He walked in with his notes under his arm, put them on the lectern without looking, turned round—

Back row. Corner seat by the door. Yellow. He stopped walking.

She waved. Just her fingers, over the top of the desk. In the front row, Bai Tianyu twisted round to see what Dr. Wei was staring at. Twisted back. His eyes went huge.

Miles picked up the chalk.

“Good morning. Today: why nothing in the universe is allowed to sit still.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It wasn’t his best lecture. Not his worst, either. He drew the bowl. He drew the little ball rolling at the bottom. He explained why a normal ball can stop and a quantum one can’t. But every time he turned round, his eyes went to the back row. And every single time, she was looking at him. Not at the board. At him. Chin in her hand.

He wrote ħ on the board. Then he noticed he’d crossed the h four times. Four lines. One h. Excellent. Very professional.

Bai Tianyu’s hand shot up.

“Dr. Wei, why are there four lines on the h?”

“Emphasis.”

“Do we need four lines on ours?”

“One is fine.”

“Will we lose marks for four?”

“Nobody will lose marks for any number of lines.”

“What about zero lines?”

“Zero lines is a different constant, Bai Tianyu. Please use one.”

At the back, someone made a muffled noise into a cardigan sleeve. He didn’t look. He absolutely didn’t look.

“So.” He cleared his throat. “The uncertainty principle says the particle can’t have exactly zero position and exactly zero momentum at the same time. So it can’t sit perfectly still at the bottom. So the lowest energy isn’t zero. It’s this.” He tapped the board. “Half ħω. Zero-point energy.”

A hand went up in the middle rows. A girl with glasses.

“Dr. Wei, so it’s, like, always moving? Forever?”

“Yes. Nothing is allowed to be completely at rest. Not even at absolute zero.”

The girl wrote it down. Underlined it twice. In the back row, Shen Yu Jie put her hand up.

The whole theatre turned round. Nobody put their hand up in the back row of C. The back row was for sleeping. Everybody knew that.

“Yes. Back row.”

She stood. She didn’t have to. Nobody stood. She stood anyway, yellow dress, enormous cardigan, three pens in her hair today, and her voice carried all the way to the front.

“Dr. Wei. Is that true of people too?”

✦ ✦ ✦

A hundred and forty heads swung from her to him. Bai Tianyu’s mouth fell open.

“I’m sorry?”

“Zero-point energy. You said nothing is ever allowed to be completely at rest. Is that people too? Or just particles?”

Somebody in the middle giggled and got shushed.

He knew what she was doing. Being funny. Being bold. Standing up in his lecture to see what he’d do with it. Same as turning up on Wednesdays.

Make a joke, Wei. People are too big for quantum effects. Easy laugh. Move on.

He opened his mouth and answered the actual question.

“I think it is. A bit.” He looked at the chalk in his hand. “You can try to keep still. Take everything away. People, plans, all of it. You can sit in a room with a cactus for three years and tell yourself you’re fine.”

He looked up.

“But something’s always left over. The lowest you can go isn’t zero. It’s never zero.”

Nobody moved. At the back, she wasn’t smiling any more. She was standing completely still.

Which was ironic, he thought, from a long way off. Given the topic.

Then, from the front row, loud, in total sincerity—

“Dr. Wei, is that going to be on the exam?”

The theatre exploded.

“No.” Miles had to raise his voice over it. “No. It’s not on the exam.”

“Is the cactus on the exam?”

“Nothing about the cactus is on the exam.”

“Does it have a NAME?” Somebody near the top.

“Moving on.”

“IT HAS A NAME!”

“Moving on.” He turned to the board so fast he nearly took the duster with him. “Raising and lowering operators. Page forty.”

Behind him, a hundred and forty people turned to page forty and absolutely did not stop talking about the cactus.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Jie was out of the corner door before the lights came up. She got as far as the vending machines on the ground floor and put her forehead on the glass. Cold. Good. Her face needed it.

What had she done?

She’d asked a joke question. He was supposed to give a joke answer. Everybody laughs, everybody moves on. Instead he’d stood there with chalk on his fingers and said never zero like he meant it. In front of everyone. And now her knees had stopped working. Her phone buzzed.

She did not put the phone down. She found xiaoyu_phys. Second-year. Glasses. The glasses. The girl who’d asked “Forever?” and underlined the answer twice. Fine. Okay. Totally fine.

She bought a can of coffee she didn’t want and drank it like it had personally wronged her.

Her phone rang. Tao Tao, obviously.

“You’re jealous of a second-year.”

“I’m not jealous. I’m CONCERNED.”

“About what?”

“Her grades! She underlines everything twice. That’s a sign of anxiety.”

“Jie Jie.”

“She asked if it moves forever. Obviously it’s forever. He’d literally just said—”

“You’re defending his lecture from a nineteen-year-old.”

“Somebody has to!”

“Where are you right now?”

“…The vending machines.”

“Are you drinking that canned coffee you hate?”

Yu Jie looked at the can in her hand.

“No.”

“Go to the lab. Do your graphene. Stop stalking children.”

“I’m not stalking. I’m reviewing the literature.”

Tao Tao hung up on her. Yu Jie looked at xiaoyu_phys’s profile one more time. Then she closed it. Then she opened it again, just to check the glasses. They were nice glasses. That was the worst part.

✦ ✦ ✦

He finished the lecture. He had no idea how. The students filed out past him. Three different girls gave him looks he couldn’t read. One boy patted his shoulder.

“Deep lecture, Dr. Wei.”

“Thank you? I think?”

“Is the cactus okay, though?” A girl at the door. “Like, honestly?”

“The cactus is fine.”

“Okay but are you—”

“Page forty. Thursday.”

She went. The back row was empty. He climbed up to it. Five years of teaching in C, and he’d never once been up there. From the back, the board looked tiny. The lecturer didn’t. You could see everything from up here. Every time he turned. Every time he looked up. Exactly where his eyes went.

Oh. So that was what she’d been doing for an hour.

On her desk was a White Rabbit wrapper, smoothed out flat. Inside, in purple biro, round handwriting:

½ħω. Never zero.

He stood there longer than he meant to. Then he folded it once and slid it into his wallet, behind his staff card. Somebody had to tidy the theatre.

Wallet. Not bin. Again. This was becoming a pattern, and he was a physicist. He knew what a pattern was.

✦ ✦ ✦

Back in 412 he shut the door and put his face in his hands. A cactus for three years. Out loud. To a hundred and forty people.

Somebody knocked. Tuesday. Not even lunch. Office hours didn’t start till three.

“It’s open.”

Dr. Fang Hao put his head round the door. Astrophysics, office 413, thirty-five, round face, married to a pastry chef. The biggest gossip on the fourth floor. He was holding a paper bag that smelled of butter.

“Croissant?”

“No, thank you.”

He came in anyway, shut the door, sat on the corner of Miles’s desk and ate half a croissant in one bite.

“Sho,” he said, through crumbs. “I hear you gave a very moving lecture.”

Miles closed his eyes.

“Four hundred and twelve likes, Miles. ‘Lonely quantum particle.’ A second-year wants you to be her potential well.” He swallowed. “Also a girl stood up in the back row. Final year. Yellow dress. Gao’s group.”

A pause. A long, buttery pause.

“Same yellow dress that comes up here every Wednesday, quarter to four on the dot, and doesn’t leave till six.”

Miles opened his eyes. “How do you know that?”

Fang Hao knocked on the wall between their offices. It sounded like a cereal box.

“Cardboard. Two hours of you two yelling about potential wells. Every week. Last week she called you lazy and you said you’re right.” He took out the second croissant. “You have never said you’re right to anyone. Not me. Not Zhou. Not the facilities man about the radiator.”

“She was right.”

“I know she was right. I heard.” Bite. “Is she in your course?”

“No.”

“Do you mark anything of hers?”

“No.”

“Supervise?”

“No. Gao does.”

“Then technically, fine. Technically.” Fang Hao pointed the croissant at him. “But she’s still a student in this department. And I’m not the only one with ears.”

“Nothing is happening.”

“I know nothing’s happening. You’re you.” Fang Hao brushed crumbs off his trousers. They landed on the second-year marking. “Just be careful, all right? Gao’s noticed. She asked me why her best student keeps coming back down from the fourth floor with chalk on her cardigan.”

“What did you tell her?”

“That you have a lot of chalk.” He got up. “She didn’t believe me either.”

“And Zhou?”

“Zhou doesn’t read posts. Zhou reads boundary conditions.” Fang Hao squinted at him. “Do you even know her name?”

“Shen Yu Jie.”

“Instantly. No pause. Full name.” Fang Hao put the croissant down on the marking. “Oh, Miles. You’re in so much trouble.”

“I know the names of all my second-years.”

“Name the boy with the green backpack.”

“…”

“There it is!”

He got as far as the door. Turned.

“For the record? Lovely lecture. I nearly cried, and I wasn’t even there.”

Door shut. Then it opened again.

“Potential well, Miles!”

Shut.

✦ ✦ ✦

Half past three. Office hours. Fifteen second-years, one radiator, no air. Her trainers squeaked past on the lino. Ponytail. Tuesday.

Miles was out of his chair and in the corridor before he’d decided anything.

“Shen Yu Jie.”

She stopped. Turned. Her face was doing something careful.

“Dr. Wei.”

“You left something. In C.”

“Did I?”

“A wrapper.”

“Oh no. Littering.” Hand on her heart. “Are you going to report me?”

“I tidied it.”

“Into the bin?”

He didn’t answer. His ears answered for him. She watched them go pink with enormous interest.

“Dr. Wei? Where did you tidy it to?”

“Wednesday,” he said. “Come on Wednesday. I have something to say to you.”

“Say it now.”

“No.”

“Is it about the cactus?”

“No.”

“Is it about my question?”

He looked at her. She looked back, chin up. The brave face was good. Her fingers were twisting the strap of her bag into a rope.

“There are fifteen second-years behind this door,” he said.

“Fourteen!” Bai Tianyu, from inside. “Doudou went to the toilet!”

“Thank you, Bai Tianyu.”

“You’re welcome, Dr. Wei! She’ll be back in two minutes!”

She pressed her lips together hard.

“Wednesday, then,” she said. “Quarter to four.”

“Quarter to four.”

She went off down the corridor and didn’t look back once. He knew, because he watched the whole way. He went back in. Fourteen faces looked up at him.

“Where were we?”

“THE CACTUS,” said everyone.

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles opened his top drawer.

Purple pen. Plastic cat. Bag of White Rabbits. All still there. He turned the pen over in his fingers.

Is that true of people too?

He’d told a hundred and forty second-years that nothing was allowed to be completely at rest. That there was always something left over.

He’d been talking about physics. Mostly.

He put the pen back and took out the wrapper, and put it in the drawer too, next to the pen. Then he took it out again and put it back in his wallet. Wallet felt safer. Who’d look in his wallet?

What was he doing? He was a grown man with a staff card and a pension. He was hiding sweet wrappers in his wallet like a schoolboy.

He shut the drawer. He pulled a pad of paper towards him and wrote one word at the top.

RULE He underlined it twice.

Then he sat there until the whale called, and he still hadn’t written a single word under it.

chapters.title: Miles Wei Has One Rule
chapters.desc: Miles turns her down with a graph he drew with a metre rule. She adds an end date: the twentieth of June, four o’clock.
chapters.epigraph: “Not while you’re a student in this department.” “And when I’m not?” “…I didn’t think about that part.”
chapters.content:
“Say it to me.”

It was Wednesday morning. Very early. Fang Hao had come in for a telescope call with Chile and found Miles sitting in 412 in yesterday’s jumper, staring at a pad of paper with one word on it.

RULE.

“I’m not saying it to you.”

“Then say it to the cactus.”

“I don’t talk to cacti.”

“Then say it to me, Miles, or you’re going to say it to her for the first time and it’ll come out as a lecture on Lagrangians.” Fang Hao sat in the student chair. It creaked. “Go on. I’m her. I’m twenty-two. I’m wearing yellow.”

Miles looked at him. Then at the pad. Then at him again.

“You’re a student in this department,” he said at last. “Nothing can happen.”

“Ouch. Too cold. She’ll cry.”

“She won’t cry.”

“Everyone cries. I’d cry. Do it gentler.”

Miles tried again. Gentler. It came out like a weather warning.

“Better.” Fang Hao winced. “Worse, but better. What if she does cry?”

“Then I’ll—” He opened his top drawer and took out a packet of tissues. “My sister makes me carry these.”

“Put them back. Do not hand her tissues. What if she asks whether you want to?”

“She won’t ask that.”

“Miles.”

“She won’t.” He put the tissues back. “Nobody asks that. It’s not a question people ask.”

Fang Hao looked at him with deep pity and went next door to talk to Chile.

✦ ✦ ✦

That afternoon, the chalkboard was clean.

Yu Jie stopped in the doorway. Every equation from last week, gone. The black paint actually shone. In the middle, in neat white chalk, there was one graph.

A horizontal axis: TIME. A vertical axis with no label at all. And across the middle, a perfectly flat line, edge to edge.

Above it: Professional distance. Below it, smaller: (constant).

Dr. Wei was behind his desk. Not at the board. Hands folded. A doctor with bad news.

“Please sit down.”

She sat. Notebook against her chest. The chair didn’t even creak. Had he oiled it?

“Is this about the lecture?”

“Partly.”

“I’m sorry. I shouldn’t have stood up, it was—” Her voice wobbled. Just once.

His hand went towards the top drawer. Tissues. He stopped it halfway. Do not hand her tissues.

“It was a very good question.” He looked at his hands. “I shouldn’t have answered it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d practised. Obviously.

Every few sentences his eyes slid left, like he was reading notes off the inside of his skull.

“You’re a student. In this department. I’m a lecturer. I don’t teach you. I don’t supervise you. I’m not on any of your committees.”

“I know.”

“But we’re in the same building. There are rules about that. And there are things that aren’t rules but should be.” Eyes left. “Also, my colleague next door can hear everything.”

“Dr. Fang.”

“Who has told me. Kindly. That people are talking. That Professor Gao has noticed. And that a second-year posted online that I compared myself to a lonely particle.”

“You did, a bit.”

“I know I did.” He took his glasses off, rubbed his eyes, put them back on. “So. I’ve made a rule. For me. Not for you. You can do what you like.”

“That’s very generous.”

“It’s not generous. It’s fair. I can’t keep seeing you on Wednesdays without telling you what it is.”

He got up, went to the board and tapped the flat line.

“Not while you’re a student in this department.”

She looked at the line.

“Nothing,” he said. “No—” a vague little wave with the chalk “—anything. You can still come on Wednesdays. I’ll still make tea. We can still fight about the bent oscillator. That’s physics. Physics is allowed.”

Tap.

“But this stays flat. That’s the rule.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t say anything at first.

She’d been turned down before. Twice. She was Shen Yu Jie. She was pretty, and her family owned half the harbour, and boys didn’t usually turn her down. They followed her around holding her bags.

Both times had been horrible anyway. Once with a laugh. Once with a lecture about how she was too much.

This wasn’t that.

He’d drawn her a graph.

He’d wiped his whole board, the board he’d painted himself, so the graph would be the only thing on it. He’d said fair. And he’d said anything with that helpless little wave, like he didn’t trust himself to say what anything was.

Well. Wasn’t that interesting.

She put the notebook down on his desk.

“Can I ask a question?”

“Of course.”

“Is it a rule because you don’t want to? Or because you can’t?”

The chalk stopped moving.

She won’t ask that, he’d told Fang Hao. This morning. With total confidence.

She watched him think. She was learning his face now. He was a terrible liar. She doubted he’d ever even tried. His eyes went to the flat line. The floor. The cactus. Her.

“It’s a rule.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It’s the only one I’m allowed to give.” He set the chalk on the ledge. “That’s sort of the point of rules.”

“Who’s not allowing you? You made it.”

“Yes.”

“So you could unmake it.”

“I could.” He looked pained. “I won’t.”

“Why not?”

“Because I’d be very bad at it. And it would cost you more than me.” He pushed his glasses up. “That’s the bit I can’t do arithmetic around.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She looked at the graph.

Then she got up, walked to the board, and picked up the chalk he’d just put down.

“And when I’m not?”

“Sorry?”

“Not while I’m a student in this department. And when I’m not?”

He blinked.

“Your time axis is wrong.” She tapped it. “It doesn’t go on forever. It can’t. I’m final year. I graduate in June.” She looked at him over her shoulder. “So when exactly do I stop being a student in this department?”

“When you—graduate. Obviously.”

“Which is when?”

“The ceremony’s on the twentieth of June. It finishes at four.” He paused. He couldn’t help himself. Precision was a disease. “Technically you’re a student until it ends. That’s when you get the certificate. From four o’clock, you’re an alumna.”

“Four o’clock. Twentieth of June.”

She turned back to the board.

At the far right end of his beautiful flat line, she drew a short vertical mark. Very neat. Beside it, small: 20 June, 16:00.

Then she drew what came after.

Nothing. She stopped the line at the mark. On the other side she left the board black and empty and shining.

She put the chalk back on the ledge and stepped away.

“There. Now it’s a proper graph. Constant on a finite interval.” She turned round. “You didn’t say anything about after the interval.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He stood in front of his own board and stared at it.

His flat line. Her mark. The empty space after it.

She watched it land on him. He’d stayed up making a kind, careful rule. And without noticing, he’d tied it to a date nine months away. Now the date was on his wall. In her handwriting.

“…I didn’t think about that part.”

“I know.” She picked up her bag. “You’re very clever, Dr. Wei. But you only ever solve for the bit you’re looking at.”

“That’s not fair.”

“You said fair was important.”

“I meant—” He gave up. He looked at the mark again. “That’s nine months.”

“Two hundred and sixty-nine days. Roughly.”

“Roughly?”

“I’ll get you an exact number.” She smiled at him. “I’m very good at counting.”

He made a noise. She’d never heard a lecturer make that noise. It sounded like a kettle that had been told some bad news.

“Two hundred and sixty-nine?”

“Roughly!”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went to go. She stopped.

He had chalk on his cheekbone again. Left side. The tiger was back.

She shouldn’t. Physics was allowed. Faces probably weren’t.

She did it anyway.

She reached up and wiped it off with her thumb. One swipe. His skin was warm under the dust. He went completely rigid. Didn’t breathe. She could actually feel him not breathing.

“Chalk,” she said. Her voice came out wrong. “You had chalk.”

“Thank you.” Barely a sound.

Her thumb was still on his cheek. Why was it still there?

She snatched her hand back and shoved it in her cardigan pocket. Traitor.

“Rule,” he said. Very low. Not to her, exactly.

“I know.”

“It’s only been up for—”

“Four minutes. I know.” She was bright red. She could feel it in her ears. “That didn’t count. That was hygiene.”

“Hygiene.”

“Chalk dust is a respiratory hazard, Dr. Wei.”

He looked at her. His jaw was doing something. Then he turned to the graph, fast, and studied it like it had just insulted him.

She cleared her throat. Looked at the graph too. Safer.

“Also, nobody draws a line that straight freehand.” She narrowed her eyes. “Did you use a ruler?”

He looked at the floor.

“The metre rule. From the second-year teaching lab. I borrowed it before anyone was in.”

“Dr. Wei!”

“It had to be constant. That was the whole point.”

She pressed her lips together so she wouldn’t smile at him. Failed. Completely.

“Same time next Wednesday? For physics.” She was at the door. “Which is allowed.”

He glanced at the board. A little helpless.

“Yes. Physics is allowed.”

She was halfway out of the door when he said her name.

“Shen Yu Jie.”

“Mm?”

“Roughly is a terrible word.”

She turned round slowly. “Then you count it, Dr. Wei.”

“I’m not going to count it.”

“Okay.” She was grinning so hard her face hurt. “Don’t count it.”

“I won’t.”

“Good.”

“Good.” He was looking extremely hard at the cactus. “It’s a waste of time. Counting.”

She left before she could do anything stupid, like go back in.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went down four flights without touching a single one of them.

Outside, in the September sun, she opened the calendar on her phone and scrolled. Past October. Past New Year. Past spring. The twentieth of June. New event. Four in the afternoon.

The name box blinked at her.

She typed: The end of the interval.

Saved.

Then she screamed into her cardigan sleeve, just a bit, and a passing first-year gave her a wide berth.
