“It wasn’t a rejection.” Yu Jie was lying on her bed with her phone on her chest. “It was a scheduling conflict.”

“Jie Jie. A man told you no with a ruler.”

“With a metre rule. He borrowed it. From the teaching lab. Before anyone was in.” She put her hands over her face. “Tao Tao, he got up early to borrow a ruler so his no would be straight.”

“That’s insane.”

“I know!”

“That’s the most insane thing I’ve ever heard and I once watched a boy propose with a petri dish.” Tao Tao chewed a crisp. “So what are you going to do?”

“Count.”

“Count what?”

Yu Jie turned her phone round. The twentieth of June. Four in the afternoon. The end of the interval.

Tao Tao stared at it.

“What did he say? When you drew the line?”

“He said, ‘I didn’t think about that part.’”

“No.”

“Like this.” Yu Jie did his face. Blank. Stricken. Glasses slipping. “I didn’t think about that part.”

Tao Tao fell over sideways onto the rug and lay there.

“He’s going to lose.” Tao Tao was flat on her back, staring up. “Oh my god. That poor man is going to lose so badly.”

“It’s not a competition.”

“Jie Jie, everything is a competition with you. You argued with the hospital about your own blood type.”

“They had it wrong!”

“They had it right and you made them check twice!”

Yu Jie put the phone face down on her chest.

“Then I’ll win,” she said. “Two hundred and sixty-nine days. I’m very patient.”

“You are the least patient person alive.”

“I’m patient about this.”

Tao Tao lifted her head off the rug and squinted at her.

“Oh, you’re so much worse than I thought.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The cleaner came into 412 just before ten with her trolley.

Miles was still there. Standing in front of the board. He’d been standing there, on and off, since six. Twice he’d picked up the rubber. Twice he’d put it down again.

“Dr. Wei? Shall I do the board for you?”

“NO.”

She froze with her cloth in the air.

“No. Thank you. Sorry. No.” He cleared his throat. “I’ll do it.”

“You’ve been saying that for an hour.”

“I’m doing it now.”

“You said that at nine, Dr. Wei.”

“I meant it at nine.”

She gave him a look, and went off to do 413.

He picked up the board rubber.

He wiped off the flat line. Professional distance. (constant). The time axis.

He got to the little mark at the end. 20 June, 16:00.

The rubber stopped.

He touched his own cheekbone. Left side. Where her thumb had been.

Miles put the rubber down.

He left the mark there in the bottom right-hand corner, small and neat in her handwriting, where nobody else would notice.

It stayed there all year.

chapters.title: A Countdown Disguised as a Semester
chapters.desc: Yu Jie makes a countdown calendar with an atom for every day. Miles finds it, counts the squares twice, and asks to kiss her on the back stairs.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s a very well-made calendar. The atoms are a good touch. Physically inaccurate, but a good touch.”
chapters.content:
The calendar was Tao Tao’s idea. Technically.

“If you’re going to be insane about it, at least be organised.” Saturday. Tao Tao was on the floor of their room with her feet up on Yu Jie’s bed. “Make a chart. Tick off the days. Like a prisoner.”

“I’m not a prisoner.”

“You’re counting down nine months until a man you’ve known for three weeks is allowed to buy you a coffee. That is literally what prisoners do.” A shrimp crisp hit Yu Jie on the ear. “Also I’ve opened a betting pool.”

“You’ve what?”

“Half the biology department’s in. The odds on ‘she gives up by Christmas’ are terrible. I warned everyone.”

“Who bet on that?”

“Ah Peng.”

“Ah Peng’s in chemistry.”

“He heard about it at the canteen. He put in twenty.” Tao Tao looked smug. “I put fifty on June.”

Yu Jie didn’t answer. She’d already got out a large sheet of graph paper.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took her all afternoon. Pencil first, then ink. One small square for every day, from today to the twentieth of June. She laid them out in rows like a periodic table. Weekends pale blue. Exam weeks red. Holidays yellow. The last square, bottom right, she drew bigger than the rest and outlined in gold.

Then she sat back and looked at it.

Two hundred and sixty-six squares. She felt slightly ridiculous. Then proud. Then ridiculous again.

“You need a symbol.” Tao Tao had come to lean over her shoulder. “For crossing them off. Something meaningful. Not an X. An X is very prison.”

Yu Jie thought about it. Then she picked up a fine purple pen, and in the first square, today’s, she drew a tiny atom. A dot in the middle. Three little elliptical orbits round it. The cartoon version that nobody had believed in for about a hundred years.

“Why an atom?”

“Because it’s always moving. Even when it looks still.” She capped the pen. “Zero-point energy.”

Tao Tao looked at her for a while.

“You are the most hopeless person I have ever met,” she said. “And I once dated a boy who wrote me a song about mitochondria.”

“Was it good?”

“It rhymed ‘cristae’ with ‘kiss me.’”

“That’s beautiful.”

“Jie Jie, it was in the key of nothing.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She folded the calendar into quarters and kept it in the back of her physics notebook. That way she could draw the atom wherever she was. The lab. The library. The bus home on Sunday, up the hill to the big white house above the harbour. Her mother called it the family residence. Yu Jie called it the museum.

Sunday dinner at the museum was at seven. It had been at seven for twenty-two years. It would be at seven after the sun exploded.

Her mother sat at the end of the long table. Shen Ruolan was fifty-four and looked forty. Perfect skin. Perfect posture. A voice like a sharp knife wrapped in silk. Her father sat at the other end and read his phone. Her brother Yu Ming, thirty-four, who ran the company, sat on her mother’s right and said nothing unless spoken to. The soup came.

“You look tired.”

“I’ve been in the lab, Ma.”

“You’re always in the lab.” Her mother tasted the soup. “Your skin suffers. Your hair suffers. You have ink on your hands, Yu Jie. Ink. Like a schoolgirl.”

Yu Jie put her hands in her lap.

“The Lus are coming to the Foundation gala in December. Their son’s back from Geneva.”

The spoon stopped halfway to Yu Jie’s mouth.

“Lu Zhiyuan. The diplomat. Twenty-nine. Very good family. He’s been posted back home for two years now, the Foreign Affairs Office.” Her mother smiled. “I showed his mother your photograph. The one from your cousin’s wedding, in the blue dress. She was very impressed.”

“Ma.”

“Wear the blue dress. And do something about your hair.”

“Ma, I’m not—”

“You’re twenty-two, darling.” The gentlest voice. Which was always the sharpest one. “You’re a beautiful girl from a very good family. You’ve spent four years in a laboratory doing something nobody in this family understands. That’s fine. It’s a hobby. Every girl needs a hobby.”

“It’s not a hobby. It’s physics.”

“Yu Ming, tell your sister.”

“Listen to Ma.” Her brother didn’t even look up from his plate.

Yu Jie stared at him. He kept eating. Across the table her father scrolled. Nobody else had heard a thing.

“Thank you, Yu Ming.” Her mother picked up her spoon. “But it’s time to think about your real future. You’re the Perfect Jewel, darling. That’s what everyone calls you.” She smiled down the table. “Jewels are meant to be worn.”

Yu Jie looked at her soup. Under the table, in her lap, the physics notebook was open on her knees. The calendar was unfolded inside it. She was holding the purple pen.

She drew the day’s atom without looking down. Nobody saw. Nobody ever looked at what was in her lap.

✦ ✦ ✦

Fifth Wednesday. Miles found the calendar by accident.

She’d brought a notebook with a problem in it, as usual. She’d put it on his desk and gone to fill her water bottle at the cooler in the corridor. A folded sheet of graph paper slid out of the back of the notebook and fell open on his desk.

He looked at it. He didn’t mean to. He was going to fold it straight back up. But it was a grid, and he was a physicist. He couldn’t look at a grid without understanding it. It was a medical condition.

Small squares. Rows like a periodic table. Weekends in blue. Exams in red. The last square, bottom right, bigger, outlined in gold. And beside it, in purple, in her round handwriting, 20 June. 16:00. The end of the interval.

The first eleven squares each had a tiny purple atom drawn in them. A dot with three orbits. One a day.

Bohr model. Of course it was the Bohr model.

He counted the empty squares. Then he counted them again, because he didn’t trust the first number. It wasn’t a hard sum. His hands weren’t steady.

Two hundred and fifty-five.

He sat at his desk with the calendar in front of him and didn’t move. Then, footsteps in the corridor. Coming back.

He folded it along its creases, exactly as it had been, and slid it into the back of her notebook. He closed the notebook. He squared it up on the desk where she’d left it. When she came back in, he was at the board with his back to her. Writing.

She didn’t notice anything. He wrote slowly, so his hand would stop shaking.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a counting problem. Not quantum mechanics. Something simpler. Almost a puzzle. A particle that took one step left or right every day, with a probability for each, and a question about how many days it’d take, on average, to reach a certain point. A random walk. The kind of thing they set first-years to warm up.

She looked at it. Puzzled.

“This is easy.”

“Humour me.”

She sat down and worked it. It took her four minutes. She wrote the answer at the bottom and turned the notebook round. 255

She looked at the number. Then up at him. Then the number. Then him. Her face went pink from the collar up.

He was standing at the board with his hands in his pockets, looking at the cactus.

“That’s a nice number,” he said, eyes on the windowsill.

“You saw it!”

“It fell out.” He didn’t look at her. “It’s a very well-made calendar. The atoms are a good touch. Physically inaccurate, but a good touch.”

“Physically inaccurate?”

“Electrons don’t orbit like that. That’s the Bohr model. It was abandoned in 1925.”

“I KNOW it was abandoned in 1925!”

“But it’s the one everyone draws. It’s the one that looks like an atom.” A pause. “I understand.”

She put her head down on his desk, on top of the notebook, and stayed there.

“I’m going to die,” she said into the paper.

“Please don’t. There are two hundred and fifty-five days left. It would be a waste.”

She lifted her head.

He was still looking at the cactus. But the tips of his ears had gone red.

“Dr. Wei. Your ears.”

“Blood flow. It’s a thermoregulatory response.”

“To what?”

He looked round the room. She watched him do it. Bookshelf. Radiator. Cactus. Window. He was searching the whole office for a stimulus that wasn’t her, and he couldn’t find one.

“Insufficient data,” he said.

She put her head back down on the notebook and laughed until the radiator joined in.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six she packed up. He said he’d walk her to the back stairs. The light on the landing had been broken since August. It had not been broken since August. Facilities fixed it on Monday. He knew, because he was the one who’d reported it.

She knew too. She’d walked past it this morning. She didn’t say anything.

The corridor was empty. Office 413 had been dark since half past five, when Fang Hao went home to his wife. Miles held the fire door. They went through. It swung shut behind them, and they were on the landing between the fourth floor and the third, by the narrow window. The last of the light came in grey over the trees.

She turned round to say goodbye. He was closer than he’d meant to be. Close enough to see the ink on the middle finger of her right hand. Chalk on her sleeve. She was holding the notebook against her chest again, the way she had on the first Wednesday. A shield.

“Two hundred and fifty-five,” he said.

“I know.”

“I counted them twice. While you were at the cooler.”

“You said counting was a waste of time.”

“It is.” He made himself look at her. “I’ve been doing it anyway. Every night. Since the graph.”

She stopped breathing. He was fairly sure. So had he.

“I drew a rule on my board,” he said. “And every day since, I’ve tried to work out how to keep it for two hundred and fifty-five more. The numbers don’t work. I’ve checked them. They don’t.”

One of the pens in her claw clip was sliding out. The green one.

He reached up and pushed it back in. His knuckles brushed the side of her neck, just under her ear. She shivered. He felt her do it.

He didn’t take his hand away.

“I’m going to break it.” His voice wasn’t steady at all. “My own rule. I’ve never broken a rule in my life. I want to break this one, here, on these stairs. But not unless you want me to.” His hand stayed where it was, at the edge of her hair. Not moving. “So I’m asking. Do you?”

She let go of the notebook. It slid down between them and smacked onto the step. Nobody looked at it.

“Yes,” she said. “Since the whale.”

He kissed her.

✦ ✦ ✦

He did it the way he did everything. Carefully. Like he was afraid of getting it wrong.

His mouth was warm and not quite sure of itself. His hand slid from her hair to the back of her neck and stayed there. For a second he only held her like that, lips barely on hers. Waiting to see if the building would fall down. It didn’t.

She put both hands flat on his chest, on the grey jumper. His heart was going hard under her palms. As fast as hers. Faster? She pressed closer.

He made a startled noise against her mouth. Then he kissed her properly.

Careful didn’t last. Her back found the cold wall by the window. His glasses knocked her cheekbone and he didn’t stop to fix them. She went up on her toes in her trainers, and he bent down to meet her, and he kissed her like he’d been doing sums about this for a month and was finally allowed to show his working.

When he pulled back, it was only an inch. He rested his forehead on hers. He was breathing like he’d run up all four flights. The tips of his ears were scarlet.

“Your ears,” she whispered.

“I’m collecting more data.”

He kissed her again. This time she laughed into it. She didn’t stop kissing him back.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards they sat on the step. Her notebook between their feet. His arm along the step behind her. Not quite round her. Still asking. She leaned back into it. Problem solved.

“Nobody can know,” he said. “Not in this building.”

She went still against his arm.

“Not because it’s wrong. It isn’t.” He said it fast, before she could. “You’re twenty-two. I don’t teach you. I don’t mark anything of yours. I read the university code on Sunday night. All forty pages.”

“You read the code?!”

“Twice.” He looked at the window. “It’s your work. Fang Hao hears through the wall. Gao counts the chalk on your cardigan. If people knew, then every mark you got, every prize, your thesis—someone would say it came from me.”

“It wouldn’t be true.”

“No. That wouldn’t matter to them.” His jaw went tight. “I won’t have that.”

“So we hide.”

“Until you graduate. Four o’clock on the twentieth of June.” He turned his head and looked at her. “After that I’ll hold your hand in the fourth-floor corridor. In front of Fang Hao. And Professor Zhou. And the facilities man. And anyone else who wants to watch.”

“You promise?”

“I’ll put it in writing. With a signature.”

“On the board?”

“Not on the board,” he said, alarmed, and she laughed so hard she had to hold on to his jumper.

She got her phone out. Found the event. Turned the screen so he could see. The end of the interval.

“Still the right name,” she said. “It just means something different now.”

He read it. Then he took the phone out of her hand, put it face down on the step, and kissed her again with the light going and the whole building empty under them. Like he was signing something.

“Give me your number,” she said, when she could.

“Why?”

“Because you’re my boyfriend and I don’t have your number, Dr. Wei.”

He went red. He gave it to her anyway. She saved it while he watched. Radiator.

“Radiator?”

“Nobody looks twice at a radiator.”

He took his own phone out. Typed. Turned it round so she could see her own name in his contacts. Wednesday.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went home and lay on her bed and stared at the ceiling. For an hour. Tao Tao demanded to know what had happened, every five minutes, louder each time.

“He saw it,” she said at last.

Tao Tao sat up so fast she hit her head on the bookshelf. “He saw it? The prison calendar? With the atoms?”

“He said the atoms were physically inaccurate.” Yu Jie put her arm over her eyes. “Then he set me a problem where the answer was the number of days left. He counted them while I was getting water. Then his ears went red.”

Tao Tao didn’t say anything for once.

“Jie Jie.” Dead serious. “That man is counting too.”

“He kissed me.” It came out from under her arm.

Tao Tao screamed. Somebody in the room below banged on the ceiling.

“On the back stairs.” Her face was burning. She could still feel the cold wall on her shoulder blades. “He asked first. He said he’d never broken a rule in his life. Then he said nobody can know. Not in the department. Not till June.”

Tao Tao sat down on the end of the bed with a shrimp crisp halfway to her mouth.

“So what’s the calendar for now?”

Yu Jie took her arm off her eyes. She looked at the gold square at the bottom of the page.

“It’s for the day I can kiss him in front of people.”

“Oh my GOD.”

“And you can’t tell anyone. Not even the betting pool.”

“I’m the bank of the betting pool!”

“Tao Tao.”

“Fine! Fine.” Tao Tao stuffed the crisp in her mouth. “But I’m changing my bet.”

Her phone buzzed on her chest.

Radiator: Home?

Yu Jie: yes

Radiator: Good.

Yu Jie: thats it?? good??

Radiator: Good night.

Yu Jie: DR WEI

Radiator: Miles.

She stared at that last one until the screen went dark.

That night, when Tao Tao was asleep, she got out the calendar and the purple pen and drew the day’s atom. Then, tiny, in the corner of the square, almost too small to see, she drew a second one.

For him.

chapters.title: The Coffee Cup Physics Jokes Were Not Flirting
chapters.desc: A joke on a sticky note starts a war, Dr. Fang keeps score, and Professor Gao walks in on the worst joke yet.
chapters.epigraph: “Why can’t you trust atoms? They make up everything.” — sticky note, yellow, Wednesday
chapters.content:
The first sticky note was on the jasmine tea. Sixth Wednesday. Door propped with Principles of Quantum Mechanics. White mug steaming in front of her chair. And stuck to the side of the mug, just above the handle, a small square yellow sticky note. His handwriting. Neat, a bit cramped.

Why can’t you trust atoms?

(Answer on the bottom of the mug.)

She picked the mug up and turned it over, slowly, so the tea wouldn’t go everywhere. A second, smaller note on the bottom.

They make up everything.

She looked up. He was at the board with his back to her. Writing. Not turning round.

“That’s a terrible joke.”

He kept writing. His shoulders looked extremely pleased with themselves.

“Did you test it on Dr. Fang first?”

The chalk paused.

“…He didn’t laugh.”

She laughed so hard she spilled the tea.

“Oh no. Oh no, no, your marking—”

“It’s fine.” He was already there with the tissues his sister made him carry. He mopped the tea off a second-year’s homework with great seriousness, then held the soggy page up to the light. “Bai Tianyu. He won’t notice. His handwriting already looks like this.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She took both sticky notes home and put them on the wall above her desk, next to the calendar. Tao Tao looked at them and said nothing at all. From Tao Tao, that was the most devastating comment possible.

It lasted until bedtime.

“They make up everything,” Tao Tao read out, in the dark.

“Go to sleep.”

“He wrote that. A grown man. With a doctorate.”

“It’s a classic.”

“It’s on a mug, Jie Jie. He put it on a mug so you’d have to turn the mug over. He planned the reveal.”

Yu Jie pulled the duvet over her head. It didn’t help. She was smiling into the pillow like an idiot.

“You’re smiling.”

“You can’t see me.”

“I can hear it.”

“Go to SLEEP, Tao Tao.”

“They make up everything,” Tao Tao whispered again, delighted. Yu Jie threw a pillow at her in the dark.

The next Wednesday there was another. What did the photon say when the porter offered to carry its luggage?

(Bottom.)

“No thanks. I’m travelling light.”

She groaned out loud.

“That’s worse. How is that worse?”

“I worked on it.”

“You worked on it?”

“Twenty minutes.” He looked wounded. “It’s a very efficient joke.”

The Wednesday after that: A neutron walks into a bar and asks how much for a drink. The barman says, “For you? No charge.”

She groaned so loudly that Fang Hao knocked on the wall from 413.

“Sorry!” she yelled.

“DON’T BE SORRY. TELL HIM TO STOP.”

She stuck them all above her desk. A small yellow row, growing.

Yu Jie: i have a question about neutrons

Radiator: Go on.

Yu Jie: do they ever get charged for anything

Radiator: No.

Yu Jie: not even rent

Radiator: Saving that.

Yu Jie: SAVING IT FOR WHAT

Radiator: Peer review.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three Wednesdays in, she struck back. The tea had its note, as usual. Schrödinger’s cat walks into a bar. And doesn’t. She read it. Rolled her eyes. Stuck it in her notebook. Then they argued about the bent oscillator for two hours.

And she was losing. Six o’clock. Fang Hao’s door had been shut for half an hour. The corridor was quiet. Dr. Wei was at the board, halfway through a line that was going to prove the second term could be thrown away after all.

She could see where it was going. He was right. She hated it.

“—so if we take the limit here, the correction goes like—”

She got up. She pushed Principles of Quantum Mechanics out of the doorway with her foot. The door swung shut.

“—like the square of—what are you doing?”

She took the chalk out of his hand.

“—the square of the—”

She kissed him in the middle of his sentence. He made a startled noise into her mouth. Then his hands came up into her hair. The clip slid. A pen hit the floor. He kissed her back until her notebook had fallen off the chair behind her and she had both fists in the front of his jumper.

When she let him go, he turned and looked at the board. The line stopped halfway across. He stared at it like it belonged to a stranger.

“I was proving something.”

“Were you?”

“I was winning.” He sounded genuinely betrayed. “I don’t know where it was going. I can’t remember the next step.”

“Oh no.” She gave him back the chalk. “What a shame.”

“That’s cheating.”

“That’s physics. Physics is allowed.”

“Kissing isn’t physics.”

“Everything’s physics, Dr. Wei. You told the second-years that.” She looked at his mouth. “Also, that joke was terrible.”

“I know.” He kissed the corner of her mouth. Quickly. Like he’d stolen it. “I’ve got a better one for next week. I’m saving it.”

His collar was sticking up on one side, where her fists had been. She grabbed it and yanked it flat. Hard. He let her, ears pink.

“There. Now you look like a lecturer.”

“What did I look like before?”

“Like someone who just lost an argument.”

Ten minutes later he opened the door again and propped it with the textbook. When she left, she stopped outside.

Under his office hours sign, under the little green cat in the box, she stuck a pink sticky note.

Dr. Wei: Why did the physics lecturer break up with the biology lecturer?

There was no chemistry.

— A student who is definitely not stuck on quantum mechanics

She walked off down the corridor and didn’t look back.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found it the next morning. He was unlocking his door with his bicycle helmet still on and an egg sandwich from the machine in his other hand. He saw the pink square under the sign. He stopped.

He read it twice. Then he stood in the fourth-floor corridor of the Hall of Science on a Thursday morning, in his helmet, holding an egg sandwich. And he made a noise he hadn’t made since he was seventeen.

A snort. Through his nose. He tried to swallow it. He couldn’t. The door of 413 opened. Fang Hao put his head out. He was holding a croissant.

“Was that you?”

“No.”

Fang Hao looked at the helmet. The sandwich. The pink note. He came out into the corridor and read it, chewing. Then he looked at Miles with an expression of enormous, delighted horror.

“Oh. Oh no. Oh, Miles.”

“It’s nothing.”

“You snorted.”

“I had a cold.”

“You have never had a cold. You cycle in the rain with your mouth open.”

“That’s not how colds work.”

“Don’t change the subject!” Fang Hao waved the croissant at the pink note. “You’ve started a war.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a war. Every Wednesday, a yellow note on her tea. Every Wednesday evening, a pink one on his door. Fang Hao started keeping score on a sheet of paper taped to the inside of his own door, where the corridor couldn’t see. Two columns. Y and P. Marks out of ten.

He showed it to anyone who asked. By the second week of November, that was most of the fourth floor.

One Wednesday he caught them both at the door. He was holding a pen like a judge’s gavel.

“Today’s yellow. Read it out.”

“No.”

Yu Jie peeled it off the mug. “Why are chemists great at solving problems? They have all the solutions.”

“Five.”

“FIVE?” Miles looked betrayed. “That’s a pun on two levels.”

“Both levels are bad. Five.” Fang Hao wrote it down. “Shen Yu Jie, your pink from Monday is still leading. Eight and a half.”

“You can’t give her higher marks than me just because she’s—”

“Funnier?”

“I was going to say new.”

“She’s funnier, Miles.” Fang Hao went back into 413. “Science doesn’t care about your feelings!”

Yellow: “I’d tell you a joke about thermodynamics, but it would lose energy and go off on a tangent.” 6/10. Points off for being too long.

Pink: “Dr. Wei, are you made of copper and tellurium? Because you’re Cu-Te.” 9/10. DEVASTATING. Miles went red for an hour.

Yellow: “Never trust a quantum physicist. They’re always uncertain.” 4/10. Weak. Is he okay?

Pink: “Dr. Wei, if you were an angle, you’d be acute one.” 8/10. I choked on a croissant.

“They’re not flirting,” Miles told him. The third time Fang Hao came in to read him the scores.

“Miles.”

“They’re physics jokes. It’s a scientific exchange. A form of peer review.”

“She called you Cu-Te. On your door. Zhou saw it on his way to the lift.”

Miles went cold.

“He stood there for a full minute. Didn’t say anything.” Fang Hao looked at him with pity. “Then he got in the lift, and I heard him laugh. Zhou. I didn’t know he could.”

Miles put his face in his hands.

“They’re not flirting,” he said, through his fingers.

This was, strictly, true. Flirting was what people did before. He’d looked it up. He didn’t tell Fang Hao what came after. That it happened on Wednesdays, around six, with the door shut and the radiator calling. That from half past five he couldn’t stop looking at the clock, until her chair creaked and she got up and came to him. Or he went to her. It depended who was losing.

“Then why do you keep every single pink one in your top drawer?”

Miles lifted his head. Fang Hao pointed his croissant at the desk.

“You opened it yesterday to get a pen. It was full of pink paper. And a purple pen with a cat on it. And sweets.” He took a bite. “Cardboard walls, Miles. And I have extremely good eyes.”

“I’m keeping them for the record.”

“What record?”

“A record.”

“Of what?”

Miles thought about it. Carefully. Honestly. That was the problem with him.

“Everything,” he said.

Fang Hao stopped chewing.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second Wednesday of November, Professor Gao came up to the fourth floor. She didn’t knock. Gao Meiling never knocked. She was fifty-eight. She’d run the condensed matter group for twenty years. Two national prizes. A reputation for terrifying her students into brilliance. She smoked thin cigarettes on the balcony outside her lab, which was forbidden, and nobody had ever had the nerve to tell her.

Quarter past five. She opened the door of 412 and stood there. Inside, her best student was sitting in Dr. Wei’s chair with chalk on her cardigan, arguing loudly about whether a second-order correction meant anything physical. Dr. Wei was perched on the edge of his own desk, chalk on his face, arguing back. Between them, a mug of jasmine tea with a yellow sticky note on it.

Both of them shut up. Gao looked at the board. Both their handwriting, all over it. She looked at the mug. At the sticky note. She walked over, peeled the note off and read it.

Why did the physicist break up with the electron? She was too negative. (Not true. She is very positive. This joke does not apply to anyone in this room.)

She read it twice. She looked at Miles. Then at Yu Jie. Then she stuck it back on the mug. Exactly where it had been.

“Shen Yu Jie.”

“Yes, Professor.”

“Your thesis draft is due on Monday. I haven’t seen a single page.”

“Yes, Professor.”

“My office. Eight o’clock. Tomorrow.”

Miles stood up off the desk. “Professor Gao, the draft’s late because of me. We’ve been working on—”

“Did I ask you, Wei?”

“No.”

“Then it isn’t because of you.” She didn’t take her eyes off her student. “Is it, Shen Yu Jie?”

Yu Jie’s chin came up. “No, Professor. It’s because of me.”

“Good. Eight o’clock.”

“Yes, Professor.”

Gao turned to go. In the doorway she stopped and looked back at Miles. Her face gave away nothing at all.

“Dr. Wei.”

“Professor Gao.”

“That is a very bad joke.”

She shut the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

They sat there. Through the wall, from 413, Fang Hao started laughing so hard he had to cough.

“She put it back,” Yu Jie whispered. “Exactly where it was.”

“She’s a condensed matter physicist. They like things on the right lattice site.”

Yu Jie looked at the note on the mug. She is very positive. This joke does not apply to anyone in this room.

“Dr. Wei. Who in this room is very positive?”

He looked at the board with tremendous concentration.

“It’s a general statement. About electrons.” Still facing the board. “There are about ten to the twenty-nine of them in this room. Give or take the books. I was being inclusive.”

She laughed so hard she had to put her forehead down on the desk. Through the wall, Fang Hao, who’d only just stopped coughing, started again.

Miles waited. He waited until the coughing stopped. Until the door of 413 opened and shut. Until Fang Hao’s footsteps went off down the corridor towards the lift, humming. Then he came round the desk. She still had her forehead on her arms. He bent over her, and he kissed the back of her neck, once, where her hair was coming down out of the clip.

She froze.

“That one,” he said, against her skin, “applies to someone in this room.”

She didn’t lift her head for a full minute. When she did, her face was the colour of the sticky notes on his door, and she pointed at him with a shaking finger.

“You can’t DO that before Gao’s eight o’clock!”

“Why not?”

“Because now I’m going to think about it all night.”

He thought about that. Then he picked up the chalk.

“Good,” he said, and went back to the board.

chapters.title: Her Supervisor Is Very Interested
chapters.desc: Professor Gao warns Yu Jie on the smoking balcony, then climbs to the fourth floor to warn Miles. He answers by reading four papers on her thesis.
chapters.epigraph: “A man like Wei will hold to a rule until it kills him. Make sure it isn’t you it kills.” — Professor Gao Meiling
chapters.content:
Gao’s lab was on the second floor, at the end of a corridor that smelled of liquid nitrogen and burnt toast. Nobody knew why it smelled of toast. One theory said a cryostat had a fault. The other said Professor Gao ate toast at her desk at six every morning and refused to open a window. Yu Jie believed the second one.

She knocked on the office door one minute before eight. She’d been standing outside for ten.

“Balcony.”

She went through. Past three desks buried in papers. Past a whiteboard covered in phase diagrams. Out through a glass door with a sign on it: NO SMOKING ON BALCONIES: UNIVERSITY POLICY 14.2. Professor Gao was leaning on the railing. Smoking.

Yu Jie looked at the sign. Then at the cigarette. She couldn’t help it.

“Do you smoke out here because it’s forbidden, Professor?”

“I smoke out here because it’s eight in the morning and I’ve been reading thesis drafts.” A pause. “Not yours. Yours doesn’t exist.”

She didn’t turn round. Small woman. Short grey hair. A lab coat she’d clearly been wearing since about 1995. She held the cigarette between two fingers like a pencil.

“Sit.”

There was one plastic chair. Yu Jie sat on it. Gao smoked and looked at the car park.

“Forty-one final-years,” she said eventually. “In twenty years. Six of them brilliant. You’re the seventh.”

Yu Jie opened her mouth.

“Don’t. I’m not finished.” Ash went over the railing. “You’re also the only one who’s spent the autumn of her final year hiding under a yellow dress and a pile of bad jokes.”

“I—”

“Still not finished. Strained graphene. Topological phases. A good problem. I gave it to you in June because I thought you could do something with it nobody else in this building could.” Another drag. “It’s now November. You’ve sent me one email. It said, and I quote, going well!!! will send soon!!! Three exclamation marks.”

“I’ve been working on it!”

“On Wednesdays, you are on the fourth floor.”

Yu Jie stopped breathing for a second.

✦ ✦ ✦

Gao turned round at last. Sharp black eyes. They went over her student from the trainers up. “Everybody knows what’s going on. Fang Hao has a scoreboard. Zhou laughed in a lift. Half the second-years think Dr. Wei is a tragic romantic hero because he compared himself to a particle.” She tapped ash. “I want to know what you think is going on.”

Yu Jie looked at her hands. She could lie. She was good at lying. She did it every Sunday at seven, smiling at her mother over the soup. The lab, Ma. Just the lab.

She didn’t want to lie to this woman. So she told her the safe half.

“He has a rule. Nothing while I’m a student in this department.” She swallowed. “He drew me a graph.”

Gao’s eyebrows went up. About a millimetre.

“A graph.”

“A flat line. Professional distance, constant.” Her face was going hot. “I put an end date on it. The twentieth of June. Four o’clock. He didn’t argue.”

Gao stared at her. Then she laughed. Short and dry. More of a cough.

“Of course he drew a graph. Did he use a ruler?”

“…A metre rule.”

“OF COURSE HE DID.” She stubbed the cigarette out on the railing. “And what are you doing till June? Counting?”

“…I made a calendar.”

“Go on.”

“With an atom. For every day.”

“Bohr atoms, I suppose.”

Yu Jie nodded. Gao looked up at the sky. She seemed to be asking it for patience. It didn’t seem to be giving her any.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Listen to me.” Gao sat on the railing. That was also not allowed. “I’m going to tell you something. Then I’m going to tell you what to do. Then you’re going to do it.”

“Yes, Professor.”

“I know Miles Wei. I was on the panel that hired him. Five years I’ve watched him.” Her voice didn’t change. “Best physicist in this department under forty. Loneliest man I’ve ever met. He doesn’t know either of those things.”

Yu Jie’s hands went tight in her lap.

“He shut himself in that office with a cactus. Painted his own wall. Never once came to a department dinner. Eats the same sandwich every day.” Gao looked at her. “His mother rings the department secretary to ask if he’s eating.”

Yu Jie hadn’t known that. It made her chest hurt. Actually hurt, under the ribs.

“Something happened to him. When he was young. I don’t know what. He decided wanting things was dangerous, and he stopped. He made himself a rule. He’s very good at rules.” Gao leaned in. “A man like Wei will hold to a rule until it kills him. Make sure it isn’t you it kills.”

Yu Jie didn’t say anything. She was thinking about the back stairs. Five weeks ago. His hand at the back of her neck. His voice, not steady. So I’m asking. Do you?

He’d already broken it. For her. He’d asked first, and then made a new rule on the spot to keep her safe. Gao didn’t know him as well as she thought.

Yu Jie kept that to herself. She found she liked having something to keep.

“So here’s what you’ll do.” Gao stood up. “Stop hiding. Write that thesis. Make it the best this department’s seen in ten years. Defend it in May in front of a committee and make them weep. Graduate in June with every prize there is.”

“And then?”

“Then, at four o’clock on the twentieth, do whatever you like. Climb the stairs in your yellow dress. Throw sticky notes at him. I don’t care.”

“And until then?”

“Until then, Wednesdays are fine. Physics is allowed. I asked Fang Hao. Apparently you two have been doing real work up there. He says the bent oscillator might be publishable.” Gao opened the glass door. “But you send me twenty pages by Monday.”

“Twenty?!”

“Or I come up to the fourth floor myself and confiscate the tea.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She did come up to the fourth floor that afternoon. Not for the tea. Miles was marking. Bai Tianyu had written, in answer to a question about the hydrogen atom: the electron is basically just vibing. Miles was trying to work out how many marks that was worth.

The door opened. No knock. Gao came in, shut it behind her, and stood in front of his desk with her hands in the pockets of her ancient lab coat. He stood up.

“Professor Gao.”

“Sit down, Wei. I’m not your mother.” She didn’t sit. She was looking at the board. A few equations. And in the bottom right-hand corner, tiny, in round handwriting that wasn’t his: 20 June, 16:00.

Miles followed her eyes. He went red to the ears.

“She told me about the graph.”

“I—”

“I’m not here to tell you off.” She turned from the board. “I don’t know what you’ve done. I’m not going to ask.”

He kept very still.

“She’s twenty-two. You’re not her supervisor. You don’t teach her. What grown people do on their own time is not my business.” She looked at him a second longer than she needed to. “If you marked her, we’d be having a very different conversation.”

“I don’t.”

“I know you don’t. I checked.”

Of course she’d checked.

“When?”

“September. The day after the cactus lecture.” Gao didn’t even blink. “Lin told me you’d asked about her pen.”

“You’re the best young physicist in this building, Wei. I’d hate to have that other conversation.”

He was no good at lying. So he said nothing, and his ears said everything for him.

“One thing. Then I’ll go.”

She came right up to the desk.

“That girl has spent her whole life being told she’s decoration. Her mother calls her the Perfect Jewel in front of guests. Her father doesn’t look up from his phone. Her brother runs a company.” Level voice. “Not one of them has ever asked her about a single equation.”

“I didn’t know that.”

“Why would you? She doesn’t say it. She makes jokes.” Gao leaned on the desk. “Until this autumn she was hiding what she can do. Because she thought nobody wanted it. And then she came up four flights of stairs, and you gave her a problem nobody knows the answer to.”

He couldn’t say anything. His throat had shut.

“So keep your rule. Keep it until June. Keep it out of this building.” Gao’s voice dropped. “But don’t you dare make her pay for it. Don’t you dare let her think what you want from her is anything less than what she can do. Don’t make her go back to hiding.”

“I wouldn’t.”

“No?” Gao tilted her head. “What does she tell her mother she does on Wednesdays?”

He opened his mouth. He didn’t know.

“The lab.” Gao didn’t blink. “I know, because her mother rang me in October to check.”

“What did you say?”

“I said yes.” Gao looked at him flatly. “So now I’m lying to Shen Ruolan for you two. I’d like that to be worth it.”

“It will be.”

“Good.” She straightened up. “Keep giving her the hard problems, Wei. That’s allowed. It’s your job.”

She went to the door. Opened it. Then she looked back at the corner of the board.

“And for heaven’s sake, get a better joke book.”

The door shut.

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles sat. Then he pulled the second-year marking back towards him. Found Bai Tianyu’s electron. Gave it two out of five. Wrote in the margin: Not wrong, exactly. Please explain what “vibing” means in terms of a wave function. I would genuinely like to know.

Then he took a fresh yellow sticky note. He wrote on it slowly. He crossed out twice. He didn’t write a joke.

That night he read the first paper. Then the second. At some point the third. At some point after that, his phone buzzed on the pile.

Wednesday: did gao come up to you

Miles: Yes.

Wednesday: did she yell

Miles: No.

Wednesday: what did she say

Miles: Get a better joke book.

Wednesday: oh my god

Wednesday: are you okay

Miles: Yes. Busy.

Wednesday: busy with WHAT its midnight

Miles: Reading.

Wednesday: reading what

Miles: Go to sleep. You have twenty pages to write.

Wednesday: HOW DO YOU KNOW ABOUT THE TWENTY PAGES

He turned the phone face down and opened paper number four.

✦ ✦ ✦

Wednesday. Quarter to four. She came in, and the note on the side of her tea said:

Professor Gao says your thesis is on strained graphene. I’ve read three papers on it this week. I have questions. Real ones. Would you mind explaining it to me?

(No joke today. Sorry. The joke book is being replaced.)

She read it twice. Then she put the mug down and looked at him. He was standing at the board with a clean piece of chalk held out to her. Waiting.

“You read three papers on strained graphene. This week.”

“Four. The fourth one was wrong, so I’m not counting it. I read it twice to make sure.”

“For me?”

He looked at the chalk in his hand.

“For the physics.”

She kept looking at him.

“And for you,” he said.

She got up and took the chalk.

He didn’t let go straight away. His thumb stayed against hers on the white stick. Warm. On purpose. Through the wall, Fang Hao’s radio was playing something terrible. Miles looked at her mouth. Then, with an effort she could actually watch him make, at the board.

“Fang Hao leaves around half five,” he said. Low. “Graphene till then.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She started with the lattice.

She talked fast. She always talked fast when it was hers. Honeycomb. Strain. What happens to the electrons when you stretch the sheet unevenly. She filled half the board. He asked real questions. Hard ones. Twice she had to stop and think, and once she said “Oh. Oh,” and rubbed out a whole line.

Half past five. Fang Hao’s door. Fang Hao’s footsteps. The lift. She didn’t notice. She was halfway through the edge states.

“—so at the boundary you get these states that can’t be removed, they’re protected, it doesn’t matter how you deform the middle, they just stay, which is the whole point, because if the strain’s uneven you’d expect them to—”

He kissed her.

Mid-sentence. No warning. One hand on her jaw, tipping her face up from the board. Chalk still in her fingers. She made a noise against his mouth. Surprise, mostly. Then not surprise at all.

When he let her go, she blinked up at him.

“I was explaining.”

“I know.”

“I was at the good part.”

“I know. I was listening.” He was breathing a bit hard. “I’ve wanted to do that since protected.”

“That was four minutes ago!”

“I was being patient.”

She hit him in the chest with the chalk. It left a white mark on his jumper, right over his heart. He looked down at it.

“Now you’re marked,” she said. “Hygiene.”

“That’s not what hygiene means.”

She went back to the board, pink to the ears, and finished the edge states. He didn’t interrupt again.

When she left, the corridor was cold. November had got into the building. He stopped her at the door. Took the two sides of her big grey cardigan and did up the buttons. All of them. Bottom to top. Right up to her chin.

“It’s thirty metres to the stairs,” she said.

“It’s eleven degrees out there.”

“You checked?!”

He did up the last button and didn’t answer. She walked to the stairs with her cardigan buttoned like a schoolgirl and didn’t undo a single one.

chapters.title: A Study Group of One
chapters.desc: She drags him to a Saturday study group, and it goes well until the head of department walks in. Miles runs, then waits fifty-six minutes for her at the bike rack.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s a study group. Physics is allowed.” “It’s a café.” “Physics happens in cafés. Ask Einstein.”
chapters.content:
“It’s a study group.”

“It’s a café.”

“It’s a study group in a café. Physics happens in cafés. Ask Einstein.”

“Einstein worked in a patent office.”

“And he went to cafés after!”

It was Friday. Not Wednesday. That was already against the rules. She was standing in the doorway of 412 holding a flyer. LIBRARY CAFÉ: OPEN SATURDAYS 9–9.

“My friends are failing thermodynamics. All three of them. It’s a crisis. You’re the only person I know who can explain entropy without making people cry.”

“I made a second-year cry about entropy last term.”

“That was Bai Tianyu. He cries about everything. He cried at a dumpling.”

“It was a very sad dumpling. It had fallen on the floor.”

“Ten o’clock. Tomorrow. One hour. Purely academic.” She waved the flyer at him. “You don’t even have to sit next to me. Sit next to Tao Tao. She bites, but only people she likes.”

He looked at the flyer. Then at the bottom right-hand corner of his board, where 20 June, 16:00 sat in small round writing.

“Physics is allowed,” she reminded him.

“In cafés.”

“Especially in cafés.”

“…One hour.”

She smiled like she’d won the national lottery.

✦ ✦ ✦

The library café was on the ground floor of the main library. Long room. Big windows. Terrible coffee. Best cakes on campus, because Fang Hao’s wife baked them. On Saturday mornings it was packed with students pretending to work.

Miles arrived three minutes early on his old green bicycle. In his backpack: two textbooks, a pad of paper, four pencils, and an egg sandwich in case the café didn’t do egg.

Yu Jie was already there. Big table by the window. Three other people. Tao Tao he recognised. Fang Hao had shown him her photo from the betting pool. Small and fierce, a bleached streak in her hair, a T-shirt that said I’M HERE FOR THE MITOCHONDRIA. Next to her, a tall sleepy boy from chemistry called Ah Peng, who appeared to be wearing pyjama trousers. And a quiet girl from engineering called Li Wen. Glasses. Three highlighters lined up in front of her in colour order. She looked at Miles like he was an exam.

“Dr. Wei!” Yu Jie stood up. “This is the study group. Study group, this is Dr. Wei. He’s going to save your lives.”

Tao Tao looked him up and down without blinking.

“So you’re the cactus man.”

Yu Jie kicked her under the table.

“OW.”

“Sorry. Cramp.”

“You don’t get cramp, you do yoga with your feet—”

“Hello.” Miles got it out to the whole table, fast. “Hello. Thermodynamics.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He sat next to Tao Tao. He’d said he would. Opposite side of the table from Yu Jie. As far away as the table allowed. Tao Tao had already shifted her chair two inches closer and was watching him like a cat watching a bird.

“Your ears are pink,” Tao Tao told him.

“It’s warm in here.”

“It’s November.”

“It’s warm for November.”

Then Ah Peng pushed a sheet of homework across the table.

“Dr. Wei, I don’t understand anything about entropy. I don’t even understand what the word means. I think it’s fake.”

Miles forgot about the table. And the distance. And Tao Tao. And everything else.

“It’s not fake. It’s the most real thing there is. Can I borrow that napkin?”

He drew on the napkin. A box with a wall down the middle. Dots on one side. Then the same box with the wall gone, and the dots spread through the whole thing.

“Why do the dots spread out?”

“Because… they want to?”

“They don’t want anything. They’re dots. They move randomly. So why do they always end up spread out? Why do they never all go back to one side?”

Ah Peng stared at the napkin. He looked like it might bite him.

Li Wen spoke up from the end of the table. Slowly. “Because there are more ways to be spread out than there are to be on one side?”

Miles lit up. Same as he had on the second Wednesday, when Yu Jie found his mistake.

“Yes! That’s it. That’s all entropy is. Counting the ways. Messy is more likely than tidy, because there are more ways to be messy.” He tapped the napkin. “That’s why your room gets untidy on its own and never tidies itself. That’s why ice melts. That’s why time only goes forwards.”

“That’s why time goes forwards?” Ah Peng was wide awake now.

“That’s one of the best explanations we’ve got.”

Li Wen uncapped a pink highlighter and wrote MESSY = MORE WAYS across the top of her notes. Underlined twice. Across the table, Yu Jie had her chin on her hand. She watched him and didn’t say a word.

✦ ✦ ✦

Around half past ten, under the table, she took off her left trainer.

He felt her foot find his ankle. Just her toes. Striped sock. Resting on the bone like it had got there by accident.

He was halfway through a sentence about the Carnot cycle. He lost the end of it.

Ah Peng waited, pen raised.

“…Isothermal.” Miles stared at the napkin like it held the secrets of the universe. “The next stage is isothermal. The temperature stays the same.”

It did not. Across the table, she moved her chin to her other hand and looked out of the window. The picture of innocence. Her foot slid an inch higher, under the hem of his trousers, and stayed there.

“Dr. Wei? Are you okay?”

“Yes, Li Wen. Thank you. Why?”

“You’ve written isothermal three times.”

He looked down. He had.

“Emphasis,” he said.

Tao Tao turned her head slowly and looked at Yu Jie. Yu Jie looked at the ceiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

The hour turned into two. Then three. He did their homework with them, one problem at a time, on napkins, because he forgot to take his pad out and nobody reminded him. He explained the Carnot cycle with a cup of coffee. He explained heat engines using Ah Peng’s pyjama trousers. Nobody, Ah Peng included, ever fully recovered. He found three mistakes in Li Wen’s textbook, and she wrote them in a special notebook like they were treasure.

At some point Tao Tao stopped watching him like a cat. She put her chin on her hand too.

Around twenty to one, Ah Peng put his pen down.

“Dr. Wei, why aren’t all lecturers like you?”

He sounded actually upset about it. Miles looked up from the napkins. Surprised. He’d forgotten there was anyone else there.

“They are. Mostly. You just have to ask the right questions.”

“I never ask questions. I’m scared they’ll think I’m stupid.”

Miles put his pencil down.

“The stupidest thing I ever did,” he said, “was not ask a question when I was your age. For a whole year. Because I didn’t want anyone to know I didn’t understand.” He looked at Ah Peng. “Then I had to learn the whole thing again later. Alone. Much more slowly.”

“What was it?”

“Doesn’t matter. Ask the question. The worst thing that happens is someone explains it.”

Nobody at the table said anything.

Yu Jie was looking at him. Her face had gone soft all over. She wasn’t moving.

He looked back. A second too long. Then the café door opened, and Professor Zhou Lin, head of department, walked in with his wife to buy a cake.

“Who’s that?” Tao Tao, under her breath.

“Head of department.”

“Oh no.”

“Shh.”

“Jie Jie, your foot is—”

“Shh!”

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles saw him first. He saw Professor Zhou see the table. Four students. Napkins everywhere. And Dr. Miles Wei in the middle of them, three hours into a Saturday, looking across the table at a girl in a yellow cardigan with exactly the face a hundred and forty second-years had posted about.

Zhou didn’t say anything. He nodded once, politely. He went to the counter.

But Miles was already on his feet. Backpack packed before anyone could speak. Textbooks. Pencils. The uneaten egg sandwich. He didn’t look at anyone.

“I have to go. I’m sorry. I forgot. A meeting.”

“On a Saturday?” Tao Tao’s eyebrows went up.

“Yes. Very important. Thank you. Good luck with the exam. Ask questions.” He was already at the door. “Messy is more likely than tidy!”

The door swung shut behind him. At the table, nobody said anything at all.

“Oh, Jie Jie.” Tao Tao put her crisps down.

Yu Jie was looking at the door. Her face was perfectly calm. It was her Sunday face. The one she wore at the museum at seven, over the soup.

Under the table she put her trainer back on. Her foot was cold.

She picked up one of the napkins he’d left. The box with the wall. The dots spreading out. Underneath, in his small neat handwriting: There are more ways to be messy. She folded it carefully and put it in her pocket.

“Is he coming back?” Ah Peng was still staring at the napkins.

“No. Do your homework.”

“But who’s going to explain the—”

“I’ll explain it.” Yu Jie pulled his sheet over. Her voice was perfectly steady. “Messy is more likely than tidy. Write that down.”

“He said that.”

“I know he said that, Ah Peng. I was there.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She came out an hour later. Her phone had been in her bag the whole time.

Radiator: Which door.

Radiator: There are two.

Radiator: I’ll wait at the bikes.

Radiator: I’m at the bikes.

He was at the bikes. She stopped. He was standing next to his old green bicycle, holding the handlebars, not looking at her.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

“You had a meeting.”

“I didn’t have a meeting.” He looked at the ground. “Zhou came in. I saw his face. I saw what it looked like. Me. On a Saturday. With you. Three hours. And your foot.” He pushed his glasses up. “And I panicked. I don’t panic. I’m very bad at it. I didn’t know what to do, so I left.”

She’d done that. She’d put her foot up his trouser leg in a café full of students, because she wanted to see his face. And his face had done exactly what she wanted. In front of the head of department.

Impulsive. Her mother’s word. You never think, Yu Jie.

“You could’ve said goodbye.”

“I know. I’m sorry.” He finally looked at her. “Your friends. Are they all right?”

“Ah Peng says he’s switching to physics.”

“Today?”

“He said on Monday. He said you changed his life with a napkin.”

“It was a good napkin.”

“It was a paper napkin, Dr. Wei.”

“The best physics is on paper napkins. Ask—”

“Don’t you dare say Einstein.”

“I was going to say Fermi.”

He looked alarmed. “He mustn’t. He’s very bad at it.”

She laughed. She didn’t mean to.

“It was the best three hours I’ve had in years.” He was looking at the handlebars, not her. “That’s the problem.”

Then he unzipped his backpack. Took out the egg sandwich, still in its plastic triangle. Held it out across the bicycle at the full length of his arm.

“You didn’t eat. You gave Ah Peng your cake at eleven, because he said entropy made him hungry. You didn’t order anything else.” A pause. “I noticed. Before.”

“Before you ran away.”

“Yes. It’s egg. It was all the machine had. Sorry.”

She took it. It was warm from his backpack, which was not hygienic. She didn’t care at all.

“How long have you been standing here?”

He looked at his watch. “Fifty-six minutes.”

“Dr. Wei! It’s November.”

“I’m aware of the date.” He didn’t look up. “I didn’t know which door you’d use. There are two.”

She grabbed his hand off the handlebar. It was freezing. Actually freezing, like a tin can from the fridge.

“Oh my god.”

“It’s fine.”

“It is NOT fine.” She took his other hand too and shoved them both into her cardigan pockets, with hers, and held on. “Fifty-six minutes. Are you insane? You could’ve texted again.”

“I texted four times.”

“You could’ve texted five.”

“Four felt like the limit.” He was looking down at her. His hands were in her pockets. Hers were wrapped round them. “Five felt like a man who’d been standing at a bike rack for an hour.”

“You were that man!”

“Yes, but I didn’t want you to know.”

She squeezed his fingers inside her pockets until they started to warm up. He let her. He stood still and let her.

✦ ✦ ✦

He got on his bicycle. He put on his helmet. He looked at her once more.

“The napkin. You took it.”

She put a hand in her pocket. She didn’t take it out.

“You left it.”

He looked at her pocket. Then he looked round once. Empty path. Bare trees. Blank library windows. The way he checked an equation before he trusted it.

Then he leaned across the handlebars and kissed her. Hard and quick. Helmet already on. The bicycle between them.

She stood there with her mouth open and an egg sandwich in her hand.

“That was the meeting,” he said. His ears had gone red under the helmet strap. “I didn’t lie. I just had the time wrong.”

He rode off down the long path between the trees. He always wobbled for the first few metres. He wobbled more than usual. She watched him go.

That night she drew the atom in the day’s square. Then, beside it, tiny, she drew a box with a wall down the middle. Dots spreading out on both sides.

Two hundred and ten to go.

Radiator: Home?

Yu Jie: yes. ate the sandwich

Radiator: All of it?

Yu Jie: ALL of it

Radiator: Good.

Yu Jie: your hands warm yet

Radiator: Yes.

chapters.title: Miles Gets Sick and Nobody Notices
chapters.desc: Miles is sick and nobody notices except Yu Jie, who turns up with soup, a thermometer and oranges, and meets his sister on speakerphone.
chapters.epigraph: “This is not allowed.” “I’m a student delivering soup. It’s community service.”
chapters.content:
Yu Jie: your lecture got cancelled??

Yu Jie: r u ok

Yu Jie: dr wei

Yu Jie: miles

Yu Jie: its wednesday btw

Yu Jie: so why arent you answering

Four more after that. Nine messages. Two days. Zero replies. The twelfth Wednesday, the door to 412 was shut.

Not propped. Shut, and locked. She tried the handle twice. She knocked. She stood in the corridor with her notebook against her chest and listened. No chalk. No whale. No voice saying it’s open, unless you’re from facilities. The door of 413 opened. Fang Hao looked out. For once he wasn’t eating anything.

“He’s not here.”

“Where is he?”

“He cancelled his lecture yesterday. And tomorrow’s. Emailed at six in the morning. One line. Unwell, apologies, will reschedule.” Fang Hao frowned. “He’s never cancelled anything. Five years. He taught with a broken wrist once. Wrote on the board left-handed. Nobody could read it. He did it.”

Her hands went tight on the notebook.

“Has anyone checked on him?”

Fang Hao opened his mouth. Closed it.

“I sent him a message. He didn’t answer. I assumed he was asleep.” He looked at her properly then. “He lives on his own. He doesn’t really know anyone. His family’s four hours away.”

“Where does he live?”

Fang Hao rubbed his face.

“That is not the kind of thing I should be giving a student.”

“Dr. Fang.”

“Shen Yu Jie, I could get in real—”

“Dr. Fang.”

He sighed. He went back into his office. He came out with a sticky note. Yellow, naturally.

“Staff flats. The old block behind the sports ground. Number fourteen, third floor.” He held it out. “I didn’t give you this. If anyone asks, you found it in the bin.”

“Thank you.”

“Go.” He was already turning away. “And text me if he’s dead, I’ll need to cancel Friday.”

“That’s not funny!”

“I know.” He didn’t look like he thought it was funny either.

✦ ✦ ✦

The staff flats were a tired five-storey block from the eighties. The lift was broken. The noticeboard in the lobby was mostly about recycling. She ran up three floors with a plastic bag in each hand.

Bag one: a flask of chicken congee from the canteen. Ginger tea from the shop by the gate. Paracetamol. Tissues. A thermometer. Bag two: oranges. Tao Tao had said you always bring oranges. It was the law.

Number fourteen had a plain brown door. No name. On the mat outside sat a small cactus in a blue pot, exactly like Schrödinger. She knocked. Nothing.

She knocked again. Louder. Her heart was going so hard she could feel it in her teeth.

Slow footsteps. Then a long pause on the other side of the door. Someone looking through the peephole and not believing it. The door opened six inches. He looked terrible. Grey jumper over pyjamas. A scarf. Socks with holes in them. Hair straight up on one side. Glasses crooked. His face was flushed red and his eyes were glassy, and his nose was so blocked his voice sounded like it was coming through a sock.

“Shen Yu Jie. It’s Wednesday.”

“I know.” She held up the bags. “You’ve got a fever. You cancelled two lectures. Dr. Fang says you once taught with a broken wrist. Therefore you’re dying.”

“This is a staff building.” Through the sock. “Half the chemistry department lives on the second floor.”

“I know.”

“This is not allowed.”

“I’m a student delivering soup. It’s community service. I’m sure there’s a box I can tick.” She pushed the door. “Let me in. You’re swaying.”

He was swaying. He let her in.

✦ ✦ ✦

The flat was small and clean and everything in it was a book. Books on shelves. Books on the floor. Books in neat stacks on the kitchen counter, sticky notes poking out. A sofa. One armchair. A table with one chair. A kettle. A window looking over the sports ground, with three more cacti on the sill in blue pots.

She checked the kitchen. A jar of instant coffee, which he didn’t drink. A packet of crackers gone soft. An egg.

One egg.

“How old is this egg?”

“It’s an egg.”

“Miles. How OLD is the egg.”

“…It’s from before.”

“Before what?”

“Before I got sick. Probably.” He thought about it. “Possibly before October.”

“Oh my god.” She put it in the bin. He watched it go with real sorrow.

“When did you last eat?”

He’d sat down on the sofa all at once. His legs had made the decision without him.

“Monday. I think. I had a sandwich.”

“An egg sandwich.”

“…Yes.”

She took out the thermometer and held it out to him.

“Stay back. You’ll catch it.” He coughed. “And then Gao will want to know where from.”

“Then take it yourself. I’ll stand over here. Very professionally. At a distance. With the soup.”

He took it himself. The little screen beeped. Thirty-nine point one. Something went cold in her stomach.

She did the arithmetic without wanting to. A sandwich on Monday. An email at six on Tuesday morning. Then nothing. Two days in this flat with a fever going up, one egg in the fridge and nobody at the door. If she hadn’t come, who would have? Nobody. Not until somebody noticed the lecturer who taught with a broken wrist hadn’t turned up to teach at all.

She could see it. She couldn’t stop seeing it. Him on the kitchen floor. Long and thin on the cold lino. Glasses skidded under the counter. Kettle still on.

Her hands had started shaking. She put the thermometer down on the arm of the sofa so he wouldn’t see.

“Right.” Her voice came out almost normal. “Lie down. Before you fall down.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She did everything at a distance. Nearly everything. She heated the congee in his one saucepan. Put it in his one bowl. Made him sit at his one chair and eat it while she stood by the window across the room, very professionally, holding the oranges. She made the ginger tea. She found his only blanket in a cupboard and put it on the arm of the sofa and pointed at it until he lay down and pulled it over himself. She lectured him the whole time.

“You live on egg sandwiches. You don’t have any food. There is not one vegetable in this flat. You have ONE egg.”

“It’s a good egg.”

“You have more cacti than plates!”

“Cacti are low maintenance.”

“When you got sick you didn’t tell anyone. You emailed at six in the morning and locked yourself in. What if you’d fallen? What if you’d hit your head? Nobody would’ve found you till Thursday office hours, when Bai Tianyu came looking for you to ask if gravity is real.”

“Gravity is real.” It came from under the blanket.

“I know gravity is real!”

“He did ask me. Last week. Theory or fact.” He coughed. “It was quite a good conversation.”

“That is not the POINT. The point is you could’ve died in here with one egg. And the last thing anyone got from you would’ve been an email that said apologies. And I’d have found out from Fang Hao. In a corridor. And—”

He got up. It took him two tries. The blanket slid onto the floor. He crossed the room in his holey socks, swaying. She stopped talking because she thought he was going to fall, and she put out both hands to catch him.

He took her face in his hot hands instead and kissed her. It was clumsy. His nose was blocked and his mouth was too warm, and he had to stop after a few seconds just to breathe. He didn’t let go of her face.

“I’m sorry I frightened you.” Still through the sock. “Your hands were shaking. When you read the thermometer. I saw.”

“They weren’t.”

“They were.”

“I’m not scared. I’m annoyed.” Her eyes were stinging. Stupid eyes. “There’s a difference.”

“Is there?”

“YES.”

He just looked at her. Glassy. Patient. He didn’t argue. That was worse.

“Now you’ll catch it,” he said. Deep regret. A man reporting a failed experiment.

She looked at him. Crooked glasses. Hair standing up. Fever all over his face. Then she grabbed the front of his grey jumper, pulled his head down, and kissed him back. Harder. On purpose. Until he made a muffled noise and had to grab the windowsill.

“Then I’ll catch it,” she said. “Now will you please lie DOWN?”

He lay down. She put the ginger tea on the floor beside the sofa and sat down next to it, back against the sofa, where he could reach her. He looked at her over the blanket. Then at the bag of oranges she was still holding, like it was a piece of evidence he couldn’t explain.

“You brought oranges.”

“Tao Tao says it’s the law.”

“My sister brings oranges. She throws them at me.” He shut his eyes. “Nobody else has ever brought me oranges.”

✦ ✦ ✦

His phone rang. It was on the floor, next to the tea. He looked at the screen and shut his eyes again.

“My sister. She rings on Wednesdays. If I don’t answer, she rings my mother. Then my mother rings the department secretary.”

“Then answer.”

He answered. He put it on speaker, because his hands were shaking too much to hold it.

“There you are.” A woman’s voice. Very loud. Very blunt. “You sound awful. Are you sick? You sound sick. Have you eaten? You haven’t eaten. I can hear it. You sound like a man who’s eaten one sandwich since Monday.”

Yu Jie put her hand over her mouth.

“Lan. I’m fine.”

“You’re not fine. You never say fine. You say ‘I’m all right’ when you’re fine. ‘Fine’ means you’re dying.” A pause. “Is someone there? I can hear breathing. Miles. Is there a person in your flat?”

Miles looked down at Yu Jie, sitting on his floor with her shoulder against his arm. Total panic. Yu Jie looked back up at him.

Then she leaned towards the phone and said politely, in her best Sunday-dinner voice, “Hello. I’m a student. From the physics department. I brought congee.”

The phone went quiet.

“A student. In his flat.”

“Delivering soup. It’s community service.”

More quiet.

“Is she pretty?”

“Lan.”

“I’m asking a medical question. I’m a nurse. It affects his recovery.” A pause. “Student. What’s his temperature?”

“Thirty-nine point one. He took it himself. I stood by the window.” This had been true at the time.

“Right. Make him drink water. A litre at least. Paracetamol every six hours, not more. If it goes over thirty-nine and a half, or he gets confused, or he can’t keep water down, take him to the clinic. I don’t care what he says. He’ll argue. He always argues. Ignore him.” Then her voice changed. “And thank you. Nobody ever checks on him. He doesn’t let them.”

“He let me.” It was out before she could stop it.

A pause.

“Did he.” Not a question.

“I’m hanging up now.”

“Miles, wait, what’s her n—”

He hung up.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stayed until his temperature came down. Three hours. She sat at his one chair at his one table across the room and worked on her thesis on her laptop. Every hour she said, “Temperature.” He took it and read it out.

Thirty-nine. Thirty-eight point seven. Thirty-eight point two.

“Shen Yu Jie.” Eyes shut.

“Mm.”

“You’ve been typing the same sentence for twenty minutes. I can hear it. Type type type. Delete delete delete.”

She took her hands off the keys. “You’re supposed to be resting.”

“I am resting. I’m resting and listening.” A pause. “What’s the sentence?”

“It’s about edge states.”

It was not about edge states. It was he has more cacti than plates and I would like to buy him some plates. She’d typed it and deleted it nine times.

“Liar,” he said kindly, from under the blanket.

She typed it a tenth time. Looked at it. Deleted it again. Put her chin on her hand and watched the blanket go up and down across the room.

At some point his breathing changed. He’d fallen asleep. She got up and crossed the room in her socks.

He was on his side with the blanket up to his chin, glasses still on, crooked. One hand hanging off the edge of the sofa, fingers curled. Asleep he looked younger. The frown he wore when he was thinking about four things at once had gone.

She took his glasses off. Carefully. Folded them. Put them on the floor by the tea. She touched his hair. The bit that always stuck up. She smoothed it flat. It sprang straight back up. Typical.

She bent and kissed his forehead. Still too hot. He didn’t wake. But he reached out in his sleep, found two of her fingers, and gripped them.

She knelt there on the cold floor until her knees ached. She didn’t take her fingers back.

✦ ✦ ✦

When he woke it was dark outside, and she’d gone. Thirty-seven point eight. The flat smelled of ginger. A bowl of congee sat on the table under a plate, still a bit warm. The paracetamol was next to it with a note: Every 6 hours. Next one at 10 p.m. Not before. Your sister will know.

A bag of oranges on the counter. And the fridge, which that afternoon had held one elderly egg, now held four more boxes of congee, a bag of green vegetables, milk, a loaf of bread, and a small plastic tub with a yellow sticky note on the lid.

He took it out. Orange segments. Peeled. Every single bit of pith picked off.

Why did the lecturer catch a cold?

Because he left his door open all autumn.

(Close it at night. Open it on Wednesdays.)

He stood in front of his open fridge in his pyjamas and holey socks, holding a tub of perfectly peeled oranges. He could afford plates. His salary had gone into the same account every month for five years, with the rent from his grandparents’ old flat on the coast, and most of it was still sitting there. He lived here because it was four minutes from the lab by bicycle. He’d never bought a second plate because there’d never been a second person to eat off one.

He ate every segment standing up. He took the paracetamol at exactly ten. He texted his sister one word before she could ring their mother.

Miles: Alive.

The reply came in four seconds.

Wei Lan: Marry her.

He put the phone face down on the counter. It buzzed again.

Wednesday: did you take the 10pm one

Miles: Yes.

Wednesday: temp

Miles: 37.8.

Wednesday: good

Miles: You picked the pith off.

Wednesday: shh

Wednesday: now go and close your door

He looked down the hall. He’d left it on the latch when she went. He went and shut it. Then he stood in the hall in his holey socks with his hand still on the latch, grinning like an idiot.

chapters.title: He Laughs in a Seminar
chapters.desc: Yu Jie takes apart a visiting professor’s slide in the seminar, and Miles laughs out loud for the first time in thirteen years. Then an invitation arrives with her family’s crest on it.
chapters.epigraph: “Dr. Wei laughed.” “Out loud?” “Out loud. Zhou dropped his pen.” — overheard, fourth-floor kitchen
chapters.content:
The department seminar was the most boring hour of the week. Everybody agreed. Including, most weeks, the speaker. Friday afternoons. The small lecture room on the third floor with the broken blind. Somebody from another university presented their research to thirty physicists, and half of the physicists checked their email. Professor Zhou sat in the front row and asked one question. Always the same question, in different words.

“But have you considered the boundary conditions?”

Fang Hao brought cake. His wife’s. Afterwards there was warm white wine in plastic cups, and everybody stood around talking about funding. Miles went every week. Third row, left side, by the broken blind. He listened properly. He asked one question if he had one, and none if he didn’t. He left before the wine.

Final-year students were allowed to come. Almost none of them did. On the first Friday in December, Fang Hao caught him on the stairs.

“Huang. From the capital. He’ll talk for an hour and take questions like they’re insults.”

“Forty minutes.”

“You’ve timed him?”

“I’ve read his papers. They’re long. He likes the sound of his own slides.”

“Is that a joke? Was that a joke, Miles?”

“It was an observation.”

They went in together just before four. She was in the second row on the right. Fang Hao stopped dead in the doorway.

“Is that—”

“Yes.”

“In the seminar?!”

“Final-years are allowed.”

“Nobody’s allowed, Miles. Nobody comes.” Fang Hao sat down next to him in the third row, eyes enormous. “She came to the seminar.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d been back at work a week. The fever had gone. His fridge had stayed full all week, mysteriously. On Monday a box of dumplings appeared outside his door with no note. On Tuesday, a cardboard box from a homeware shop on Harbour Road. Inside: four white plates.

Four. The sticky note on top said: So the cacti don’t have to share.

Fang Hao looked at the plates. He looked at the dumplings. He said nothing at all, extremely loudly.

“Don’t.”

“I didn’t say anything!”

“You were going to.”

“I was going to say plates, Miles.” Fang Hao bit into a croissant. “Just the word. Plates. That’s all.”

On Thursday there was another bag of oranges. He hadn’t said anything to her about the flat. Not in words. On Wednesday she’d come, quarter to four as always, and the door had been open. The tea had been on the desk with a sticky note that said Thank you. Nothing else. No joke. She read it and put it in her notebook and they did physics for two hours.

At six, when the corridor emptied, she shut the door herself. Then she sat on the edge of his desk. Right on top of the second-year marking.

“You’re sitting on Bai Tianyu.”

“Good. He deserves it.”

“He got a three this week. That’s his best ever.”

“Then he can handle it.”

“Shen Yu Jie, if you crease his three—”

Then she grabbed the front of his jumper and pulled him in and kissed him until he forgot what he’d been arguing about. It took about four seconds. He was a little ashamed of the number. Nobody mentioned oranges. Or plates. She caught his cold, though. A small one.

Radiator: Pigeonhole.

Yu Jie: ??

Radiator: Second floor. Your pigeonhole.

She went and looked. A flask of ginger tea. No note.

Yu Jie: how did you know im sick

Radiator: You sneezed at the end of the corridor. Twice.

Yu Jie: thats CREEPY

Radiator: It’s acoustics.

Yu Jie: miles

Radiator: The corridor is very good for acoustics.

Now here she was in the second row of the seminar. Dark green jumper instead of yellow. Her hair down for once. Taking notes. He sat in the third row on the left. She didn’t turn round. But he saw her shoulders change when he sat down.

✦ ✦ ✦

The visiting speaker was Dr. Huang, from the capital. He was famous, and he knew it. He was presenting a new model of electrons in a sheet of carbon one atom thick, stretched and twisted. Strained graphene. He talked for forty minutes, fast, with a huge number of slides. At the end of every slide he looked at the audience like he was expecting applause.

Miles listened. It was a clever model. It was also, around minute thirty, slightly wrong. Slide nineteen. There was an assumption that didn’t hold if the strain was uneven. He was writing himself a note about it when he looked up.

In the second row, Shen Yu Jie had stopped writing. She was sitting bolt upright. Looking at slide nineteen.

He knew that look. Second Wednesday. His bent oscillator. Four seconds. Oh no, he thought. Oh, good.

Dr. Huang finished. Polite applause. Zhou raised his hand and asked about the boundary conditions. Dr. Huang answered at length. Two more questions from the audience. Safe ones. Then a hand went up in the second row. Chairs creaked. Thirty physicists turned to look at the final-year student with her hand up. Zhou twisted round in his seat. Dr. Huang squinted.

“Yes? The young lady?”

She stood up.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Slide nineteen.” Clear voice. Not nervous at all. “You assume the strain’s uniform across the sample. In real devices it isn’t. It’s worse at the edges. If you put uneven strain into your model, your gap closes. The phase you’re describing goes away.”

She paused.

“I’ve been working on this for my thesis. With non-uniform strain I don’t think it survives. Unless your samples are very small. Which you didn’t say.”

The little room on the third floor went dead quiet. Dr. Huang looked at her. His smile had gone a bit stiff.

“That’s an interesting point. For a student. But uneven strain is a second-order effect.”

“Not at the edges.”

“The edges are a small part of the sample.”

“Your samples are small. So the edges are most of it.” She tilted her head. “Aren’t they?”

In the front row, Professor Zhou sat up.

“Boundary conditions!” Zhou looked thrilled.

Someone snorted. Dr. Huang’s smile got stiffer.

“I think if you look more carefully at the—”

“I have looked. I ran it. Last Wednesday.” Politely. “With help.”

She didn’t look at the third row on the left. Thirty heads did it for her.

Fang Hao whispered it, delighted. “Oh no. Oh, she’s good.”

Miles sat by the broken blind and kept his face straight. Dr. Huang followed their eyes. He looked at Miles. Miles looked back.

“Dr. Wei? Is this your student?”

“No. She’s Professor Gao’s.” A pause. “But she’s right. About slide nineteen. I was writing it down myself.”

He held up his notebook. Small letters: Slide 19. Uneven strain. Gap closes?

“She just saw it faster.”

At the back of the room somebody made a sharp noise. Professor Gao. She’d come in late and was standing by the door with her arms folded, looking fiercely pleased.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dr. Huang recovered. He was a professional. It was an interesting question, he said. He’d look into it. Thank you. Moving on. Yu Jie sat down, pink, and wrote something in her notebook so she wouldn’t have to look at anyone. One more question. The chair thanked the speaker. People clapped. Then Dr. Huang, gathering up his laptop and clearly wanting the last word, leaned into the microphone. Little laugh.

“Well! I see this department produces very confident students. I’ll have to be careful next time. Maybe I should bring my own lecturer to defend me.”

Polite laughter. And Shen Yu Jie, without looking up from her notebook, spoke into the gap after it.

“You’d need a very strong one. My gap doesn’t close.”

A beat. Then a few people laughed. At the back, Fang Hao put his hand over his mouth. And in the third row on the left, by the broken blind, Miles Wei laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

This was nothing like the snort at the pink sticky note. It came out of him loud, before he could stop it, and it filled the whole room. Helpless. Surprised. His head went back. His notebook slid off his knee onto the floor.

He hadn’t laughed like that since he was seventeen. Thirteen years. Since a library, and two girls fighting in it, and the day he decided it was safer to want nothing.

The room stopped. Zhou had turned all the way round in the front row. He’d dropped his pen. Fang Hao was staring. Gao’s eyebrows had gone up into her hairline. Dr. Huang stood at the lectern with his laptop half shut and his mouth a bit open. Thirty physicists who had worked in the same building as Dr. Miles Wei for five years. They’d never heard him make a sound louder than I have a question about the boundary conditions. They sat and looked at him laughing by the broken blind.

He stopped. He looked round at all the faces.

Next to him, Fang Hao leaned over. Very quietly.

“Was that you?”

“No.”

He went red. Ears first. Then all the way down to his collar.
