“Sorry. I’m sorry. That was—sorry.” He picked his notebook up off the floor. “It was a good joke.”

In the second row, Yu Jie had turned round in her seat. She wasn’t smiling. She looked stunned. Like she’d just watched an experiment do something no theory predicted.

He looked back at her. Across two rows of chairs. In front of the whole department. For one second he forgot that nobody was supposed to know.

Then he remembered. He looked down at his notebook. The chair said, “Well! Wine’s in the corridor,” and the room broke into noise, and the second was over.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t stay for the wine. He never stayed for the wine. Dr. Huang caught him at the door. Plastic cup in hand. Smile back on.

“Wei. Your students are very forward.” A laugh. “That girl will need some manners if she wants a postdoc anywhere I’ve got friends.”

Miles looked at him.

“I’m refereeing your paper. The one with slide nineteen in it. The journal sent it to me last month.” He tucked his notebook under his arm. “I was going to ask for revisions. I’ve changed my mind. I’ll recommend they reject it. Everything after section four depends on that assumption.”

The smile went.

“You can’t let a student’s—”

“Her name is Shen Yu Jie.” Flat. “You’ll want to spell it right. When you thank her in the next version.”

He walked past him to the stairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was on the stairs. She wasn’t waiting, exactly. She was holding a plastic cup of warm white wine she wasn’t drinking and reading a notice about fire drills with tremendous attention. Two steps up from the third-floor landing. Exactly where anyone going to the fourth floor would have to pass.

He passed. One step above her, he stopped.

“That was a very good question. Slide nineteen.”

“That was a very good laugh.” She stared hard at the fire drill notice. “Four seconds. Nearly five. I counted.”

He stared at her.

“You counted.”

“I’m a physicist. I needed a baseline.” She turned her head and looked up at him, and her eyes were bright. “For next time.”

“Next time?”

“You’ll do it again.”

“I don’t—that’s not—”

“You will. I’ll make you.” She went back to the fire drill notice. “I’m going to make you laugh in front of Gao.”

“Gao was there.”

“In front of her face.”

He opened his mouth. Nothing came out. He went on up the stairs. She heard him walk straight into the fire door at the top. Thump. Then through it. She gave it a minute. She left the wine on the windowsill and went up after him.

The fourth floor was empty. Everyone was downstairs with the plastic cups. He was standing just the other side of the fire door, rubbing his forehead. When she came through he took his hand away and looked at her.

He’d been waiting. He didn’t say anything.

He took her wrist and pulled her in, out of the line of the little window in the fire door, and kissed her against the wall by the fire extinguisher.

Not carefully. Not at all. He kissed her like the laugh was still in him and had to go somewhere. One floor down, thirty physicists were talking about funding. Wine bottles clinked. None of it mattered. Her hands found the back of his neck. His found her waist under the green jumper, warm on her bare skin. She gasped against his mouth.

He did it again. When he let her go, she had to lean on the wall.

“That,” she said, not very steadily, “was a lot longer than five seconds.”

“Twenty-two.” His glasses were crooked. “New baseline.”

“You counted?!”

“I’m a physicist.” He straightened her jumper with both hands. Carefully. Like he was putting a page back in order. “I’ll need more data.”

“Huang’s still downstairs.”

“I know.”

“You can’t go back down like that. Your collar.”

“I’m not going back down.”

“You’re hiding? Dr. Wei. From a man with forty slides?”

“From a man with forty slides and a plastic cup,” he said. “Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He went to the kitchen with his collar undone, to fill the kettle and get his face back. Two postdocs were in there with plastic cups. They didn’t see him in the doorway.

“Dr. Wei laughed.”

“Out loud?”

“Out loud. Zhou dropped his pen.”

“No.”

“Dropped it. I saw it roll under Gao’s—”

Miles reversed out of the kitchen without the kettle.

On his desk there was an envelope. A real one. Thick. Cream-coloured. Heavy paper, the kind he associated with weddings and lawyers. His name on the front in black calligraphy: Dr. Miles Wei. On the back, pressed into a circle of dark red wax, a crest. A letter S, wound round what looked like a ship’s anchor.

He was still holding it when Fang Hao came in without knocking, with two plastic cups.

“You LAUGHED. I brought you wine. You never stay for the wine, so I’ve brought the wine to the—what’s that?”

“An invitation.”

“Ooh. Wax. Who still uses wax?” Fang Hao put the cups down on the marking. “Open it.”

He opened it.

The Shen Foundation requests the pleasure of your company at its Annual Winter Gala in celebration of its new endowment to the City University Department of Physics Saturday, the twentieth of December The Harbour Hotel, seven o’clock Black tie

“Black tie,” Fang Hao read over his shoulder. “Oh, you’re doomed.”

Underneath was a separate card. Handwriting Miles didn’t know. Elegant. Sharp. Slanting.

Dr. Wei. Professor Gao tells me you are the department’s most promising young lecturer. As the Foundation’s new gift will fund the physics department for the next ten years, my husband and I would be delighted to meet you. — Shen Ruolan

Fang Hao stopped reading out loud.

“Shen.”

“Yes.”

“Shen Ruolan. Miles. That’s Shen Holdings.”

“I know who Shen Holdings are.”

“Half the harbour! The new hospital wing! The Shen Building, forty floors, it’s got a helipad—”

“I know.”

“And your yellow dress is called—”

“Shen Yu Jie.” Miles sat down. “I know.”

Fang Hao sat down too. On the desk. On Bai Tianyu.

“You didn’t know,” he said slowly.

“She has biro on her shoes.”

“Miles.”

“She picked the pith off an orange, Fang. Every bit. With her fingernails.” He looked at the card. “Who does that? If they’ve got a helipad?”

Fang Hao didn’t make a joke. That was how Miles knew it was bad.

“Gao says her mother calls her the Perfect Jewel,” Fang Hao said. “In front of guests.”

“Gao told me.”

“Are you going?”

Miles looked at the card. My husband and I would be delighted to meet you. Then at the corner of the board. 20 June, 16:00.

“Gao says I have to.”

“That’s not what I asked you.”

Miles didn’t answer. Fang Hao picked up one of the wine cups, drank it in one go, and took the other one with him when he left.

✦ ✦ ✦

He got his phone out. He opened her name. Wednesday.

He typed: Your surname. He deleted it.

He typed: Shen? He deleted that too.

Through the wall, Fang Hao was telling somebody new. Out loud. In a seminar. Zhou dropped his PEN.

Miles put the phone face down on the invitation.

The plan had been to hide. From Fang Hao. From Zhou. From the second-years and the cardboard walls.

Nobody had said anything about hiding from a harbour.

chapters.title: Miles in a Rented Suit
chapters.desc: He looks like he’s about to defend a thesis. His sister takes over. Dr. Fang provides croissants and terrible advice.
chapters.epigraph: “Black tie means a bow tie, Miles. Not a black tie.” — Wei Lan, on video call, despairing
chapters.content:
He didn’t own a suit.

Correction. He owned one. Grey. Bought at twenty-five for his PhD defence, worn once more at a cousin’s wedding, then hung at the back of the wardrobe in the staff flat. It had stayed there for five years. Nobody had asked it to come out.

On Monday night he got it out. It had a moth hole in the left lapel. It was two sizes too big across the shoulders, because he’d been eating egg sandwiches since 2020 and not much else. It smelled of wardrobe.

He put it on and looked in the little mirror on the back of the bathroom door.

He looked like a man about to be told his thesis had failed. Also like a man who’d deserve it.

✦ ✦ ✦

“No.”

Fang Hao didn’t even put down his croissant. Tuesday lunchtime, office 412. Miles had brought the suit to work in a carrier bag because he didn’t know what else to do with it, and Fang Hao had smelled fear through the wall.

“It’s grey.”

“Miles. That is not a suit. That is a cry for help.”

“It was for my defence.”

“Your defence was five years ago! You were a different shape. You were a different species.” Fang Hao poked the lapel. His finger went through the moth hole. They both looked at it. “Oh, it’s got a door.”

“It’s a small hole.”

“It’s a portal. And the invitation says black tie. You know what black tie means?”

Miles thought about it. He liked to be accurate.

“A black tie.”

Fang Hao shut his eyes. He took an enormous bite of croissant, like a man who needed the strength.

“Ring your sister,” he said, with his mouth full. “I can’t do this alone. I’m one man. I have a wife and a mortgage.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He rang Wei Lan that night. On video, because Fang Hao said that counted as an emergency.

She picked up in the hospital staff kitchen in her scrubs, eating noodles out of a plastic tub. Same face as his. Shorter. Louder. Never once in her life unsure about anything.

“You never video call. Something’s happened.” She pointed her chopsticks at the screen. “Is it the soup girl?”

“There’s a gala.”

The chopsticks stopped.

“A gala.”

“The Shen Foundation. They’re giving the department money. Gao says I have to go. The dean’ll be there.” He held the invitation up to the camera. Wax seal and all. “It says black tie. Fang Hao says I don’t know what that means.”

“What do you think it means?”

“…A black tie.”

Wei Lan stared at him for three full seconds. Her noodles dripped.

“Black tie means a bow tie, Miles. Not a black tie. A bow tie. And a dinner jacket. Black. Satin on the lapels.” She jabbed the chopsticks. “You’ll go to the place on Harbour Road tomorrow and you’ll send me a photo from the changing room. Every outfit. And I’ll say no to all of them until you get it right.”

“I don’t need—”

“Is she going to be there?”

He didn’t answer. That was an answer. Wei Lan leaned so close to her phone that all he could see was one eye.

“Miles. The girl with the oranges. Is she going to be at this gala?”

“Her name’s Shen Yu Jie.” He put the invitation down. “It’s her family’s gala.”

The eye went away. Wei Lan sat back slowly.

“Shen. As in—”

“As in the Shen Building. As in half the harbour.” He looked at the wax crest. An S round an anchor. “I didn’t know. She never said. She’s got biro on her trainers, Lan. She eats White Rabbits out of her cardigan pocket. She peeled the pith off my oranges.”

His sister didn’t say anything for a bit. She put the noodles down. That was serious. Wei Lan never put noodles down.

“Oh, Miles.”

“What?”

“Nothing.” She picked them up again. “Harbour Road. Photos. And get a haircut. You look like a dandelion.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He went on Wednesday morning, before the not-office-hours.

He sent eleven photographs from the changing room. She said no to ten of them. No. No. You look like a waiter. No. Why is it BROWN. The eleventh was black, slim, satin lapels, a white shirt with tiny buttons. The bow tie came already tied, on a strap. Wei Lan said he’d strangle himself with a real one, and he’d be found dead in a ballroom, and she’d have to tell Mum.

Wei Lan: That one. Buy it, don’t rent it. You’ll need it again.

Miles: Why would I need it again?

She sent back a picture of a ring. No words. Just the ring.

He put his phone in his pocket. He bought it, though.

The tailor was about a hundred years old. Tape measure round his neck. Pins in his mouth. He took up the trousers and looked at Miles in the mirror the whole time. Tall, thin, hunched, glasses crooked. A man in a beautiful jacket with the face of a man in a lift that had stopped between floors.

“Big night?” Through the pins.

“A gala.”

“For a girl?”

Miles went red from the collar up. The tailor took the pins out of his mouth.

“Shoulders back. No. Back. Like a man who knows something nobody else in the room knows.”

Miles stood up straight. It felt strange. Like being stretched.

“I do know a few things nobody else knows,” he said. “I’m a physicist.”

“Then stand like one.” The tailor went to get his receipt book. “And stop looking at the door.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Wednesday. Quarter to four. She came in, sat down, picked up her tea. Then she saw the envelope on his desk.

Cream. Heavy. Red wax.

He watched her face do it. All of it went. The cheek, the noise, the Wednesday. What was left was polite and pale.

“You got one.”

“Your mother wrote to me.”

“Oh god!” She put her tea down. “What did she say?”

“That Gao says I’m promising. That she’d be delighted to meet me.” He pushed his glasses up. “That the Foundation’s gift will fund this department for ten years.”

“It will. She’ll mention it. Every time she sees you. Probably in the first sentence.”

He looked at her. She looked at the wax.

“Shen.”

“I was going to tell you.”

“When?”

“I don’t know! June? Never? When you’d got used to me?” Her voice went up. “You’d have been weird. Everyone’s weird. They find out and they start talking to me like I’m made of glass. Or like I’m a cheque.”

“I don’t think you’re a cheque.”

“You don’t know that yet!”

“I do. You picked the pith off my oranges with your fingernails.” He meant it as evidence. It came out a lot softer than evidence. “Is that why you came up four floors? Because nobody up here knew?”

She didn’t answer for a second. Then she nodded at the wax. Small and miserable.

“Up here I’m just loud.”

“You are very loud.”

“Thank you.”

“I meant it as a compliment…”

“I know you did, that’s the problem.” She wiped her eyes with the heel of her hand, fast, like she was cross with them. Then she spotted the pin. “You’ve got a pin in your jumper.”

He looked down. A tailor’s pin, stuck in his left elbow right next to the hole. He pulled it out.

“The tailor. For the gala.” A pause. “I don’t have to go. I could tell Gao I’ve got a fever. There’s a precedent.”

“No.” It came out much too fast. “Come. Please.” She stopped. Started again, carefully, like she was rubbing out a line of working. “I’ve just never had anyone there before. Anyone who knows I can do the harmonic oscillator.”

“Then I’ll be somewhere you can find me. Not in a corner.”

“You always stand in the corner.”

“I’ll ask Fang Hao where people stand.”

She held out her hand for the pin. He gave it to her. She put it in her cardigan pocket with the White Rabbit wrappers. She didn’t give it back.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six, Fang Hao’s door. Fang Hao’s footsteps. The lift.

She got up and shut the door herself. Then she came round the desk to where he was leaning on the edge of it, and stood between his knees, and fixed his collar. It didn’t need fixing. She did it anyway. Tugged it. Flattened it. Tugged it again.

“You’ll be in a dinner jacket. I’ll be at the top of the stairs with my mother’s hand on my elbow.” Tug. “I won’t be able to touch you all night. Not once.”

“I know.”

“So I’m doing it now. In advance.”

She kissed him. Took her time. His hands went to her waist and stayed there. When she pulled back to breathe, he followed her, and she put one finger on his mouth.

“That’s Saturday’s. Don’t use it all at once.”

He looked at her over her finger. Glasses crooked. Then he took her hand off his mouth and kissed the finger. The middle one. Right where the ink was.

She forgot what she’d been going to say. Completely. It was just gone.

“I’ll ration it,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He got a haircut on Thursday. He said “shorter”. The barber looked at the bit at the back that always stuck up, sighed like a man at a funeral, and did his best.

On Friday Fang Hao came in with two croissants and sat on Bai Tianyu’s homework.

“Right. Gala rules.”

“There are rules?”

“There are always rules. Rule one. Don’t talk physics for more than five minutes at a time. Rich people get bored. Talk about boats.”

“I don’t know anything about boats.”

“Buoyancy, Miles. You know buoyancy. Lie.” Bite. “Rule two. Don’t stand in the corner. Stand by the food. Everyone comes to the food.”

“I don’t eat at parties.”

“Hold a plate anyway. It gives your hands a job.” Another bite. “Rule three. When you see her, and she’s with her family, and they’re dripping in diamonds, and her mother’s walking her up and down in front of men who own shipping companies—”

He stopped. He looked at Miles. Miles didn’t say anything at all. His ears did, though.

“Rule three is don’t leave early.” Fang Hao’s voice had changed. “You always leave early. Whatever happens. Stay till the end.”

“Why?”

“Because she’s going to be a Perfect Jewel in that ballroom all night. And at some point she’s going to look across it. And she’s going to need one person in there who knows she’s got biro on her shoes.” He brushed crumbs off his trousers. “That’s you, idiot. Don’t leave.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Friday night, sixth floor, the flat by the east gate. The dress was hanging on the wardrobe door in a dust bag. Tao Tao unzipped it two inches and zipped it straight back up.

“Nope. Too beautiful. I can’t look at it directly.”

“It’s just a dress.”

“It’s the colour of the sky at five in the morning, Jie Jie. Nobody’s just anything in that.” Tao Tao flopped onto the bed. “Will he be there?”

“Fang Hao’s giving him rules.”

“FANG HAO’S GIVING HIM RULES?”

“Don’t shout! The woman downstairs will bang on the ceiling again.”

Her phone went. Ma. Yu Jie looked at the screen like it was a bill. Tao Tao mimed zipping her mouth shut and then didn’t zip it at all.

“Yu Jie.” Her mother’s voice, pleasant as ice cubes. “The car will come at five. Hair at the house. Don’t eat anything with garlic.”

“Yes, Ma.”

“Professor Gao tells me you’re in her laboratory every Wednesday. Until seven, she says.” A tiny pause. “She’s very fond of you.”

Yu Jie’s mouth went dry. Gao. Gao had said that. Out loud. To her mother.

“She’s a monster, Ma. She makes me count atoms.”

“How dreary. Well. You’ll have something to talk about with the dean.” Another pause. “And the young lecturer. Dr. Wei. I wrote to him. Gao says he’s the clever one. Is he?”

Her toes curled up in her socks.

“He’s… fine. He’s very boring. He eats the same sandwich every day.”

“Good.”

Her mother rang off.

Tao Tao was sitting bolt upright.

“Boring?”

“What was I supposed to say?! He’s the best thing that’s ever happened to me and he kissed my finger?”

“He kissed your—which finger—”

Yu Jie threw a pillow at her. Then she lay on her back and held the phone against her chest. Gao. Lying to Shen Ruolan for the second time. For them.

She was going to write that woman the best thesis in ten years if it killed her.

✦ ✦ ✦

Before he went home, Miles opened his top drawer.

Pink sticky notes, a whole stack of them. A bag of White Rabbits, still half full. And the purple pen with the plastic cat on the end, the question mark painted on its head. She’d dropped it in September. He’d told her he hadn’t seen it. He was a terrible liar and she’d never asked again.

He took out the pen. He looked at it for a while. Then he took out two White Rabbits as well, in case.

Saturday. Quarter past six. He stood in front of the little mirror in the dinner jacket, the white shirt with tiny buttons, the bow tie on its strap. The bit at the back of his hair, against all known laws, lay flat.

He looked like somebody who was going somewhere he wanted to go. Who was that?

He took a photo and sent it to his sister.

Wei Lan: Oh.

Wei Lan: Oh, Miles.

Wei Lan: Don’t talk about entropy.

Wei Lan: DON’T LEAVE EARLY

He put the phone in his inside pocket. Then the two sweets. Then the purple pen with the cat on it, right over his heart, where it poked him every time he breathed.

If he was going to stand in a room full of diamonds all night, he wanted something in his pocket that had been hers before anybody called her a jewel.

It poked him again. He let it.

chapters.title: The Shen Family Gala
chapters.desc: The Perfect Jewel at the top of the stairs. Two married women who recognise him across the room. And a very large man by the pillar, glaring.
chapters.epigraph: “Miles Wei. As I live and breathe. In a tuxedo.” — Aurelia Chen
chapters.content:
The ballroom of the Harbour Hotel smelled of lilies and money. Chandeliers. An ice sculpture of a ship, melting into a silver tray. Four hundred people in black and jewels. A banner over the stage: THE SHEN FOUNDATION: INVESTING IN TOMORROW.

Miles looked for the nearest corner. There it was. Behind a potted palm. Nobody would find him till spring. Rule two, idiot.

He went to the window by the dessert table instead. He picked up an empty plate. Then a glass of water, for the other hand. Both hands had jobs now. Fang Hao would be thrilled.

“You’re holding a plate.”

Professor Gao. Black dress, clearly older than most of the waiters. She was holding a glass of red wine like it had insulted her family.

“Fang Hao says it gives my hands a job.”

“Fang Hao’s never been to a gala in his life.”

“He’s read about them.”

“Hm.” She looked him over. Shoes. Jacket. Hair. “Who did the haircut?”

“A barber. He sighed a lot.”

“He did well.” She drank half the wine in one go. “The dean wants to shake your hand. Shake it. Smile. Don’t explain gravitational lensing to his wife. She’ll cry. Last year it was dark matter and she had to go and lie down.”

“I wasn’t going to—”

“You were.” She was already going. “Stand up straight, Wei.”

He stood up straight. Across the room, Professor Zhou caught his eye and nodded. A careful nod. The nod of a man who’d heard his youngest lecturer laugh out loud in a seminar and still hadn’t recovered.

Miles nodded back. Was there a correct way to hold an empty plate? Everyone else seemed to know it.

Then the dean arrived. Round, beaming, a wife in purple on his arm.

“Dr. Wei! Our rising star! Gao never stops talking about you.”

Gao, three metres behind him, mouthed I do.

“Thank you, Dean.”

“And what is it you do, Dr. Wei?” The wife. Bright, kind, doomed. “In very simple words. I was hopeless at school.”

Miles looked at Gao. Gao looked at the ceiling.

“Light,” he said. “It bends. Round heavy things.”

“Oh! How lovely. Like what?”

“Galaxies. Black holes.” He felt the words lining up behind his teeth. Six papers’ worth. Gao’s eyebrow went up a millimetre. He shut his mouth. Opened it again. “Also… people. Sometimes. Metaphorically.”

“People.” The dean’s wife put a hand on her chest. “Oh, that’s beautiful. Isn’t that beautiful, Wen?”

“Very beautiful,” said the dean, who had not been listening.

They moved on. Gao walked past him with her wine.

“Metaphorically,” she muttered. “God help us.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Hold still.”

He jumped. Water went all down his wrist. Two hands came round from behind him and took hold of his bow tie. He knew those hands. At sixteen they’d stolen his physics notebook and read the front page out to the whole library.

Untie. Cross. Fold. Three movements. Exactly like the reunion.

“There.” A pat on the knot. “Now you look like someone who’s allowed to be here.”

He turned round. Gold dress. Sapphires like quail’s eggs. The same wicked, delighted face. She looked about twenty. How was that allowed?

“Miles Wei. As I live and breathe. In a tuxedo.”

“Aurelia Song.”

“Chen. Aurelia Chen.” She tipped her head back. “And this is my husband, who has heard a great deal about you.”

Miles hadn’t heard anyone come. A man in grey was simply there now, at her shoulder, hand already out. Calm eyes. Very pleasant.

“Mostly unprintable.”

Miles shook the hand. His was wet and freezing. Chen Si didn’t seem to mind. He went on shaking it for exactly as long as was polite. Meanwhile Aurelia leaned back against his shoulder and murmured something without turning her head.

Miles caught one word. Jealous. He looked at Chen Si. Chen Si looked back. Mild face. Not mild eyes. Not even slightly.

Oh no. About him? About two years of Aurelia doing calculus she didn’t need, to sit near him in a library? He’d been a stick insect with a fringe!

Chen Si let go and put his hand on the small of his wife’s back. And left it there.

“You tied it like a man who understands fluid dynamics and not knots,” Aurelia told him. “I’d know that bow tie anywhere. Are you still doing light?”

“Light bending. Round galaxies.”

“Still bending. Good for you.” She smiled wickedly past his shoulder. “And of course you remember Elowen.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He turned round. Again. He was going to get dizzy. Elowen. Elowen Zhao, now. Dark green silk. A glass of water, same as his. Her smile was small and amused and much warmer than he remembered. There was a green stain on her thumb. Stems, cut that morning.

And by the marble pillar behind her stood the largest man in the room. Miles remembered him. At the reunion he’d walked up to this man, out of breath, holding an empty glass. He’d asked him what he did. Import and export, the man had said, and Chen Si had coughed into his napkin.

Zhao Zhendong was wearing black and no expression. He was glaring at Miles. Openly. Steadily. Like it was his job and he was good at it.

“Miles. It’s good to see you.” Elowen turned her head. “Zhendong. You remember Miles.”

“Yes.”

That was all. Yes. He didn’t blink.

“Hello,” Miles tried. “I’m—still Miles.”

Aurelia made a sound of pure joy. Then she lifted her voice. Not much. Just enough to carry to the pillar.

“Zhendong, Elowen has three hundred white roses to do for a wedding tomorrow, and you’re driving her to the flower market at half past three in the morning to carry the buckets.”

Elowen went pink. Zhao turned his head and looked at Aurelia for a long, flat second.

“Hm.”

Then he moved half a step closer to his wife. And looked back at Miles. And glared.

“You look well,” Miles told Elowen. It was true. It was also the only sentence he had left.

“She’s very well. I’m not saying anything. I’m just standing here.”

“Aurelia.”

“Nothing! I’m furniture. I’m a lamp.”

The corner of Zhao’s mouth moved. On another man it might have been a smile. Then it was gone.

Elowen was studying Miles over her water. “You’ve stopped apologising to things.”

“Have I?”

“You walked into the door on the way in. I saw. You didn’t say sorry to it.” She tilted her head. “At school you said sorry to a fire extinguisher.”

“It was a very big fire extinguisher.”

“When did you stop?”

He thought about it honestly. “September.”

“What happened in September?”

“Someone told me it was weird.”

“It was weird,” Elowen agreed.

Aurelia’s eyes had gone narrow and bright. “Who told you?”

“A student.” He pushed his glasses up. “She was very loud about it.”

Aurelia smiled like a cat. “She.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The quartet stopped.

“Ladies and gentlemen, the Shen family.”

The room turned to the white marble staircase. The father first. Tall, silver hair, no expression. The mother in pale grey silk, diamonds at her throat, a smile so perfect it looked painted on. The son, about thirty-five, checking his phone on the stairs.

And one step behind her mother, coming down slowly with a hand on the banister: her. A long dress the colour of the sky just before it gets light. Hair up in a smooth coil. Diamonds in her ears. Not one pen. Not a single one.

Miles forgot he was holding a plate.

She was smiling. It was a small, polite, perfect smile. He’d never seen it before. Fifteen Wednesdays and not once. It went nowhere near her eyes. Her eyes were on a spot above four hundred heads. On nothing.

At the bottom of the stairs her mother took her elbow and turned her to face the room. Best side out. Like a vase.

“Look at Ruolan,” Aurelia breathed. “That smile. She practises it in a mirror.”

“Aurelia.” Chen Si, very mild.

“She does! Her hairdresser told my hairdresser.” Aurelia narrowed her eyes at the staircase. “And the girl’s dress is from Paris.”

Elowen didn’t look up from her water. “Milan.”

“It is not—” Aurelia looked again. Her mouth fell open. “Oh, that’s Milan. How did you—”

“The hem.”

“You don’t know anything about hems!”

“I know about edges. Forty-two.”

Aurelia made a noise like a kettle.

Miles wasn’t listening. He was thinking about a girl with her head on his desk, laughing so hard at a cactus joke she couldn’t breathe. The yellow sundress. The pink sticky note on his door. Cu-Te.

And Gao, in his office. She’s been hiding what she can do. Because she thinks nobody wants it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother started bringing them over. Men. One at a time.

Aurelia leaned in, like a race commentator. “Shipping. Owns eleven boats and can’t swim.”

Miles counted. He didn’t mean to. He couldn’t stop.

“Bank. Bank again. Oh, that’s the restaurant one, he’ll tell her about every restaurant. Every one. Darling, how long did he do at our table?”

Chen Si didn’t even look round. “Forty minutes.”

“Forty minutes!”

“Four,” Miles said, before he could stop himself.

Aurelia’s head turned. “Four what?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re counting.”

“I’m not.”

“You said four.”

He watched the next man bow over the hand. “…Five.”

“Oh my god.” Aurelia grabbed her husband’s sleeve. “He’s counting them!”

“I can hear him, my love.”

Number five was about forty-five. Very clean fingernails. He stood much too close. Halfway through a sentence he put his hand on her arm to make a point. The point ended. The hand didn’t.

Miles had never had an opinion about a stranger’s fingernails in his life. He had one now. It was detailed. It had sub-sections. He’d kissed the inside of that elbow on Wednesday. Right there, where the skin was thin. She’d laughed and pulled away because it tickled. Then she’d given it back. Again. Do it again.

“Miles.” Elowen, beside him. “Your plate.”

He looked down. He’d been gripping it so hard the rim had printed a red line across his palm.

“It’s a very good plate,” he heard himself say.

Aurelia had gone quiet. For Aurelia that was a medical event. She was following his eyes across the ballroom. To the island of light by the stage. To the girl in the dawn-coloured dress, and the hand on her arm.

Then she turned and looked at his face instead.

“Oh,” she said. “Oh, Miles.”

“What?”

“That’s Ruolan’s girl. The Perfect Jewel.” She didn’t blink. “She’s at your university. Physics, I heard. Ruolan’s livid about it.”

“Is she.”

“Miles Wei. Look at me.”

He didn’t. He’d had thirteen years of practice at not looking at things. It didn’t help at all.

“She’s a final-year. In my department.” He kept his eyes on the plate. “I don’t teach her.”

“I didn’t ask if you taught her.”

“I’m aware.”

“I didn’t ask anything. I said oh.”

“You said oh, Miles.”

“Which is a whole question! Everyone knows that’s a whole question.” She swung round. “Elowen. Isn’t that a whole question?”

Elowen considered it. “It is, a bit.”

“Not you as well.”

“I’d answer her,” Chen Si offered, still to the chandelier. “If she doesn’t hear it from you, she’ll hear it from someone else. Then she’ll be cross with you instead of curious.”

“I’m never cross.”

“I’m not allowed to lie, my love.”

“There’s nothing to answer.”

Aurelia looked at him. Then at the red line across his palm. Then at his ears, which he could feel getting hotter by the second, like a pair of very small, very stupid radiators.

“Nothing,” she said. “Right. Of course. Silly me.”

Elowen put her glass down on a passing tray. She had the look he remembered from the school library. Tired and sharp and much too clever. Chen Si studied the chandelier with great politeness.

“I’m going to get some cake,” Miles announced, to nobody.

Elowen didn’t even turn her head. “You don’t eat cake.”

“I’m going to hold some.”

✦ ✦ ✦

His phone buzzed against the purple pen in his inside pocket. He shouldn’t have looked. He looked.

Wednesday: stop holding that plate like a shield

Wednesday: also hi

Wednesday: you look

He typed back with his thumb, under the edge of the plate.

Miles: Rule two.

You look. No full stop. Like she’d been interrupted. Or like she hadn’t found the end of the sentence.

He looked up. Across four hundred people, past the ice ship and the quartet, she’d turned her head. Straight at him.

The perfect smile went. Just gone. What was there instead was startled and wide open and very like relief. Like he was a door she’d been hunting for in a room with no doors.

He didn’t smile back. His face had stopped working. He let her see whatever was on it. Then her mother’s hand tightened on her elbow. She turned back to man number six. The Perfect Jewel came down over her face like a shutter.

Aurelia let out a breath. Very gently, for Aurelia. “Well. That’s not a rule.”

Miles didn’t answer. He’d been caught by three people at once. Four, if you counted the chandelier Chen Si was pretending to look at.

And by a fifth. By the pillar, Zhao Zhendong had stopped glaring. He looked across the room at the girl in the dawn-coloured dress. Back at Miles. At the girl again. Slow. Like a man doing a sum and not liking it.

“Hm.”

“Oh, that’s new.” Aurelia, delighted, behind her hand. “He’s stopped glaring at you. Miles. Darling. You should be terrified.”

“I am.”

“Good. Hold on to the plate.”

He held on to the plate. He’d have preferred the glaring.

chapters.title: Yu Jie Is Not Jealous of Women Married to Dangerous Men
chapters.desc: She is a little jealous. She would like that noted privately. Then Aurelia Chen corners her in the powder room.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not jealous.” “You’ve folded that napkin into a swan, unfolded it, and folded it into a smaller swan.”
chapters.content:
“Ruolan’s daughter, Yu Jie. She’s at the university. Physics, can you imagine?” Her mother’s hand on her elbow. Her mother’s little laugh. “She’ll grow out of it.”

That was man number one. He owned boats.

“Do you sail, Miss Shen?”

“I get seasick.”

“Ha! Ha. You’ll grow out of it.”

Everyone thought she’d grow out of things. She was starting to think she might grow out of them.

Number two was a bank. Number three owned eleven restaurants.

“The second one does a crab you would not believe. The fourth one, now, the fourth one has a chef from Lyon—”

“How interesting.”

“—and what is it you study, Miss Shen?”

“Oh, just physics.” And the little laugh. The one she’d been taught. So it sounded like pottery.

Just physics. She thought of the chalkboard in 412 and felt sick.

Number five was a widower of about forty-five, with spotless fingernails. He looked at her like a vase in an antique shop he might put a deposit on. Halfway through a sentence about his yacht, he put his hand on her arm. The sentence ended. The hand didn’t.

She looked down at it. Then up at him, sweetly.

“Your cufflink’s upside down.”

“What? Oh—oh dear—”

He spent ten minutes turning it round. He didn’t touch her again. Small wins. You took them where you found them.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d spotted Miles between number three and number four. By the food. By the food! Real dinner jacket. Satin lapels. Hair cut short, so the stupid bit at the back almost lay flat. Holding an empty plate. Standing so straight it looked like somebody had put a broom handle down his back.

He looked like—

She had words in three languages, plus maths. None of them were good enough. He looked like somebody she’d cross a ballroom for, if her mother’s hand weren’t on her elbow.

Then a woman in gold walked up behind him and took hold of his bow tie. Untie. Cross. Fold. Like she’d done it a hundred times. Like she had every right in the world to touch his collar.

Yu Jie had undone that collar on Wednesday! Two buttons, door shut, because she’d wanted to see his collarbone, and he’d stood still and let her. She had every right. She just wasn’t allowed to use it in here.

Her mother turned to greet the dean. Four seconds. Yu Jie got her phone out.

Yu Jie: stop holding that plate like a shield

Yu Jie: also hi

Yu Jie: you look

She’d been going to write like mine. Her mother turned back. The phone went in the bag. It buzzed against her hip a minute later.

Radiator: Rule two.

She snorted. Out loud. Number six looked alarmed.

“Are you all right, Miss Shen?”

“Bubbles. Champagne. Up my nose.”

She wasn’t holding a glass. He didn’t notice. None of them noticed anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Who’s the woman in gold?” Number six, following her eyes. “With the thin chap.”

“Aurelia Chen.”

“Oh! Chen.” He lowered his voice like the name might hear him. “Your father would never—”

“No.”

Her father did business with everybody. Once, at dinner, under his breath, he’d said the Shens would never do business with Chen Si. Then he’d changed the subject. Nobody had brought it up again.

“And the one in green?”

“Elowen Zhao.”

“Ah.” He went pink. “The florist.”

Her mother had a lot to say about the florist. Always at dinner. Always in her not done voice. From the Walled City. With that man. They say he bought her whole shop on the first night. That man was by the pillar, looking at Miles like he wanted to fold him up and post him somewhere.

And Miles stood between them. Gold and green. Both gorgeous. Both smiling at him like they had something old together. They did. You didn’t look at someone like that unless you’d known them forever.

Fang Hao had said it once, through the cardboard wall, not knowing she was there. He hasn’t laughed since school. Two girls. Big drama.

Number seven talked about golf.

“I’m off a twelve now. Twelve. Do you play?”

“No.”

“You’d love it. It’s all angles, you know. Physics, really.”

“How interesting.”

She folded her napkin into a swan. Number seven peered at it.

“Is that a bird?”

“It’s a swan.”

“Ha! Clever hands. You should try putting.” He mimed it. “It’s all in the wrists, you know.”

Yu Jie smiled at him. So is strangling.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was not jealous. She’d like that noted. She was a scientist. She’d looked at the evidence. Both women were married, loudly and publicly, to men who could buy the harbour. Aurelia’s hand kept drifting back to her husband’s sleeve. Elowen checked the pillar every few seconds, like a lighthouse.

So. Nothing to be jealous of.

She unfolded the swan. She folded it into a smaller swan. It was just that they’d known him. At seventeen. Before the rule and the cactus and the one sad egg. They’d known a boy who laughed. And Yu Jie, who’d made him laugh in front of the whole department, who knew what he sounded like saying her name against her mouth, had to stand over here in her mother’s diamonds and hear about a handicap.

“—so I said to the caddie—”

Miles looked up. Straight at her. She forgot to smile. Golf, diamonds, swan, all of it, gone. She just looked at him, and something came onto her face that she couldn’t stop.

Her mother’s hand tightened.

“You’re staring.” Without moving her lips. “Who is that?”

“Nobody. A lecturer. From the department.”

Her mother followed her eyes. To the thin man in the new tuxedo, between Aurelia Chen and Elowen Zhao.

“Ah. Gao’s young one. I wrote to him.” A tiny narrowing. “He’s very thin.”

“He eats the same sandwich every day.”

“How sad.” A pause. “Gao says he’s brilliant. Gao says you’re brilliant. Gao says a great many things on the telephone.”

“She’s very… thorough.”

“She’s very loud. She told me you were in her laboratory until seven every Wednesday, as though I’d asked.” Her mother’s smile didn’t flicker. “I hadn’t asked.”

Yu Jie’s stomach dropped through the floor. Gao. Gao had volunteered it.

“It’s a big project, Ma.”

“I’m sure.” Her mother turned her back round, firmly. “Smile, darling. This gentleman’s family owns the airport.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She escaped during the speeches. Her father was on the stage being flat and expressionless about tomorrow. Her mother was beside him, glowing. Her brother was at the bar on his phone. For the first time all night, nobody had a hand on her elbow.

She went down a corridor of mirrors to the powder room. It was the size of her whole flat. Velvet sofas. Gold taps. An attendant with a tower of tiny towels.

“Towel, miss?” The attendant, kindly.

“No. Thank you.” She sat down on a velvet sofa. “…Yes. Two, please.”

She put her face in both towels. No crying. Not at galas. She’d made that rule at fourteen, at her first one, after her mother told her in the car that she’d laughed too loudly at dinner and embarrassed the family.

She got her phone out.

Tao Tao: hows the zoo. any rich boys worth eating

Yu Jie: nine. all inedible. hes here

Tao Tao: IN A TUX??? SEND A PHOTO OR I WILL DIE

Yu Jie: hes talking to aurelia chen AND elowen zhao. they both knew him at school. theyre both married to men who look like they kill people for a living. theyre both gorgeous. im not jealous

Tao Tao: youre a little jealous

Yu Jie: i would like that noted privately

Tao Tao: also reminder ah peng bet youd give up by christmas. FIVE DAYS. dont you dare give up i need his money

Yu Jie: im not giving up

Yu Jie: im just in a powder room having a

The door opened.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia Chen came in, in a shimmer of gold, and stopped. She looked at the velvet sofa. At the girl on it, with the diamonds and the perfect hair and the phone clutched in both hands.

“Oh, good. I was hoping it was you.”

She sat down on the other end of the sofa without asking. Crossed her legs. Looked Yu Jie up and down with open, cheerful interest. Like Tao Tao with a new mushroom.

“You’re Ruolan’s girl.”

“Yu Jie.”

“Yu Jie. Physics. City University.” A pause, beautifully timed. “With Miles.”

Yu Jie put the phone face down on her knee.

“Sweetheart.” Aurelia’s smile was slow and wicked. “You looked at him across that ballroom like he was the last lifeboat off the Titanic. And he looked back like he’d been hit by one. I’ve known Miles since he was sixteen. His face has never done that. Not once.” She leaned in. “So. How long?”

“There’s nothing.” Steady. Good. “He’s a lecturer. I’m a student. He has a rule.”

“Of course he has a rule.” Aurelia rolled her eyes at the gold ceiling. “He had one at sixteen! No girlfriends until university. He wrote it in the front of his physics notebook.”

“How do you know that?”

“I stole the notebook and read it out loud.”

“You didn’t.”

“In the library. To everyone.” No shame at all. “Then Elowen and I had a fight about him that the school still talks about. He went white, walked out, and chose a textbook over both of us.” A shrug of one gold shoulder. “Correct choice. I was a nightmare. Elowen was asleep on her feet. We didn’t want him. We wanted to win.”

Yu Jie looked at her.

“Did you love him?”

It was out before she could stop it. Aurelia’s smile went crooked.

“No. Not really.” She thought about it. “I loved that he didn’t want me. Nobody ever didn’t want me.” Her head tilted. “Do you?”

Yu Jie didn’t answer. Her face didn’t move. She’d been trained by the best.

It didn’t matter. Aurelia read it anyway.

“Oh, sweetheart.”

“I’m not jealous.”

“You’ve folded that napkin into a swan, unfolded it, and folded it into a smaller swan.”

Yu Jie looked down. The napkin was in her lap. She’d brought it with her. Why had she brought it with her?! It was a tiny swan now. Practically a duckling.

She tried to look dignified. “That was… origami. For calm.”

“Mm. Very calm. I could see it from the bar.” Aurelia sat back. “Fine. There’s nothing. Tell me about the nothing. What’s he like? Now, I mean. Grown up.”

“I don’t—he’s a lecturer, I hardly—”

“Sweetheart.”

Yu Jie lasted about two seconds.

“He stood at a bike rack for fifty-six minutes,” she blurted. “In November! Because he didn’t know which door I’d come out of. And then he gave me an egg sandwich. Out of his backpack. It was warm, it was disgusting, I ate all of it—”

She stopped. Her face was on fire.

“That didn’t happen.”

“Of course it didn’t.” Aurelia’s eyes were shining. “Fifty-six minutes.”

“He counted.”

“Of course he counted!” Aurelia pressed both hands to her chest like she’d been shot. “Oh, this is the best night I’ve had in years.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia got up and fixed her lipstick in the gold mirror. She talked to Yu Jie’s reflection instead of to her face, which was somehow easier.

“He thinks wanting things gets people hurt. Did you know that? He watched two girls tear each other apart over him and decided it was his fault. So he stopped being anything anyone could want.” Lipstick, top lip. “He made himself boring on purpose. He used to be funny. He did impressions of the physics teacher.”

Yu Jie’s throat went tight.

“He laughed,” she said. “Two weeks ago. In a seminar. Out loud.”

Aurelia’s hand stopped an inch from her mouth.

“That was you?” She spun round. “Somebody put it online! Some second-year! Dr. Wei LAUGHS. I watched it six times. Chen Si had to take the phone off me.” She stared. “What did you say?”

“I told a professor from the capital that my gap doesn’t close.”

Aurelia looked at her for a second. Then she threw her head back and laughed so loud the attendant dropped a towel.

“Oh, I like you. Oh, Ruolan is going to HATE this!” She held out a hand and pulled Yu Jie up off the sofa. “Come on. Speeches are nearly done. If your mother finds you in here with me she’ll have a stroke, and I’m not ready to be blamed for that yet.”

At the door she stopped. Looked back. Not wicked this time.

“I’m married to a man the papers call a gangster. Elowen’s married to one who sells guns. Neither of us wants anything you’ve got. Except one thing.” She opened the door. “He laughed for you. He never once laughed for us.”

She went out in a blaze of gold. Yu Jie stood there with her phone and her duckling and her heart going much too fast.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tao Tao had sent eleven more messages. All capitals. She typed one word back.

Yu Jie: later

Then she put the phone in her silver bag and walked back down the corridor of mirrors. Twenty of her went past. Dawn-coloured dress. Diamonds. Perfect hair. Not a single pen.

At the last mirror, by the ballroom door, she stopped. She reached up and slid one of the long silver pins out of the coil. One strand came loose and fell against her cheek.

Her brother came round the corner, thumb on his phone.

“Ma wants you.”

“Coming.”

“You’ve got—” He waved vaguely at his own head. Didn’t look up. “Something.”

“I know.”

He’d already gone. Nobody in her family ever looked up.

Her mother wouldn’t notice. Miles would. She’d bet Tao Tao’s whole book on it.

chapters.title: Elowen Asks Him One Question
chapters.desc: Five years ago he asked her on a balcony. Tonight, on a terrace over the harbour, she asks him back.
chapters.epigraph: “Are you happy, Miles?” He had never once, in thirty-one years, thought about it.
chapters.content:
Before the speeches, Shen Ruolan found him.

She came across the room with her daughter on her arm. Like a woman walking a very expensive dog. People got out of the way. Miles thought about the potted palm and decided he wasn’t fast enough.

“Dr. Wei. At last.” A cool hand. A perfect smile. “Professor Gao speaks of you constantly. I’m so glad you came.”

“Thank you for inviting me, Mrs. Shen.”

“Not at all. The Foundation likes to meet the people it pays for.” She said it lightly. It landed like a brick. “And this is my daughter. Yu Jie. I believe she’s in your department.”

Yu Jie held out her hand. Very correct. Very polite. Total stranger.

“Dr. Wei.”

“Miss Shen.”

He shook it. Her fingers were cold. Her thumb pressed once, hard, into the side of his hand, where her mother couldn’t see. He nearly dropped his plate.

Shen Ruolan patted her daughter’s arm. “You must find her terribly ordinary. Next to your real students.”

He felt Yu Jie not breathe beside him.

“No,” he said. Carefully. Like a man walking on a frozen pond. “Professor Gao says she’s the best she’s had in twenty years.”

“Gao is very generous.”

“Gao isn’t generous at all. She’s accurate.”

A tiny pause. Shen Ruolan’s smile didn’t move. Her eyes did. They went over him once, shoes to hair, and filed him somewhere.

“How loyal the department is. Come along, darling. The harbour board is waiting.”

Yu Jie let go of his hand last. A fraction late. Then she was gone across the room on her mother’s arm, back straight, not looking round.

He looked down. On his palm, next to the red line from the plate, there was a tiny smudge of purple ink. From her thumb.

Of course. Of course she’d still got ink on her. Under all that.

✦ ✦ ✦

The speeches started at nine. By the third one, Shen Guoqiang had reached quarterly growth.

Fang Hao: Status report.

Miles: Holding a plate.

Fang Hao: GOOD. Corner?

Miles: No corner.

Fang Hao: Proud of you. Has anyone mentioned boats

Miles: Eleven boats. One man. He can’t swim.

Fang Hao: Perfect. Stay till the end.

Fang Hao’s rules didn’t say anything about speeches. Miles checked twice. Then he put his plate down by the ice ship, which had lost most of its mast, and slipped out through the glass doors onto the terrace.

Cold. Real December cold, wet off the water. The harbour was black and silver, with ship lights crawling across it. On the far side stood the Shen Building, forty floors, with its name lit up in white at the top. You could see it from everywhere in the city. Including, it turned out, from here.

He leaned on the stone railing and looked at it.

Shen.

He’d counted nine men. He wished he hadn’t. He’d remember all nine for the rest of his life now. That was how his brain worked. It never once asked permission.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You never stay for speeches.”

Elowen. A pashmina round her shoulders, the same glass of water. She came and leaned on the railing a comfortable distance away and looked at the harbour too.

“You didn’t stay for them at the reunion either.”

“I gave one at the reunion.”

“You gave half of one. You dropped the clicker.”

“It was a slippery clicker.”

Behind them, through the glass, a very large shape stood just inside the doors. It didn’t come out. It stood with its back to the speeches and its face to the terrace.

“Your husband.”

“He’ll stay in. I made him promise.” She smiled at the water. “He’s very good at doing what I want. As long as he can see me while he does it.”

“He’s been glaring at me all night.”

“He’s been glaring at you for five years.” Fondly. “He knows it’s ridiculous. His words. It’s ridiculous. He’d lose a fight to a coat stand. Then he glared at you anyway.”

“I would lose a fight to a coat stand.”

“I know. I pointed that out too.”

The wind came up off the water. Neither of them said anything for a bit. It was easy. It always had been, with her. At school they’d both stayed late in the library, her because she didn’t want to go home, him because there was nowhere else he wanted to be. Opposite ends of one table, for hours. Not a word. He’d never understood, back then, what was at her home. He’d only understood that she was tired, and didn’t want anything from him, and that was restful.

“Three hundred white roses. At half three in the morning.”

“Aurelia.” Elowen rolled her eyes. “She’ll never let it go.”

“Will he really carry the buckets?”

“Every bucket. In a suit that costs more than the market.” She was smiling properly now. “The old women who sell peonies used to hide when he came. Now they make him tea.”

“Tea?”

“In little paper cups. He drinks it. He hates tea.”

“Then why does he drink it?”

“Because they made it for him.” She shrugged. “Nobody used to make him anything. Now a lot of old women do. He doesn’t know what to do with his face.”

It was out before he could stop it. “I know that feeling.”

Elowen gave him a long look. She didn’t say anything. She turned the glass in her fingers. “Last month he closed my shop for a week without telling me. Got someone to learn the whole order book. Booked a cabin in the mountains with a hot spring. All he did was look at me and go, You haven’t had a day off in ten years.”

“Had you?”

“No. I didn’t know you were allowed.” She laughed. “We’re going north in February. To see the lights. He’s read eleven books about them. He tells me facts at dinner. I’ve never been so well informed in my life.”

Miles looked at her.

He’d known Elowen at sixteen. Grey. Exhausted. Holding the whole world up with two thin arms. Her face had never once looked like this. Not about anything.

It came out like a result. “You’re happy.”

“Yes.” Like she’d checked it herself, more than once.

✦ ✦ ✦

After a while she put her glass down on the railing. “Five years ago. At the reunion. You came out on a balcony like this one and asked me a question. Do you remember?”

He remembered. She’d been alone at the railing in a red dress, with that enormous man by the wall inside. And under all the elegance she’d looked exactly like the tired girl in the library. So he’d asked the only thing he could think of.

“I asked if you were happy.”

“You did. And I didn’t know.” She looked at him. “Nobody had ever asked me. I had to stand there and think about it. That mattered, Miles. More than you’d guess.”

He hadn’t guessed. He’d gone home and been embarrassed for a week.

“So I’ve been waiting five years to give it back.” She turned to face him properly. Her back to the harbour. “Are you happy, Miles?”

✦ ✦ ✦

He opened his mouth.

Then he shut it again.

He stood on the cold terrace and thought about it properly. The way he’d think about a problem nobody had the answer to.

The staff flat. Books on every surface. One chair, one table. Three cacti on the windowsill. One egg in the fridge, until somebody filled it with congee. The same sandwich every day at his desk, because it took no decisions. Every seminar, the same seat. Leaving before the wine. Five years in office 412 with the door shut.

Until September.

“I don’t know.” His voice came out strange. “I’ve never… thought about it.”

Elowen waited. She was very good at waiting. She’d been practising since the library.

“I thought I was all right. That’s what I tell my sister. I’m all right.” He pushed his glasses up. “I’ve got my work. I’ve got the cactus. I don’t bother anyone and nobody bothers me and nobody gets hurt. I thought that was the same as happy. Close enough.”

“And now?”

He didn’t answer for a while. He watched a ferry cross the whole harbour first.

“Since September… I’ve been happy on Wednesdays.”

He heard himself. He went red. Even in the cold. Especially in the cold.

“Wednesdays.”

“From quarter to four. Till six. And a bit after six.” He was talking to the railing now. “And one Saturday at a café. For three hours. And when she brought oranges.”

“Oranges.”

“And the rest of the week I’m all right. Like before.” He swallowed. “Except it doesn’t feel close enough any more. Not at all. It feels like—it’s Thursday. All the time. It’s always Thursday.”

Elowen didn’t laugh. She looked like she might cry, actually, which was much worse.

“She’s twenty-two,” he heard himself say. “A final-year. In my department. Her family owns that.” He nodded across the water at forty white floors. “Her mother walked nine men past her tonight. I counted. And I stood by the food and held a plate. Because nobody in there’s allowed to know that—”

He stopped.

He’d never said it out loud. Not to Fang Hao. Not to Lan. He looked at the harbour, because he couldn’t have said it to a face.

“That we’re together. Since October.”

“Ah.” Not surprised. Not even slightly.

“Nobody knows. Nobody can. Not till she graduates. Or every mark she ever got would be mine instead of hers.” He gripped the cold stone. “So we made a rule. It’s a good rule.”

“It is a good rule.”

“Then why does it feel like I’m standing on the wrong side of the room?”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen looked back through the glass at her husband. He hadn’t moved. He wasn’t going to.

“I had a rule too. For years. Don’t want anything you can’t afford to lose.” She pulled the pashmina tighter. “I made it when I was seven. The night my mother died. I kept it till I was twenty-four.”

“What happened at twenty-four?”

“A man walked into my shop in the rain and bought every flower I had.” Her mouth twitched. “Then I spent a year trying to keep my rule. It nearly killed both of us.”

Miles looked at the shape behind the glass. Then back at her.

“I’m not going to make you break yours. Keep it. Keep it till June. You’d never forgive yourself if someone used you against her work.”

“No.”

“But, Miles.” She waited till he looked at her. “That rule’s for the people in there. Not for her. You’ve been hiding what you want since you were seventeen. Don’t let her think it’s her you’re hiding.”

He didn’t say anything. His throat had shut.

“Stand three metres off her all night. Fine. Hold your plate. But let her see your face.” Elowen tilted her head. “You’re a physicist. You know about light. It bends round heavy things. It doesn’t stop going where it was going.”

He stared at her.

“Did you just make a gravitational lensing metaphor?”

“I read your paper. The one from the reunion.” Not one bit embarrassed. “I read all of them. I didn’t understand most of it. I liked the pictures.”

He laughed.

He didn’t mean to. It came out of him on the cold terrace, loud and surprised. Twice in one month! Who was he?

Behind the glass, the very large shape of Zhao Zhendong went completely still.

✦ ✦ ✦

The terrace door opened.

Not Zhao. Someone smaller. A girl in a dawn-coloured dress, diamonds in her ears, one strand of hair loose against her cheek. The gold light of the ballroom behind her. She’d clearly come out to be alone. She found it full and stopped dead.

She looked from Miles, still half laughing, to Elowen beside him. Back to Miles. Something tightened in her face. Then it smoothed out flat.

“Sorry.” Her gala voice. Perfectly polite. “I didn’t know anyone was—”

“I was just going in.”

Elowen pushed off the railing. She walked to the door. As she passed, she stopped, leaned close, and said something in the girl’s ear that Miles couldn’t hear.

The girl went pink. All the way up to the loose strand.

Then Elowen went in, straight to the man waiting by the glass. He put his hand on the small of her back without looking at her. He was looking at the terrace. At Miles. He glared one last time, very thoroughly, and steered his wife back towards the ballroom.

The door swung shut.

Miles and Yu Jie were alone on the cold terrace above the harbour. Three metres apart. With her surname lit up white across the water.

“What did she say to you?”

Yu Jie looked at him. The dinner jacket. The bow tie Aurelia had fixed. His face, still red from laughing.

“She said, He just told me he’s happy on Wednesdays.”

Miles shut his eyes.

“That woman has been dangerous since she was sixteen.”

Yu Jie lasted about one second. Then the Perfect Jewel cracked straight down the middle, and she laughed so hard she had to hold on to the railing.

“Wednesdays,” she wheezed. “Wednesdays!”

“Please stop saying it.”

“You told Elowen Zhao—”

“I KNOW what I said to Elowen Zhao!”

She wiped her eyes with one knuckle. Careful of the make-up. Then she stopped laughing. Just like that.

“What else did you say to her?”

“Nothing.”

“Miles.”

He looked at the Shen Building. That was a mistake. It looked back.

“That we’re together.”

She went completely quiet.

“Out loud?”

“Mostly to the harbour,” he admitted. “She happened to be standing next to it.”

chapters.title: The Diplomat Her Mother Chose
chapters.desc: Lu Zhiyuan is a perfect match on paper: twenty-nine, five languages, a beautiful waltz. Yu Jie hates paper. Then he offers her a deal.
chapters.epigraph: “On paper, we’re perfect.” “I hate paper.” “Good. So do I. Shall we dance anyway?”
chapters.content:
They had four minutes on the terrace.

Afterwards Yu Jie counted them. The way she counted squares on the calendar. One at a time, so she could keep them.

Minute one, they laughed. She couldn’t stop, and then he couldn’t either. A waiter came out for a cigarette, took one look at the Shen heiress and the man in the new tuxedo, three metres apart and crying with laughter at nothing, and went straight back in again.

“We’ve scared the staff!”

“He’ll tell people.”

“He’ll tell people the heiress has gone mad on the terrace. Ma will say I’ve always been highly strung.”

“Have you?”

“Since birth. Ask anyone.”

Minute two, they didn’t say anything at all. The doors were glass. Four hundred people on the other side of them, and one of them was her mother. So they stood at the cold railing with three metres between them and looked at the harbour. It was the same quiet as 412 at five on a Wednesday, when the problem was done and nobody wanted to go. The wind came up off the water. Wet. Salty. She was in silk with bare arms. She didn’t shiver. The Perfect Jewel didn’t shiver in public. They’d trained that out of her at fourteen.

He noticed anyway. Of course he did. He walked round behind her, a long way behind, and came back to the railing on her other side. Between her and the open end of the terrace where the wind was coming from. Still three metres off. Exactly three. She saw him check it against the paving stones.

The wind dropped. Not much. Enough. “You moved.”

“I wanted to look at the other half of the harbour.”

“It’s the same harbour.”

“It’s a different angle.” He didn’t look at her. “Angles are very important. Ask a man who plays golf.”

She bit the inside of her cheek so hard it hurt.

Minute three, he moved again. Along the railing. One step, then another, into the shadow of a big stone urn at the end where the gold light from the doors gave up. She followed. Nobody behind the glass could have seen them there. Not if they’d pressed their noses to it. One metre. Then less.

“Your hair.”

Her hand went to the loose strand by her cheek.

“It came down.”

“No, it didn’t. You took a pin out.” He was looking at the water. “There’s a gap in the coil on the left. About two centimetres. Where the pin was.” A pause. “Sorry. I notice things. I can’t turn it off.”

“I know you can’t.”

“It’s very inconvenient.”

“I know. I did it for you, idiot.”

His hand found hers on the cold stone, in the dark under the urn. He didn’t take it carefully. He took it like it was his, like he’d been looking for it all night and was cross about how long it had taken. He laced his fingers through hers and held on so hard it nearly hurt. She held on back. Her bare arm was against his sleeve. She could feel him breathing.

Then he lifted her hand and turned it over and put his mouth to the inside of her wrist. Right on the pulse. And kept it there. Her knees did something unscientific.

Minute four. He lifted his head. He looked at her properly, finally, in what was left of the light. The diamonds. The dress. The strand of hair.

“You don’t look like yourself tonight.”

“Who do I look like?”

“Like a photograph of you. Taken by somebody who’s never met you.”

She opened her mouth—

“Yu Jie.”

The door. Her brother. Phone in his hand.

“Ma wants you. Now! Lu Zhiyuan’s here.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Shen Yu Ming was thirty-four. He ran the logistics side of Shen Holdings. He had never once in his whole life asked his little sister a single question about anything she studied. He looked at Miles with total polite indifference. Like Miles was a pillar.

“Dr. Wei, isn’t it? From the university. My mother says thank you for coming.” Then, to her: “Now, please.”

Miles had let go of her hand before the door was halfway open. He’d stepped out of the shadow of the urn into the light. He was standing straight in the dinner jacket, hands at his sides, face calm. Professional. Three metres again. He gave her a tiny nod. Go. It’s all right. I know.

She hated that nod. She’d remember it all night. She went.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lu Zhiyuan was waiting with her mother by the dance floor. He was perfect. She saw it straight away. Like seeing a proof is elegant before you’ve checked one line. Twenty-nine. Tall. Midnight-blue dinner jacket that actually fitted him. A calm, clever face with tired eyes. The eyes of a man who’d been to too many receptions in too many countries. Father a former ambassador. Him at the foreign ministry. Five languages. Her mother had told her all of it in the car. Three times. As a list.

“Zhiyuan.” Her mother was glowing. “My daughter. Yu Jie.”

He bowed slightly over her hand. Skipped the diamonds completely. Went straight to her face.

“Miss Shen. I’ve heard a great deal about you.”

“From my mother.”

“From your mother.” Perfectly straight face. “At length. In a list.”

She blinked at him. Was that a joke? From a man in a list?

Behind him the quartet started a waltz.

“Zhiyuan learned in Vienna,” said her mother. “Go on, both of you. Everybody’s watching.”

Everybody was. Her mother had made sure of it.

He held out his hand. Then, low, just for her:

“On paper, we’re perfect. You know that.”

“I hate paper.”

His tired eyes eased.

“Good. So do I.” The corner of his mouth went up. “Shall we dance anyway? It’ll make your mother very happy, and mine. And then they’ll both leave us alone for at least an hour.”

She took the hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

He did dance beautifully. Vienna had done its job. He held her at exactly the right distance, his hand light on her back, and steered her round the floor in long smooth turns like she weighed nothing at all.

“So.” Second turn. “Physics.”

She looked at him warily. “Yes.”

“What kind?”

She nearly fell over. What kind? Since when did anyone in this room ask what kind?

Nine men tonight. Twenty or thirty at every gala before that. Not one of them had ever asked what kind.

“Condensed matter. Topological phases in strained graphene.” It came out fast, like it always did when it was hers. “It’s carbon, one atom thick. If you stretch it the right way, the electrons act like there’s a magnetic field when there isn’t one. And at the edges weird things happen. Things that might be useful for computers one day. Or might not! That’s what I’m trying to find out.”

She stopped. She’d forgotten to do the little laugh. The pottery laugh.

He was looking at her with real interest.

“That’s the most interesting thing anyone’s said to me at a party in three years.” He turned her. “Last week a man in Brussels told me about his boat for forty minutes.”

“Was it a nice boat?!”

“I have no idea. I stopped listening at minute four. I nodded for thirty-six…”

She laughed. A real one. It got out before she could catch it.

“You see?” Long smooth turn. “We have something in common already. We both find these parties unbearable. And we’re both extremely good at hiding it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the third turn she saw Miles. He’d come back in. He was standing at the edge of the floor by the food, holding an empty plate, exactly where Fang Hao had told him to stand. Watching her dance with the man her mother had chosen.

His face was calm. He looked like he was listening to a seminar. Only someone who’d spent fifteen Wednesdays in 412 would have known his knuckles had gone white on that plate. She missed a step.

Lu Zhiyuan caught her so smoothly nobody saw. He brought her round in a long turn so her back was to the food table. Then he looked over her shoulder. At the place she’d been looking.

“Ah.”

Her stomach dropped through the floor.

“Oh! The lecturer. Thin, new tuxedo.” Conversational. “He’s been in that exact spot for ten minutes with an empty plate. He hasn’t taken his eyes off you once.” Another turn. “And you’ve looked at him four times since we started. I’m a diplomat. Counting things is half the job.”

“It’s NOT what you think.”

“I don’t think anything. I’m very good at not thinking things. That’s the other half of the job.”

She didn’t believe him for one second. So why wasn’t she scared of him? She should be. She wasn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

The waltz slowed. He bent his head a fraction.

“Miss Shen. May I make you an offer?”

“If it’s golf, I’ll scream!”

“It is very much not golf. I promise. I hate golf more than you do. I’ve been made to watch it.”

She looked up at him.

“My parents have been trying to marry me off for four years. Your mother’s been trying for two. They’ve decided we’re perfect. They won’t stop until something happens.” His hand was steady on her back. “So I’d like to propose an arrangement. Not a marriage. An arrangement.”

“What kind of arrangement?”

“We let them think it’s working. Dinner when they ask. We dance at galas. We’re seen together, very correctly, at a distance. You tell your mother I’m charming. I tell mine you’re brilliant.” A beat. “Which is true. And while they’re busy planning a wedding that’ll never happen, they stop parading us past everybody else.”

“It buys us time.”

“Both of us.”

She stared at him.

“Why would you want that? You’re perfect. You could marry anyone.”

For one second he looked a lot less calm.

“I could marry anyone my parents want. That’s not the same thing.” The music was ending. “Let’s just say there’s someone I’m not allowed to be seen with, Miss Shen. Not in rooms like this one. And I’m very tired of rooms like this one.”

Oh. Oh.

She looked at the tired eyes. He looked back. Neither of them said anything else about it. They didn’t need to. The waltz ended. He stepped back to exactly the right distance and bowed. Four hundred people clapped. At the edge of the floor her mother touched her diamonds like she might faint with joy.

“Think about it.” The reception smile was back. “I’m in no hurry. I’m very good at waiting. It’s the third half of the job.”

“That’s three halves.”

“Diplomacy is not an exact science.” He looked extremely pleased with himself about it.

And for the second time that night, she forgot to laugh like a hobby.

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles put the plate down. He’d watched the whole thing. The man in midnight blue, holding her at exactly the right distance. Leaning in to say something in her ear. Her laughing. Her real laugh. The one that came out of her nose a bit at the end. He’d thought he’d mind the distance. He didn’t. He minded the laugh. He minded that someone else had found the way to it in one waltz, when it had taken him a whole Wednesday and a bent oscillator.

That was stupid. He knew it was stupid. He minded anyway.

“You’re holding a plate again.”

Gao. Second glass of wine. Possibly third.

“Rule two.”

“Rule two my foot. Eat a prawn.” She followed his eyes to the dance floor and made a noise like a kettle coming off the boil. “The Lu boy. Ruolan’s been after that one since spring.”

“He dances well.”

“He was taught by an Austrian. Anyone can dance if they’re taught by an Austrian.” She drank. “Wei. Your face.”

“What about it?”

“It’s doing the thing. The Wednesday thing. In a ballroom.” She put her empty glass on his empty plate. “Fix it or go outside.”

“I’ve been outside.”

“Then go and be outside AGAIN!”

She stalked off. He stood there holding a plate with a wine glass on it, which was somehow worse than just a plate.

Rule three. Don’t leave.

He didn’t leave.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother bent to her ear as the quartet started something new. Glowing. Lips barely moving.

“The Lus are coming to New Year dinner. Both families. I’ve spoken to his mother.” Her hand closed on Yu Jie’s elbow. “Nothing official, of course. Not before you graduate. But I thought July. July is a lovely month for an engagement.”

Yu Jie didn’t move.

“July.”

“After the twentieth of June there’s really nothing to wait for, is there, darling? The degree will be finished. You’ll have had your little hobby.” A pat on the arm. “And jewels are meant to be worn.”

Across the room a thin man in a new tuxedo stood bolt upright with an empty plate. He couldn’t have heard. He was much too far away. But he looked at her face across four hundred people and frowned. Like he’d found an equation on it and didn’t like the answer.

She looked away first.

“Of course, Ma.” Perfect smile.

She went to say goodnight to Lu Zhiyuan. Correctly. At exactly the right distance. In the little silver bag on her wrist, her phone buzzed. A reminder. She’d made it in September and set it to go off once a month, and forgotten.

The end of the interval. 20 June, 16:00.

She left it in the bag. She knew exactly what it said.

July started eleven days later.

chapters.title: Miles Takes the Long Way Home
chapters.desc: One in the morning, no coat, silver shoes that hurt. He walks her home through the sleeping city, three metres apart under the streetlights and not at all along the old wall, and stops one block early on purpose.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re walking very slowly.” “I’m calculating the optimal route.” “It’s a straight line, Miles.” “Not if you do it properly.”
chapters.content:
He stayed.

He stayed through the auction, where a man paid an unthinkable sum for a weekend on a yacht he’d probably fall off. He stayed through dessert, which he didn’t eat, and coffee, which he didn’t drink.

Around half ten, Aurelia came past on her husband’s arm. Chen Si was putting her coat round her shoulders as they walked. She stopped. She leaned up and kissed Miles on both cheeks. Then, in a whisper you could have heard on the ferry:

“Wednesdays.”

“Aurelia—”

“I didn’t say anything! I’m going home.” She patted his bow tie. “It’s still perfect. You’re welcome.”

Chen Si nodded to him. Mild. “Goodnight, Dr. Wei.”

“Goodnight.”

“Don’t let her fix anything else. She’ll never stop.”

They went. At the doors they ran into Elowen and Zhao. Elowen was putting on a green coat that Zhao was holding open for her. The two women looked at each other. Something passed between them that Miles didn’t have the maths for.

Then Zhao turned his head. He left his wife buttoning her coat and walked back across the floor. Straight at Miles. People moved.

He stopped a metre away and looked down from a great height.

“She’s a good girl. The Shen one.”

Miles looked up at him.

“Yes.”

Flat dark eyes. Not one thing in them Miles could read. Was that a threat? It felt like a threat. It also felt, very slightly, like a man handing over a coat.

“Don’t be stupid about it.”

He walked away. At the door Elowen took his arm. She looked back over her shoulder at Miles and smiled.

Threatened or blessed? By that man it was probably the same thing.

Midnight. Gao came past with her old black dress and her handbag, on her way out. She looked at him, still standing by the dessert table, still holding a plate.

“Good,” she said. That was all. Then she left.

✦ ✦ ✦

He went down the hotel steps into the cold just before one.

Black cars with their engines running. Doormen whistling. He had his phone out for a taxi when he saw her.

She was standing to the side of the steps. In the shadow of a stone pillar. Alone. No coat. Bare arms wrapped round herself. The silver bag on her wrist. And she was holding her shoes, one high silver heel in each hand, standing on the freezing stone in her stockings.

He put his phone away. He went down to her, slowly, keeping out of the light.

“You’re not wearing any shoes.”

She looked round. She didn’t look surprised. She looked like she’d been waiting.

“They’re very beautiful shoes. Italian. My mother chose them.” She held one up. “They were designed by a man who’s never walked anywhere in his life. I can’t feel my toes. I don’t know if that’s the shoes or the cold.”

“Where’s your coat?”

“In the car. With my mother.” She nodded at a long dark car with its back door open and a driver beside it. “We’re going to the family house tonight. She wants to talk about July.”

He didn’t know what July was. He looked at the open door. The driver. Her bare feet on the stone.

“You don’t want to get in that car.”

Her eyes were very bright in the dark.

“No. I don’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He took off his jacket. On the way, without looking, he moved something from the inside pocket to his trouser pocket.

He didn’t think about it. The black one with the satin lapels, the one Lan had made him buy. He held it out at arm’s length. As far as his arm would go. So his hand wouldn’t get anywhere near her. He didn’t trust it to let go if it did.

She looked at it.

“That’s not professional distance.”

“It’s a metre and a half. My arm is very long.” He held it steady. “And you’re going to get hypothermia. Then I’ll have to explain to Gao why her best student in twenty years froze to death on the steps of the Harbour Hotel in front of me. And she’ll kill me. And then there’ll be two of us, and the department can’t afford it.”

She took the jacket.

It was much too big. The sleeves came down over her hands. She stood in it with her eyes shut. It was still warm from him.

Then she opened her eyes, got her phone out with a sleeve-covered hand, and typed.

“What are you telling her?”

“That I’m going back to the flat. Because I’m in the lab early tomorrow. Because my supervisor’s a monster.” She hit send. “Gao’s going to have to back that up.”

“That’s three times she’s lied for you.”

“I KNOW. I’m going to have to name a particle after her.”

Down at the bottom of the steps, a phone rang in the long dark car. After a moment the driver shut the back door. The car pulled away.

Yu Jie let out a long white breath. Then she opened the tiny bag and felt about in it.

“You didn’t eat. All night. I watched you hold an empty plate for six hours.” She pulled out one White Rabbit and held it out at the full length of her arm. “Here. Professional distance.”

He looked at it. Then he put his hand in his trouser pocket and took out two.

“I brought these. For you. In case.”

Something else came out with them. It bounced on the step. Rolled. Stopped against her bare toe.

A purple pen. With a plastic cat on the end and a question mark painted on its head.

They both looked down at it.

“That’s MY PEN.”

“…Yes.”

“You said you hadn’t SEEN it!”

“I’m a very bad liar.” He bent and picked it up before she could. “You never asked again.”

“Because you said you hadn’t SEEN it!” She stared at him. “Where’s it been?”

“My top drawer. With the sweets.” He put it back in his pocket. Calmly. Like that was a normal thing to do with stolen property. “Since September.”

“You’re not giving it back?”

“It’s on loan.”

“To WHO?”

He didn’t answer that. He held out the White Rabbits instead.

They swapped by the very ends of the twists of paper. He ate hers on the steps of the Harbour Hotel at one in the morning in his shirtsleeves. It was better than anything they’d served all night.

“Right.” She put his two in the jacket pocket. “I need to get home. I’ve got no shoes I can walk in, and no money, because my bag is the size of a biscuit. And I’ve never called a taxi by myself in my life.”

“Never?”

“There’s always a driver.”

He looked at the biscuit bag. The Italian shoes. His jacket, hanging off her shoulders.

“How far is your flat?”

“Two kilometres. Up the hill. By the east gate.”

“I’ll walk you.” He said it before he’d finished deciding. “Three metres away. Other side of the road, if you want. I’m not putting you in a taxi with a stranger in my jacket at one in the morning. Gao would kill me twice.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t walk on the other side of the road. He did walk three metres back. She kept having to stop and wait for him.

They went up through the old harbour streets. Past the closed shutters of the fish market. Past an all-night noodle stall, where three taxi drivers at a plastic table watched them go by with enormous interest. A man in a white shirt and a bow tie. A girl in a ball gown and a man’s dinner jacket, carrying her shoes.

One of the drivers raised his chopsticks. “Evening.”

“Evening!”

“Lovely night for it.”

“For what?” Miles asked, alarmed.

The driver just grinned at his noodles.

She’d put the shoes back on after the first hundred metres, because the pavement was too cold to bear. Now she was limping. He slowed down. Then he slowed down more. She turned round.

“You’re walking very slowly.”

“I’m calculating the optimal route.”

“It’s a straight line, Miles. Up the hill. I can see the university from here.”

“Not if you do it properly.” He pushed his glasses up. “Straight up the hill is steep. In those shoes it’s twenty-two minutes and probably a sprained ankle. If you go round by the park, along the old wall, it’s longer. Thirty-eight minutes.” He looked at the pavement. “But it’s flatter. For the shoes.”
