She didn’t say anything. She just turned left, towards the park.

Twenty metres later he said, to her back: “I could give you my shoes.”

She stopped and looked at his feet.

“I’ve got thicker skin. Statistically.” He thought about it. “But they’re a forty-four and you’re a thirty-seven. You’d be walking in two boats. I’ve modelled it. It isn’t better.”

She turned round very slowly under a streetlight.

“How do you know my shoe size?”

He looked at a lamppost with great interest.

“The label inside your trainers. You take them off under my desk when you’re thinking. Every Wednesday. About half an hour in.”

“I don’t do that.”

“You do. Left one first. Always.”

She turned and walked on. He couldn’t see her face. That was probably best for everyone.

✦ ✦ ✦

The old city wall ran along the top of the park, low and grey, with old iron lamps on it. Nobody there. Bare trees. Frost on the paths. The whole city below them. The harbour. The ships. Forty white floors with her name on top.

At the second lamp he looked back once. Empty path, all the way to the gate. No windows. Nothing but frost.

He closed the three metres in four steps and took her hand.

She stopped walking. She looked down at it. His warm hand round her frozen one. She didn’t say anything. She walked on with him, slower. Her limp got worse. On purpose. So she could lean on his arm.

“You said I looked like a photograph.” She wasn’t looking at him. “Of me. Taken by someone who’d never met me.”

“Sorry. That was rude.”

“It was the nicest thing anyone said to me all night.” She stopped under the lamp and turned round. “Nine men told me I looked beautiful. You told me I didn’t look like myself.” Her breath came out white. “You’re the only one in that whole room who knows what I actually look like.”

“Yellow.” He didn’t even have to think. “Biro on your trainers. Four pens in your hair. A cardigan with White Rabbit wrappers in the pocket. One lace undone, usually the left.” A pause. “Ink on your right hand. Middle finger. You never wash it all off.”

“You’re doing it again.” Unsteady. “The noticing.”

“I can’t stop. I told you.”

Then he came the last of the way under the lamp. He put his hands inside the jacket, on her waist, on the cold silk. And he kissed her.

She was shaking. With cold, and with the whole night coming off her at once. Nine men. A waltz. Her mother’s hand. He felt it. He pulled the jacket shut round both of them and held her against him so she could feel how warm he was, and kept kissing her till she stopped. Her shoes fell out of her hand onto the frost. She went up on her bare toes on the freezing path. He lifted her the last few centimetres so she wouldn’t have to.

When he put her down she was standing on his feet.

“Your shoes are on the ground,” he said, against her mouth.

“I know.”

He kissed her again before he bent to get them. Then he didn’t give them back. He carried them. One in each hand, by the straps, like a man carrying two very small, very expensive fish.

“I can carry my own shoes!”

“You’re carrying my jacket. That’s enough to be going on with.”

At the next lamp she got there first. She stopped, spun round and pulled him down by the front of his shirt before he could even check the path. At the one after, he did it, because it was there and nobody else was. At the third she put a hand flat on his chest.

“You’re going to make us late.”

“For what?”

She couldn’t think of anything. He took that as a yes.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the end of the wall a flight of old stone steps came down to the main road by the university. They could see the east gate from there. And the row of flats opposite it. The tall one at the end with the blue door.

There was a guard in a little lit box by the gate. On the corner opposite was a 24-hour shop, very bright, where two students in pyjamas were buying instant noodles and staring out of the window. One of them had his phone out. Probably texting. Probably nothing.

Miles stopped walking.

He stopped one block early, on the corner, in the dark between two streetlamps. Where nobody in the shop or the box could see him.

She stopped too. She looked at the blue door, two hundred metres away. Then at him.

“On purpose,” he said. He nodded at the bright windows. “There are people. Students. If they see you come home at this time in my jacket, with me—” He shook his head. “I won’t give anyone anything to say about you. Not before June.”

She looked from the shop to him. Shirtsleeves, bow tie, arms crossed against the cold, her shoes dangling from his fingers.

“You walked me the long way. Thirty-eight minutes.”

“Forty-one. You stopped under three lamps.”

“I stopped?”

“We stopped.” He held out her shoes. “Mostly you.”

“And now you’re stopping a block early. Because of the rule.”

“Because of you.”

He didn’t look up when he said it. His breath went white and was gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took the shoes. She started taking off his jacket.

She had one arm out, holding it towards him by the sleeve, when he took hold of the other end of the sleeve and pulled.

She came against him all at once. His arms were round her and his mouth was on hers before either of them could think about June, or the shop, or the guard. It wasn’t careful. A whole night of standing by the food with an empty plate came out of him. She met it with a whole night of nine men and a waltz. Her hands went into his hair and wrecked the haircut. His went under the jacket to the bare skin of her back above the dress. She gasped at how warm they were and pressed closer. He made a sound into her mouth she’d have liked to keep in a jar.

When he stopped, it was because he had to. Forehead against hers. Neither of them could breathe properly.

“I was trying to give it back,” she managed.

“Don’t.” He put her arm back into the sleeve himself, carefully, like part of an experiment, and pulled the jacket shut at the front. “It’s a long block. Give it back on Wednesday.”

“People will see it.”

“People will see a jacket.” He tucked the loose strand of hair behind her ear. Looked at it. Then took it out again and let it fall. “They won’t see me. I made sure.”

She looked at him in the dark.

“Thank you. For staying till the end.”

She walked the last block alone. Barefoot. Shoes in one hand. Dawn-coloured dress, a man’s black dinner jacket, the sleeves over her hands. Past the bright shop, where the students in pyjamas stared. Past the guard, who stared. In through the blue door.

She didn’t look back. He knew she wouldn’t. She was being careful for him.

He stood on the dark corner in his shirtsleeves until a light came on, on the sixth floor.

He walked home across the sleeping campus in his shirt. He didn’t notice the cold till his key was in the lock.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tao Tao was sitting up on the sofa in pyjamas and a face mask. Waiting.

She looked at Yu Jie. Barefoot. Shoes in hand. Pink cheeks. Shining eyes. A jacket that was not hers.

“You walked. From the harbour. In those?”

“He walked me.”

Tao Tao peeled off the face mask with one slow, dramatic pull.

“Where did he stop?”

“The corner. One block early. On purpose, so nobody’d see.” Yu Jie slid down onto the floor with her back against the sofa and put her face in her knees. “He went the long way. Along the wall. He said it was flatter. For the shoes. Tao Tao. Flatter. For the shoes.”

“Oh my god.”

“And he kissed me under the lamps.”

“How many lamps?”

“Three.” Into her knees. “And the corner.”

Tao Tao looked at the jacket. At Yu Jie’s wrecked hair. At her mouth.

“Five days to Christmas,” she said finally. “Ah Peng is going to lose so much money.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, in her room, still in the dress, she took the calendar down off the wall.

She found the square for the twentieth of December. She drew the purple atom. Then, beside it, very small: three lamps, a bit of wall, and a long curved line along the bottom of the square. The long way round.

A hundred and eighty-two squares left.

And then July.

She sat on her bed in her mother’s diamonds and his jacket. She took the diamonds off, one earring and then the other, and put them in their box and shut it.

She slept in the jacket. There were two White Rabbits in the pocket. She didn’t eat them. She held them.

chapters.title: The Thesis Draft Covered in Red Pen
chapters.desc: He’s not her supervisor. He reads it anyway, all night, and finds the flaw that would have sunk her in May. She fixes it her way, and that night she crosses the snowy sports ground to his flat.
chapters.epigraph: “This is beautiful. Now prove it.” — margin note, page 41, red ink
chapters.content:
Tao Tao: AH PENG PAID UP

Tao Tao: christmas is OVER and you did NOT give up

Tao Tao: hes very upset. he says he believed in human weakness

By the fifth of January even Ah Peng had stopped talking about Christmas. Miles was on his sofa in holey socks with cold tea when an email came in, near midnight. Not from her. From Gao. No message. Just a subject line. Read this. Properly. Notes by Friday. — G. And an attachment. ShenYJ_thesis_draft1.pdf. A hundred and eighteen pages.

He knew what he should do. Write back. I’m not her supervisor. You know why.

He opened it.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was good. He’d known it would be. But he hadn’t known it would be this good. On page nine there was a paragraph about electrons running along the edge of the carbon sheet so clear that he put the red pen down and sat looking at the snow for a while. She wrote the way she talked. Fast. Bright. Impatient. Every step there underneath.

He wrote in the margins. Small. Neat. Red. p.4: Define this before you use it. The committee will be tired. Be kind to them. p.12: Lovely. p.23: You’ve written “obviously” four times on this page. Nothing in physics is obvious. If it were, they wouldn’t pay us. p.31: Axis labels too small. Zhou is fifty-nine and refuses to wear his glasses. p.39: There’s a tiny atom drawn in the margin by Figure 6. Physically inaccurate. Please leave it in. p.41: This is beautiful. Now prove it.

Somewhere around four in the morning, on page sixty-seven, it went cold in his stomach.

He sat there with the pen over the page till the sky went grey.

✦ ✦ ✦

Knock on the wall. Like a cereal box.

“Are you dead?”

“No.” Into a stack of second-year homework. He’d fallen asleep on it.

“You sound dead.”

“I was reading.”

A pause. Then the door of 412 opened, and Fang Hao came in with a croissant and the face of a man who already knew.

“Reading what, Miles?”

“A hundred and eighteen pages. Gao sent it.”

“Her thesis?”

“I’m not her supervisor. I’m a second pair of eyes.”

“Your eyes look like they’ve been boiled.” Fang Hao sat on Bai Tianyu. “And?”

“It’s extraordinary.”

“And?”

“There’s a mistake. Page sixty-seven.” Miles sat up. His glasses were printed with somebody’s homework. “The boundary conditions. It works for her rectangle. It doesn’t work in general. And her whole conclusion needs it to work in general.”

Fang Hao stopped chewing.

“Will they fail her?”

“No. They’ll just take the big result away. Very promising. Good degree instead of a great one.” He rubbed his face. “And Zhou will find it before he’s finished his tea.”

“So you fixed it.”

“No.”

“No?”

“I wrote her three questions.”

“Miles. You can see how to fix it?”

“Three pages. One figure.”

“Then WHY—”

“Because then it’s mine.” It came out sharper than he meant. “One line in the margin and it stops being hers. Even a bit. I’m not doing that. She found my mistake in four seconds in September. She can find hers in four months.”

Fang Hao looked at him for a long time. Then he put half his croissant down on the desk in front of Miles. Which, for Fang Hao, was practically a medal.

“Eat that. And what did you write on the last page?”

“How do you know I wrote anything on the last page?”

“Because you’re you.”

Miles looked at the brown envelope by his elbow. Professor Gao. Nothing else on the front.

“Nothing important,” he said, and went red to the ears.

✦ ✦ ✦

Gao called Yu Jie in on Thursday. Not to the balcony. To her desk. No cigarette. Just the brown envelope and a cup of black tea. She pushed the envelope across.

“Your draft. I asked someone to read it. Not your supervisor. A second pair of eyes.” She sipped. “I do it for all my best students. First time I’ve had one back with two hundred and twelve notes.”

Yu Jie looked at the envelope. Professor Gao. In small neat letters she’d have known anywhere. Her hands weren’t steady opening it.

Define this before you use it. She turned a page. Lovely. Another. You’ve written “obviously” four times on this page. She put her hand over her mouth.

Gao drank her tea and didn’t hurry her. Yu Jie read the whole thing right there, page by page. An hour and twenty minutes. I had to stop and think here for twenty minutes. That’s a compliment. At page sixty-seven she stopped.

Stop. Look at this line again. It works for your rectangle. Does it work for any shape? What happens at a corner?

Page sixty-nine. I think you know how to fix this. I think you know better than I do. I’m giving you four months. (Zhou will ask about the boundary conditions. When he does, I want you to smile.)

What corner? Which line? She read the line they pointed at. Twice. Her stomach turned right over.

Gao watched her face go white. Then watched the fright go out of it and something fierce come in.

“Corners.” Barely out loud. “Oh, no. Corners.”

“Can you fix it?”

“I don’t know yet!” She was already grabbing a pen. Already writing on the back of page sixty-eight. “If the boundary isn’t fixed—if you let it—no. Wait. If you—” She stopped. Looked up. Her eyes were blazing. “He didn’t tell me how. He knows. He must know. He didn’t TELL me.”

“No. He didn’t.”

“He gave me four months.”

Gao just nodded.

I think you know better than I do. Yu Jie’s eyes filled. She blinked hard.

“He thinks I can do it.”

“So do I.” Gao finished her tea. “Go and do it. And Shen Yu Jie—read the last page somewhere private.”

She read it in a locked cubicle in the third-floor toilets, sitting on the lid. Your gap doesn’t close.

Yu Jie: he read my whole thesis. all night. 212 notes. he found a mistake that would have killed me in may and he DIDNT FIX IT. he says he thinks i can

Tao Tao: jie jie that is the most romantic thing ive ever heard and its about BOUNDARY CONDITIONS

She laughed out loud. Alone. In a toilet. Crying.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took her nineteen days. Two notebooks. Four approaches that didn’t work. On day eleven, one that almost worked, and she cried for an hour out of pure rage and ate an entire bag of White Rabbits and started again. She didn’t go up to the fourth floor once. She sent him one text.

Yu Jie: not yet

Radiator: All right.

That was it. That was all he sent for nineteen days. All right? What kind of man sends all right for nineteen days? She could have killed him. She could also have kissed him till he fell over. On day nineteen, at two in the morning, on her bedroom floor in pyjamas, she found it. Not his fix. She found that out later. A different one. Cleaner. It worked for any shape. It worked at the corners. And it did something neither of them had seen coming. It made the big claim bigger.

That Wednesday, quarter to four, she stuck a yellow sticky note to the side of his tea.

Corners. Fixed. Not your way. Mine. (Better.)

He read it twice. Then he looked up at her. Red jumper. Four pens in her hair. Ink on her middle finger. Holding out a clean stick of chalk.

“Show me.”

She showed him. Forty minutes. When she finished he stood with his arms folded in front of the board and didn’t say anything at all. She started to panic.

“Say something!”

“That’s better than mine.” Quiet. “That’s much better than mine.”

“I KNOW.” Her whole face was shining. “And you wrote lovely in my margins. Nine times. I counted.”

“Eleven.”

“Nine.”

“Two are on the back of page eighty-eight. I ran out of margin.” He pushed his glasses up. “I set myself a limit of ten before I started. I went over.”

Then he opened his top drawer. He took out something and stuck a sticky note round it and put it down on the desk in front of her.

The purple pen. The cat. The question mark. I think this is yours. It keeps asking questions.

She picked it up and held it in both hands like it was hot. Then she put it straight in her claw clip, where it belonged.

The door was propped open. Fang Hao was eating something crunchy through the wall. She couldn’t touch him. But she could see his face, everything he couldn’t say with the door open. Pride. And under it something so big and so careful it frightened her a bit. Bottom right corner of the board: 20 June, 16:00.

A hundred and forty-three squares left.

✦ ✦ ✦

Fang Hao’s door. Fang Hao’s footsteps. The lift. Miles crossed the office without a word, kicked the doorstop away, and shut the door. Then he turned round and picked her up.

She shrieked. He put his hand over her mouth, which made her laugh into his palm, and carried her the three steps to the board and kissed her up against her own proof. Her legs round him. The chalk ledge digging into her back. Her corners smudging all down her red jumper. He kissed her like he’d been waiting nineteen days. He had been.

“Mine was eleven pages.” Against her mouth. “Yours is four.”

“I know.”

“It’s the most beautiful thing anybody’s ever put on that board.”

She took his face in both chalky hands and looked at him. He meant it. The way he meant the speed of light.

“Your flat,” she said, “is nine minutes from here. You told me. You counted.”

He didn’t move.

“It’s a staff building.” His voice had dropped right down. “Dr. Xue from chemistry lives underneath. The walls are worse than these.”

“Then we’ll be quiet.”

She watched him think it through. Watched him decide.

“Go home first. Eat something. Then at nine, come across the sports ground, not up the road. The back door of the block doesn’t lock. Third floor.” He swallowed. “And if you change your mind on the way—any time—that’s all right. I’ll still be there. I’ll just make you tea.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She came across the dark sports ground at five to nine, with snow in her hair.

The door opened before she knocked. He’d been standing behind it. For twenty minutes, she found out later. The heating was broken again. She could see her breath by the window. He’d put both his lamps in the main room. He’d moved the books off the sofa. There was jasmine tea on the floor, going cold. And on the table, on two of the four white plates, were dumplings. From the place by the gate. Arranged in rows. Very straight rows.

She stopped in the doorway with her coat half off.

“You used the plates.”

“It seemed important.” His ears were scarlet. “I went out at six. I didn’t know what you’d—I got pork and chive. In case.”

She dropped her coat on the floor and walked into him. He caught her. He kissed her standing in the middle of the cold room with snow melting out of her hair and running down onto his hands. Slow at first. Then not slow at all. She pulled his jumper over his head and his glasses came with it. He swore. She’d never heard him swear. He laughed, found the glasses on the floor by feel, and put them on the bookshelf. Without them his eyes looked younger and much less careful.

He took her jumper off the same way. The red one, with her corners smudged down the back. Then he stood there holding it and looking at her in her vest in the lamplight, breath white, like he’d completely forgotten what came next.

“You’ll get cold.”

“Then do something about it.”

He folded the jumper and put it on the arm of the sofa. Folded. Because he was who he was. Then he put both hands on her bare arms, all goosebumps, and ran them slowly up to her shoulders and down again. Warming her. He bent his head and kissed her shoulder. The side of her neck. The place under her jaw. Until the goosebumps had nothing to do with the cold.

“I should tell you something,” he said into her neck. “Before.”

She waited.

“I’ve done this once.” He lifted his head. Red to the ears. Made himself keep going. “At university. With someone who didn’t matter, and I didn’t matter to her, and we both knew it. That’s all.” His hands were shaking on her arms. “I’ve never done it with anyone who did. I don’t know if I’ll be any good.”

She put both hands flat on his bare chest. His heart was going under them like something trying to get out.

“You read my whole thesis in one night. You found the one thing that was wrong. And you didn’t fix it, because you wanted me to.” She slid her hands up to his shoulders. “I think you’ll pay attention.”

He laughed. It cracked in the middle. Then he picked her up again and carried her into the other room.

✦ ✦ ✦

His bed was narrow and the sheets were freezing. She yelped when they touched her back.

“Sorry—sorry—”

“Don’t apologise to me, just get in!”

He pulled the one blanket over both of them and himself over her and held still, his weight on his elbows, his face an inch above hers. He let her get warm against him. He waited till she stopped shivering. Then he kissed her. For a long while that was all he did. Lying down was different. Slower. Deeper. The whole length of him against her under the blanket, the cold outside it and the heat in. His hand moving down her side in long strokes, ribs to hip and back, like he was learning a curve by heart. Every time his palm came up over her ribs she felt it low in her stomach. Like missing a stair in the dark.

She pulled the vest over her head and dropped it off the side of the bed. He stopped breathing. Then he bent and put his mouth to the hollow of her throat. Then lower. Slowly. Like there was no hurry anywhere in the world. She clapped a hand over her own mouth because of Dr. Xue. He felt her do it and lifted his head. His eyes had gone dark.

“All right?”

“Don’t you dare stop,” she said through her fingers.

He didn’t. He was slow and careful and thorough. The way he’d been with her thesis. Every time she made a sound he stopped to look at her face, like he was checking a result, and then did it again. Until she was gripping the iron bed frame over her head with one hand and biting her other wrist.

“You’re doing it on purpose.”

“I’m being thorough.”

“You’re being smug—”

“A bit,” he admitted, and did it again.

When she tugged at the rest of his clothes he helped, clumsy with hurry. They got tangled in the blanket. They both started laughing, foreheads together, shaking with it, trying to be quiet. The laughing went on. And then halfway through it turned into something else. Breathless and close. Nobody was laughing any more.

He stopped once more. Right at the edge. He held her face in both hands in the grey light off the snow.

“Are you sure? You can still say no. I mean it. I’ll make the tea.”

She pulled his head down till his mouth was on hers.

“Yes.”

After that there was no more asking. It was clumsy and close and nothing at all like films. His elbow slipped once and he nearly went off the side of the narrow bed. She grabbed his shoulders and didn’t let go again. She kept her eyes open. So did he. That was what she’d remember. How he watched her the whole time, like he didn’t want to miss one second. How, when her breath broke, he said her name. Just her name. Low and wrecked against her temple. And held her so tight she could feel his heart going in her own ribs. Afterwards it was quiet. Snow ticked on the window. The blanket was half on the floor. Nobody was cold.

“Was I—” he started, into her hair.

“Miles. If you ask me for a mark out of ten, I will push you off this bed.”

A pause.

“Nine?”

She pushed him off the bed. He landed on the floor with a thump. Somewhere underneath them, Dr. Xue from chemistry banged on his ceiling with a broom.

✦ ✦ ✦

Before five he walked her back across the sports ground in the dark. Before Dr. Xue went out running. Before the cleaners came. Her hand inside his in his coat pocket. The snow had stopped. Their footprints went across the white field side by side. By morning the groundsman would have walked all over them. Under the last tree he kissed her goodbye. Then again.

“You’ll have chalk on your jumper on Wednesday. Gao will ask.”

“I’ll tell her it was corners.”

That morning, on the calendar, beside the purple atom, she drew a tiny window with snow falling past it.

Then she drew two white plates.

chapters.title: Rumours in the Department Kitchen
chapters.desc: A photograph on the student forum. A man’s tuxedo jacket at half past one in the morning. Then Miles hears what the postdocs are saying, and finds out he has a temper after all.
chapters.epigraph: “The Shen girl’s buying her degree, and he’s getting paid in kind.” — Dr. Ren Bo, fourth-floor kitchen, Tuesday, 12:31 p.m.
chapters.content:
“Jie Jie. Don’t be angry.”

“Why would I be angry?”

Tao Tao turned her laptop round on the sofa. Saturday night. Instant noodles. A face mask she’d forgotten she was wearing.

“Because of this.”

The university forum. A post from Thursday. Which rich girl came home in a guy’s tux in the middle of the night before christmas?? (opposite the east gate) Underneath, a photo. Blurry, orange, taken through the window of a 24-hour shop by somebody holding noodles in the other hand. A girl in a long pale dress walking barefoot towards a blue door. Shoes in her hand. A man’s black dinner jacket, sleeves down over her hands.

No face. But the shoes. The dress. The blue door. Yu Jie’s noodles went cold in her lap.

“It’s been up since Thursday,” Tao Tao said fast. “Nobody cared! Eleven comments, all about the shoes. Somebody said they were fake. I nearly replied. I didn’t—”

“Tao Tao.”

“Then this morning someone posted this.”

She scrolled. A second photo. A door. Office 412, Hall of Science. Dr. M. Wei. The green cat in the box. And stuck all over it, from the autumn, dozens of pink sticky notes in round handwriting. Under it, one comment. the shen heiress is a physics final year. just saying. look at the jacket

“How many comments now?”

Tao Tao didn’t want to say.

“Tao Tao.”

“Two hundred and… something.” Small voice. “Some of them are… about your family. About what you’re for.” She shut the laptop halfway. “Don’t read them. I’ve read them. I’m going to find every single one of those people and put fungus in their shoes.”

Yu Jie sat very still. Her face had gone her Sunday face. Calm. Pleasant. Nothing.

“Does he know?”

“Does he even know the forum exists?”

He didn’t. Yu Jie was nearly sure. He didn’t use anything. He’d once asked her what a hashtag was for.

She got her phone out. Radiator. Her thumb hovered. Then she put it face down on the sofa.

“Don’t tell him.”

“Jie Jie—”

“He’ll blame himself. He’ll do something stupid and honest.” She swallowed. “It’ll die down. They get bored. Let him not know, just for a bit. Please.”

Tao Tao looked at her for a long moment. Then she opened the laptop again, went to a different tab, and started typing.

“What are you doing?”

“Closing the betting pool.” Grim. “Refunding everybody. It’s not funny any more.” She hit a key very hard. “Except Ah Peng. Ah Peng lost fair and square.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles didn’t know the forum existed. He didn’t know until Tuesday lunchtime, when he went into the fourth-floor kitchen to make his tea, the way he had every working day for five years. And stopped in the doorway.

Three people. Dr. Ren Bo and Wu Na, postdocs from theory. A PhD student he didn’t know well. They had a phone propped against the kettle. They didn’t see him. He was always quiet.

“—four hundred and sixty comments.” Wu Na. “Someone found the jacket on the shop’s website. Same lapels.”

Ren. Thirty-three. Clever. Ambitious. Applied for a lectureship two years ago and didn’t get it.

“Course it is. Everyone knew. Fang Hao had a scoreboard. And the Shen Foundation just gave this department forty million, and their daughter’s been hanging round Wei’s office every Wednesday like a cat.” He laughed. “Come on. It’s obvious. The Shen girl’s buying her degree, and he’s getting paid in kind.”

The PhD student laughed. Uncomfortably.

“Ren! Don’t.” But Wu Na was smiling.

“What? You think a twenty-two-year-old heiress climbs to the fourth floor every week for quantum mechanics?” He scrolled. “She’ll get a first. He’ll get a lab. Everyone wins. Except anyone in this building who actually earned—”

He looked up. He saw Miles in the doorway.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nobody in the Hall of Science had ever seen Miles Wei angry. Absent. Lost in a sum. Walking into chairs. Once, laughing in a seminar. If you’d asked, most of them would have said he didn’t have a temper at all. Too gentle. Too far away.

He wasn’t far away now. He walked in. He didn’t hurry. Past Wu Na, who stepped back. Past the PhD student, who looked at the floor. He stopped in front of Ren, about a metre off.

He was a head taller than Ren. Ren had never noticed. Nobody had. Miles always stood like he was trying to take up less room. He was standing up straight now.

“Say it again.”

Level. Quiet. His lecture voice, the one for important things.

Ren tried a smile. “Wei, come on. It was a joke, everyone’s—”

“Say it again. About her.”

Ren didn’t.

“No. I didn’t think you would.”

He looked at the phone against the kettle. The blurry orange girl. The shoes. His jacket.

“That’s a student who was cold at one in the morning. Her shoes hurt. Her coat was in a car she didn’t want to get into.”

“Look, I—”

“I gave her my jacket. I walked her home. I stopped a block away so nobody would see me with her. Nobody did. I went home alone.”

“I never said—”

“That’s what’s in the photograph. The rest of my life is none of your business, Dr. Ren. And none of it has anything to do with her degree.”

Ren’s face had gone red.

“But that’s not what I want to talk about.” Miles tilted his head. “You said she’s buying it.”

“I didn’t mean—”

“She’s the best student this department’s had in twenty years.” The way he’d say the speed of light was constant. “Gao says so. I say so. Two weeks ago she fixed a problem in her thesis. Her fix was better than the one I came up with after a whole night. Much better.”

“Wei—”

“In May she’ll defend it. Zhou will ask her about the boundary conditions. She’ll answer him.” A beat. “She’ll be extraordinary.”

He took one step closer. Ren took one step back. Into the fridge.

“You didn’t get the lectureship two years ago because Zhou asked you about boundary conditions in your interview. You didn’t know the answer. You pretended you did.” Very calm. “I know, because I was there. Junior member of the panel. You talked for four minutes. It was all wrong. Everyone knew.”

Ren went from red to white.

“She has never pretended to know something she doesn’t. Not once. Not to me. Not to a famous man from the capital in front of thirty people. She’d rather be wrong in public than pretend.” He looked down at him. “That’s why she’s better than you. Not her money. Her.”

He took his mug off the drying rack. WORLD’S OKAYEST SON.

“If I hear you say anything about her again—here or anywhere—I won’t say a word to you. I’ll go straight to Zhou and the harassment office and tell them exactly what you said. Word for word. Paid in kind.” He went to the door. “I’ve got a very good memory. You know I have.”

Then he stopped. Turned round.

“And it isn’t forty million. It’s thirty-eight. If you’re going to spread rumours in a physics department, at least get the numbers right.”

He went out.

The kettle clicked off. Nobody touched it.

“Did he just…” The PhD student, faintly.

“Yes.”

“Is he allowed to—”

“Yes.” Wu Na was staring at the door. Then at Ren. She’d stopped smiling. “Ren. You absolute idiot.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Fang Hao was in the corridor holding a croissant. He’d heard everything. The cardboard walls went all the way down the fourth floor.

He looked at Miles’s face. Perfectly calm. Then at Miles’s hands. They were shaking so badly the empty mug was rattling.

“Office. Now.”

He took the mug off him, steered him into 412, shut the door, and sat him down. Then he went next door to 413. Miles heard tape ripping.

Fang Hao came back with the scoreboard. The one from October, with the Y column and the P column and Cu-Te 9/10 in red. He folded it in half. Then in half again. Then he put it in his pocket.

“That’s on me.” He didn’t sit. “The scoreboard. I thought it was funny. I thought—” He stopped. “I didn’t think.”

“It wasn’t you.” Miles’s hands were flat on the desk. He was looking at them. “It was the jacket. I should never have given her the jacket.”

“She’d have FROZEN!”

“I should have called her a taxi. Called her driver back. I should’ve—” He stopped. “I stopped a block away, Hao. I was careful. I was so careful. And a boy buying noodles took a photo, and now four hundred and sixty people are saying she’s—”

He couldn’t finish it.

Fang Hao looked at his hands. Then at the bottom corner of the board. 20 June, 16:00.

“Miles. Is there something else? Something I—no.” He held the croissant up like a stop sign. “Don’t tell me. If Zhou asks, I want to look him in the eye and say I don’t know. I’m a terrible liar. You’re worse.”

Miles shut his mouth.

He thought about the corner between two streetlamps. Her arm halfway out of a sleeve. Snow on a window. Two white plates. He didn’t say anything. His ears said all of it.

“Right.” Fang Hao nodded slowly. “I didn’t see that either.”

“Have you seen the comments?”

“Don’t.”

“Hao.”

“Some are about you. Most are about her. About her family. About what she’s for.” He looked away. “They’re kids. It’s a forum. They’ll be bored in a week.”

“She’ll have seen it.”

Fang Hao didn’t say anything to that.

“She’ll have seen it. Days ago, probably. And she didn’t tell me.” Miles put his face in his hands. “Why didn’t she tell me?”

Fang Hao pointed down the corridor at the kitchen. “Because she knew you’d do something like that.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Office hours. Tuesday. Half past three. A knock.

It wasn’t a second-year. It was Professor Zhou. Cardigan. Reading glasses in his hand, because he refused to put them on. He looked at Miles. At Fang Hao on the corner of the desk. At the tiny round writing in the bottom corner of the board.

“Dr. Fang. Would you give us a moment?”

Fang Hao went. Very fast. Zhou shut the door and sat in the chair where she always sat. He put his glasses on the desk and folded his hands.

“I’ve had three emails. A parent of a second-year, about the forum. The student paper, asking for a comment. And Dr. Ren, twenty minutes ago, saying you threatened him in the kitchen.”

“I didn’t threaten him. I said I’d report him for harassment if he did it again.” Miles kept his hands flat. “That’s not a threat. That’s a procedure.”

The corner of Zhou’s mouth twitched.

“That’s more or less what Wu Na said. She came to see me at one. She said she was ashamed of herself.” He paused. “She told me what Ren said. Word for word.”

Miles said nothing.

“I’m not here about Ren. I’ll deal with Ren. I’m here about you.” Zhou leaned forward. “There’s no complaint. Nothing to investigate. A photo of a girl in a jacket and a door with sticky notes on it isn’t misconduct. I want to be very clear.”

“But.”

“But.” Zhou took a folded sheet out of his cardigan. “In September I assigned this year’s thesis panels. Supervisor plus two internal examiners.” He put it on the desk. “I put you on hers. Second examiner. Her methods are from your field. You’re the best person in the building to examine it.”

Miles looked at the paper. SHEN Yu Jie. Supervisor: Prof. Gao M. Internal Examiners: Prof. Zhou L., Dr. Wei M.

His name. Second slot. Typed in September. He’d forgotten. Completely. The list had come round before the second Wednesday. He’d read the whole university code on a Sunday night in October, all forty pages. He’d told her on the back stairs it was fine, because he didn’t mark anything of hers.

He’d been on her panel the whole time. It had been in his inbox since the week before she knocked. Cold went right through him. Bones first.

“I’ll have to answer the paper. And that parent. Maybe the dean.”

“Maybe Mrs. Shen.”

“Who sits on the university council. Yes.” Zhou watched him over his hands. “When I do, Miles, I need to be able to say nobody with a personal interest in this student will have any part in her grade. So I have to ask you a question. Think before you answer.”

Miles already knew the question. He looked at the board. 20 June, 16:00. He looked at his own name on the paper.

“You don’t have to ask it.”

Zhou’s eyebrows went up.

“I’ll write it down. Tonight. Properly.” He pushed his glasses up. His hand had stopped shaking. “You’ll have it on your desk in the morning.”

✦ ✦ ✦

His phone went at eleven that night. He was at his one table with graph paper and a pencil and four crossed-out tries.

Wednesday: fang hao says you yelled at a postdoc

Miles: I didn’t yell.

Wednesday: he says you were TERRIFYING

Miles: I was accurate.

Wednesday: miles

Wednesday: i saw it on saturday. the forum. i didnt tell you

Wednesday: im sorry

Miles: I know why you didn’t.

Wednesday: are you angry

Miles: Not with you.

Wednesday: what are you doing

He looked at the graph paper. Draft five. Half a page. He typed I love you. He looked at it for a long time. His thumb over the send button.

Not like this. Not by text, at eleven at night, because he’d been caught. Not before he’d said it to her face somewhere he was allowed to. He deleted it. Letter by letter.

Miles: Writing something.

Wednesday: what

Miles: Go to sleep. Tomorrow’s Wednesday.

He turned the phone face down and picked up the pencil.

Draft six.

chapters.title: Miles Recuses Himself
chapters.desc: One page, written at his one table between midnight and four. The most honest document in the history of the department. Then the Wednesday rules change, and Fang Hao brings croissants.
chapters.epigraph: “I have a personal interest in this student. I wish to state clearly what it is, so that nobody else has to guess.” — Dr. M. Wei, letter to the Head of Department
chapters.content:
Eleven drafts.

The first one was four lines. I wish to withdraw from the examining panel of SHEN Yu Jie due to a potential conflict of interest. He read it back. It looked like a lie. Nothing in it was false. It was hiding something, and he’d never been able to stand a document that hid things. The second was three pages. He tore it up. The fifth had the word regrettably in it four times. He tore that up too.

By the sixth he’d stopped trying to sound like a university form. By the ninth he’d stopped being scared of it. By the eleventh, with the sky outside going from black to grey, it was one page and it was true. He typed it. Printed it. Signed it. Rode to the Hall of Science in the dark and slid it under Zhou’s door before anyone else was in the building. So he couldn’t change his mind.

✦ ✦ ✦

Professor Zhou, I am withdrawing from the examining panel for Shen Yu Jie’s thesis, from today. I should have done this earlier. I am sorry I did not. I have a personal interest in this student. I wish to state clearly what it is, so that nobody else has to guess. Since September she has come to my office on Wednesdays to talk about physics. She is the most gifted student I have taught. In October I asked her if she would consider a relationship with me. She said yes. We have been in one since. I love her. I have not said so to her yet. I know it is strange to say it first to the Head of Department. You asked me to think carefully. That is part of the answer.

It was my idea. I asked first. I decided we would keep it private until she graduates, so nobody could say her work had been helped by it. I read the university code before I asked her. I did not remember that you had put me on her panel in September. That is my failure. I should have checked. The photograph was taken on 20 December. I walked her home from the gala because she had no coat. I stopped a street away. I went home alone. I cannot be a fair examiner of her work. I should not be seen to be one. Her work is extraordinary. It deserves a panel nobody can doubt.

In January, at Professor Gao’s request, I read a draft and gave written comments to Professor Gao, not to the student. A copy is attached. They contain questions, not answers. Miss Shen solved the main problem herself, by a better method than mine. I would be grateful if that were noted. I have not discussed this letter with her. I will have to answer to her for that. If anything further is needed about my own conduct, I will cooperate. I only ask that nothing here is used in any way that harms her. None of this is her fault. If there is fault, it is mine.

Miles Wei

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhou read it standing at his desk with his reading glasses on. He only wore them when nobody was looking. He read it twice. Then he sat down, took the glasses off, and looked at the car park for a while.

Then he rang Gao.

“Come to my office. Don’t smoke on the way.”

She came three minutes later, smelling of smoke.

He handed her the letter without a word. She read it by the window. He’d known Gao Meiling for twenty-six years. He watched her get to I love her, and her face went soft for about two seconds. Then she put it back how it was.

“That idiot.”

“Yes.”

“That honest, stupid, beautiful idiot.” She dropped it on his desk. “He’s put it in writing, Lin! On the record! I asked first. I love her. He’s handed you his head on a plate. If anyone wanted trouble—if Ruolan Shen wanted trouble—”

“I know.”

“Four words. Conflict of interest. Nobody would’ve asked!”

“I know.” Zhou picked the letter up again. “Read it again, Meiling. Read who he’s protecting.”

She read it again. Her mouth went tight.

“He’s made himself the target. So there’s nothing left to aim at her.”

“Yes. I think that’s exactly what he’s done.” Zhou put it in a folder. “Thirty-four years. Most honest document anyone’s ever handed me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He called Miles in at eleven. Miles hadn’t slept. He sat in front of Zhou’s desk with his hands on his knees and his face calm. Like a man who’d prepared for the worst and was waiting to hear how bad.

“I’ve read your letter.”

“Yes.”

“I’ve accepted your withdrawal. Dr. Fang replaces you. He’s qualified and he has no personal interest. Except in croissants.” Zhou folded his hands. “I also rang legal this morning. No names. General terms. Their view is that nothing’s been breached that can’t be fixed. A lecturer in a relationship with an adult student, who declares it and withdraws the moment he finds out he’s on her panel, is doing what the policy asks.” A pause. “They’d have liked you to check sooner.”

“So would I.”

Miles’s shoulders came down.

“However.”

His shoulders went straight back up.

“Legal also say Wednesdays continue only if they’re clearly academic. Clearly supervised. Clearly visible.” Zhou looked at him. “So from this afternoon, Wednesdays move out of 412. Third-floor seminar room. The one with glass walls. Door open.”

“Yes.”

“Physics only.”

“Yes.”

He didn’t say it’s always been physics. He’d written a letter at four in the morning so he’d never have to say anything like that to this man.

“Miles.” Zhou’s voice went gentler. “Your private life is your own. Nobody will hear about that letter from me. But I was at that seminar in December. I heard you laugh. I’ve seen the corner of your board.” A pause. “I walk past your door to the lift. I read the sticky notes. Cu-Te was quite good.”

Miles went red to the collar.

“Physics only. And a third person present.”

“A third—”

The door opened. No knock. Fang Hao in the doorway with a paper bag, looking radiantly innocent.

“I volunteered! I’ll bring croissants.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Gao told Yu Jie at one o’clock. On the balcony. In the cold. Not everything. She didn’t show her the letter. Dr. Wei had withdrawn from her panel, of his own accord. Dr. Fang would replace him. The photos had been reported and taken down. Dr. Ren had been spoken to and would be apologising to Wu Na, who’d made a formal complaint about him. And Wednesdays, from today, were in the glass room on the third floor. Door open. Fang Hao present.

Yu Jie sat on the plastic chair and listened to all of it without a word. Withdrawn. Of his own accord. When? Why hadn’t he said?

“Why did he withdraw?”

Gao smoked for a bit.

“Because he wanted there to be no question that your marks are yours.”

“That’s not all. Is it.”

Gao looked at her. Sharp black eyes. They didn’t move.

“No.”

“There was a letter. There’s always a letter with him. He writes things down.” Yu Jie’s hands were tight on her knees. “What did he say?”

“That none of it was your fault. That if there was fault, it was his.” Gao tapped ash over the rail. “And some other things. Not mine to tell. You’ll have to ask him yourself.” She looked at the car park. “Tonight, I imagine. Wherever it is you two go that I’ve decided not to know about.”

Yu Jie went scarlet to the roots of her hair.

“Don’t. I’m fifty-eight. I was young once. In 1987. For about a fortnight.”

“He put it on the record.” Yu Jie’s voice cracked. “Didn’t he? So if anyone ever said anything about me, about my degree, about my family’s money, there’d already be a piece of paper in a file saying it was him.” She wiped her face, furious. “He made himself the one they’d blame. Without asking me.”

Gao didn’t answer. She stubbed the cigarette out on the rail and lit another.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first glass Wednesday was that same afternoon. The room was cold and bright. A long white table. A whiteboard instead of a chalkboard. Three glass walls onto the corridor, where people walked past and looked in.

He was standing at the whiteboard holding a marker like it had insulted his mother.

“I don’t like these.” That was hello. “They squeak. They run out. They smell of chemicals. I asked facilities for a chalkboard. They said it’s the twenty-first century.” He uncapped it. Sniffed it. Recapped it. “Chalk is still better.”

At the far end of the table Fang Hao had his feet up on a chair, marking in front of him, croissants at his elbow. He waved.

“Don’t mind me! I’m furniture. Very well-fed furniture. Proceed with the physics.”

She looked at Miles. Three metres away. Glass walls. Open door. Fang Hao chewing. He looked back.

You wrote a letter. You put your name on a piece of paper so nobody could put mine on one. What did you SAY?

She didn’t say any of it. She sat down, took out her notebook, and pulled the purple pen out of her claw clip. The cat. The question mark.

“I want to do corners again. I think there’s a second paper in it.”

For a second the calm on his face slipped.

“Show me.”

“Ninety-degree corners first,” he said. “Then any angle.”

“Any angle’s the whole point—”

“Ninety first. Walk before you run.”

“I can run!”

“I’ve seen you run. You fell over a cable in the lab in October.”

“That was the cable’s fault!”

At the end of the table Fang Hao looked up. “Are you two even speaking the same language?”

“Yes,” they both said.

Fang Hao pretended to mark for two hours after that. He didn’t turn a single page. Was he even holding it the right way up? Hard to say.

Halfway through, two second-years stopped in the corridor and pressed their noses to the glass. Yu Jie looked up. She took the squeaking marker out of Miles’s hand. She wrote across the top of the whiteboard in letters as tall as her hand: THIS IS PHYSICS. KEEP WALKING. Then she stared at them until they did.

She gave him back the marker and went on about corners as if nobody had been there at all. At the end she packed up. On her way out she stopped and put a little cardboard box down on the corner of the table, at arm’s length from him. Slid it the last few centimetres with one finger.

White chalk. Twelve sticks. The old-fashioned kind, from the second-year teaching lab.

“It won’t work on the whiteboard.”

“I know. It isn’t for the whiteboard.” She hitched her bag up. “It’s so you’ve got something in your pocket that doesn’t squeak.”

She went out through the open glass door. He stood looking at the box so long Fang Hao had to cough.

✦ ✦ ✦

Fang Hao waited till she’d gone. “She knows.”

Miles was wiping the board. It took ages. The marker never came off properly. There was always a grey ghost of everything left behind.

“Knows what?”

“There was a letter. Gao told her that much. Not what was in it.” Fang Hao brushed crumbs off his marking. “She looked at you for two hours like she wanted to climb over this table.”

“She didn’t, though.”

“No. She did corners instead.” Fang Hao stood up. “I’ve watched a lot of people fall in love in this building, Miles. Postdocs. Lecturers. One very embarrassing visiting professor from Hamburg.” He picked up his marking. “I’ve never seen two people work this hard at looking like they haven’t.”

He went to the door. Stopped.

“The second paper’s going to be very good, by the way. I understood about a third of it. Most romantic third of anything I’ve ever sat through.”

In the bottom right corner of the whiteboard, tiny, in marker, somebody had written 20 June, 16:00. Miles didn’t remember doing it.

He didn’t wipe it off.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came across the sports ground at ten that night, the way she’d learned to. He opened the door before she knocked.

She didn’t take her coat off. She stood in the middle of the room under the one lamp with her hands in her pockets.

“You wrote a letter.”

“Yes.”

“About us.”

“About me.” He leaned back against the door. “I wrote that I asked first. My idea. My rule. My mistake about the panel. I didn’t give him one thing you did. I put my name on all of it.” He swallowed. “Zhou’s got it in a folder. Gao’s read it. Nobody else will.”

“You didn’t tell me first.”

“No.” He didn’t look away. “I should have. I was scared you’d stop me.”

“I WOULD have stopped you!”

“I know. That’s why.”

She stood there with her jaw tight. The shadows under his eyes from four in the morning. The WORLD’S OKAYEST SON mug on the table with cold tea in it. The man who’d walked into Zhou’s office and handed over his own head so there’d be nothing left to aim at hers.

Then she crossed the room in three steps, grabbed two fistfuls of his jumper, and kissed him so hard his head went back against the door. It was angry. It was grateful. She didn’t know which was winning. He let her. He stood against the door with his hands open at his sides and let her do it. Until she bit his bottom lip, not gently either. He made a rough sound. His hands came up and closed on her hips and dragged her in. Then he was kissing her back, and her coat was on the floor, and she didn’t remember taking it off.

When she finally let him breathe, his glasses were on top of his head and she was standing on his feet.

“Gao said there were other things.” Against his mouth. “In the letter. Things that weren’t hers to tell.”

He stopped breathing.

“There’s one.” Barely audible. “I wrote down something I haven’t said to you yet. I said it to the Head of Department first. That’s the wrong order. I’m not making it worse by saying it against a door because I got caught.” His thumb moved on her hip. “I’ll say it properly. When I can say it anywhere.”

She looked up at him. She knew what it was. It was all over his face. He probably knew she could see it.

“Then I’ll wait.” She pulled his glasses down off his head and put them back on his nose. Crooked. “I’m very good at waiting. I’ve got a calendar.”

He kissed her again. Slower this time. Like he was saying it another way.

She let him. She let him for quite a long time. Then she took his hand and walked him backwards towards the other room.

“Wednesday’s over. Physics only was this afternoon.”

chapters.title: She Cries in a Stairwell
chapters.desc: New Year’s Eve dinner at the museum, with the Lus at the table and the forum on her mother’s phone. Not because of him. Because of her mother.
chapters.epigraph: “I let you have your little hobby. I let you have your little man. Now the hobby is over.” — Shen Ruolan
chapters.content:
Tao Tao held up both hands. “Eleven courses. Say it with me.”

“Eleven courses.”

“And you’ll survive all of them.”

“I’ll survive all of them.”

“And then you’ll come home and eat instant noodles with me like a person.”

“Like a person.” Yu Jie zipped her bag. “Tao Tao, I’ve done twenty-two of these. I know the menu better than the cook.”

She did. Every New Year’s Eve at the Shen house was the same. Seven o’clock. The big dining room. The cold plates arranged as a phoenix, from a magazine. Soup. The fish, whole, which you must never turn over, or a boat would sink and the business would fail. Much later, dumplings. Folded by the cook, never by the family. Folding dumplings, her mother said, is for people who can’t afford a cook. Yu Jie had folded dumplings once. At Tao Tao’s family’s flat, in first year. Tao Tao’s grandmother had shown her how to pleat the edge with her thumbs. She’d been so happy she nearly cried. The grandmother gave her a red envelope with a twenty in it. She still had it in her desk drawer. Never spent.

“The Lus are coming this year,” she said.

Tao Tao’s face fell. “The diplomat?”

“And his parents.”

“Oh, Jie Jie.”

“It’s fine. He’s on my side.” She picked up the bag. “Mostly.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The Lus came at half six. His father had been an ambassador three times over and sat at the table like it was a treaty. His mother wore jade and smiled at Yu Jie with the nervous hope of a woman who’d been trying to marry off her son for four years. Lu Zhiyuan was charming to everybody. Trade with her father. Shipping with her brother. He praised her mother’s phoenix. He sat next to Yu Jie at exactly the right distance and turned to her at exactly the right moments. And under the table, during the fish, he tipped his phone on his knee so she could see the screen.

Lu Zhiyuan: Course 3 of 11. Courage. Halfway to the dumplings.

She nearly laughed. She turned it into a cough. Her mother looked at her across the table. Sharp.

“Are you unwell, darling?”

“Fish bone, Ma.”

“There are no bones in this fish. Cook takes them out.”

“…Then I must have imagined it.”

Lu Zhiyuan turned to her mother with a smile so perfect it could have been on a stamp. “Mrs. Shen, this phoenix. Did you design it yourself?”

Her mother lit up. Yu Jie breathed again.

✦ ✦ ✦

It happened between the eighth course and the ninth. The staff were clearing plates. Her father had gone to take a call. Her brother was on his phone. The Lus were at the window admiring the harbour. Her mother got up, came round the table, put a hand on Yu Jie’s elbow and smiled.

“Come and help me with something, darling.”

She took her down the corridor into the little sitting room with the glass cabinets, and shut the door. Her mother’s collection. Porcelain. Jade. Two vases nobody could breathe near. And on the middle shelf, under its own tiny light, one pearl on a silver stand. Her grandmother had given it to her mother on her wedding day. The Perfect Jewel. That was where the name came from. Yu Jie had heard the story every New Year since she was four. Her mother let go of her elbow. She took out her phone, unlocked it, and held it up. The forum. The blurry orange photo. The girl. The shoes. The jacket with its sleeves over her hands. And under it, 412. Dr. M. Wei. The pink sticky notes. The photos had come down a week ago. Her mother had screenshots.

“An old friend sent me these.” Pleasant. “On Monday. She thought I should know.” She tilted her head. “Do you know how many people at that gala have seen these, Yu Jie? How many of my friends? Do you know what they’re saying about this family?”

Yu Jie didn’t answer.

“The lecturer. The thin one. I invited him. I wrote to him myself.” The smile didn’t move at all. “And he put my daughter in his jacket and walked her home at one in the morning, and the whole city’s seen it.”

“He gave me his jacket because I was cold.” Her voice was steady. She wasn’t going to say nothing happened. Not about him. Never about him. “He walked me home because I had no coat. He stopped a whole block away. He didn’t—”

“I don’t care what happened.”

Her mother said it quite gently.

“I don’t care what happened, and I don’t care what didn’t. I care what it looks like. I’ve been teaching you that since you were four.”

“Ma, please—”

She put the phone away. “I spoke to Professor Zhou on Friday. He told me the lecturer has withdrawn from your examining panel. Very polite. He called it a formality.” A tiny laugh. “People don’t withdraw from things as a formality, darling.”

“Ma—”

“And Professor Gao. Gao assures me you’re in her laboratory every Wednesday until seven. With a great many witnesses.” Her mother looked at her. “I’ve decided to believe her. That’s what one does with staff.”

Yu Jie’s nails went into her palms.

“I let you have your little hobby.” Her mother stepped closer. Expensive perfume. Very cold. “That university instead of the one I chose. That flat, with that girl who studies fungus. Those terrible shoes.”

“Ma—”

“I let you have your little man. Now the hobby is over.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Jie stood in front of the glass cabinet and didn’t move. Her nails were in her palms. Four crescents on each hand. If she pressed hard enough, the pain was something else to think about. Her heart was so loud she could hear it. A thin high rushing, like the sea in a shell. The little light over the pearl was humming. Twenty-two years. Had it always hummed?

“The Lus have agreed. The engagement will be announced at the end of June. The week after your graduation. Two hundred guests.”

“You can’t—”

Her mother reached out and tucked the loose strand of hair behind Yu Jie’s ear. The one she always let fall now. “You’ll finish your degree. It would look strange if you didn’t. And then you’ll stop. Zhiyuan’s being posted abroad. Geneva, possibly. You’ll go with him.” She smoothed the strand flat. “It’s a beautiful life, darling. It’s the life you were made for.”

“I’m not a pearl.”

Her mother looked faintly surprised.

“Of course you are. You always have been.” She turned to the door. “I made you one.”

She opened it.

“Come back to the table. The dumplings are coming. And smile. Zhiyuan’s mother is watching.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She smiled. She smiled through the dumplings and the whole steamed chicken and the sweet soup with the rice balls. At midnight the fireworks went up over the harbour and she stood at the big window with both families and smiled at them. When Lu Zhiyuan’s mother took her hand and pressed a red envelope into it with tears in her eyes and said, “We’re so happy,” she smiled. Under the table, during the sweet soup, Lu Zhiyuan had looked at her face once. Then he’d gone quiet.

Lu Zhiyuan: What did she say to you?

She didn’t answer.

No tears that night, in the canopy bed with the dolls in glass cases. None through four days of visits and red envelopes. On the fourth day she got back to the flat. Tao Tao took one look at her.

“What happened.”

“Nothing.”

“That’s your Ma voice. You’re using your Ma voice on me.”

“I’m tired, Tao Tao.”

“Did she hit you?”

“No! Tao Tao!”

“Did he—”

“NO. God. No.” Yu Jie had her hand on her door. “He’s the only good thing. He’s the only—” She stopped. “Please. I just want to sleep.”

Tao Tao put the kettle on, very loudly, so Yu Jie would know she was still there. She went in her room and shut the door.

Radiator: Are you all right?

Yu Jie: family

Every night. Same question. Same one word. She didn’t ring him. If she heard his voice she’d fall apart, and she didn’t want him to watch her fall apart over something he couldn’t fix.

Radiator: Eaten?

Yu Jie: yes

Radiator: What?

Yu Jie: dumplings

Radiator: Who folded them?

Yu Jie: the cook

She stared at that for a long time. How did he know to ask that? He didn’t. He couldn’t. He just asked things. She didn’t cry when she looked at the calendar. A hundred and twenty squares till the gold one. Then a week. Then two hundred guests. Then Geneva.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday the building opened again. She went in early. The lab was the only place in the world where nobody had ever called her a jewel.

The Hall of Science was nearly empty. She took the back stairs, the old concrete ones nobody used because the lift was quicker. Past the first floor. Past the second, where Gao’s lab was still dark. Past the third. Between the third and the fourth, on the little landing where the stairs turned, there was a narrow window. Bare trees. Grey February sky. It was where he’d kissed her for the first time. October. The light going. She stopped there. She didn’t decide to. Her legs did it. And then the whole week came up out of her at once, from somewhere very deep, like water coming up through a floor.

She sat down on the cold concrete step and put her face in her hands. And she cried. Ugly crying. The kind that hurts. Her throat shut like a fist. There was a hot ache at the hinge of her jaw. Her breath came in pieces that didn’t fit together. She pushed the heels of her hands into her eyes till she saw colours. The concrete was so cold through her jeans her legs went numb, and she didn’t move. A week of smiling came off her face all at once, and her face didn’t know what to do without it. She bit the sleeve of her jumper so no sound would get out into the empty building.

It got out anyway. Thin and high, like something caught in a door.

✦ ✦ ✦

He heard it from the corridor. He’d come in early because the heating at the flat had died again. He was walking back from the kitchen with his mug when he heard it. Faint. Through the fire door at the end.

Somebody crying in the back stairwell. Trying very hard not to. Failing. He stopped. He put the mug down on the floor against the wall. He opened the fire door.

She was on the third step from the bottom of the flight below him. Back against the wall. Face in her hands. Jeans. A big grey jumper he’d never seen. Hair down. No pens in it. Not one. Her shoulders were shaking. She heard the door and looked up. Her face was wet. Red. Blotchy. Nothing at all like a photograph.

“Oh. No. No, not you. Please.” She scrubbed at her face. “I don’t want—go away. I’m fine. I’m FINE.”

He didn’t go away. He came down the stairs fast. Sat on the cold step beside her. Pulled her in sideways, her wet face into his neck, and wrapped both arms round her.

She fought it for about one second. Then she stopped fighting. He didn’t say anything. He took a packet of tissues out of his cardigan pocket, the kind his sister made him carry, and pushed it into her hand. She took one and blew her nose very loudly. Then she started crying again, into his collar. He waited, like he did at the board. His hand went up and down her back over the big grey jumper. Slow. Even. Like he had all morning and was glad to spend it on a freezing step in an empty building.

✦ ✦ ✦

After a long time she stopped. She leaned against him with a fistful of wet tissues, looking at the narrow window.

“It isn’t you…” Thick. “I want you to know that. It’s not the forum. Or the photos. Or the letter. It’s not anything you did.”

“All right.”

“It’s my mother.”

He waited.

“She had the photos. On her phone. She took me in the room with the pearl and showed me. She said she didn’t care what happened. Only what it looked like.”

“Of course she did.”

“And then she said—” Her voice broke. She stopped. She tried again. “The engagement’s at the end of June. The week after graduation. Two hundred guests.”

His arm went tight round her.

“And then I stop. Just stop. Physics. The lab. Gao. All of it. Geneva, with a man who’s very kind and doesn’t love me. Dresses. Parties. Smiling.” She stared at the tissues. “She said I was made for it. She said she made me for it.”

“What did you say?”

“That I’m not a pearl.” A wet, broken laugh. “And she said, Of course you are. Like I’d said I wasn’t a girl. Like it was a fact. And then I went back and ate the dumplings and smiled for a week.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He looked down at her. Big grey jumper. No pens.

“My parents are retired teachers.” He said it slowly. “They live in a little flat by the sea. My dad taught maths for thirty-eight years. My mum did literature.”

She was listening.

“When I was nine I asked why light bends. That weekend my dad went to the library and brought home every book on optics they had. He sat at the kitchen table with me every night for a year.” A pause. “He didn’t understand them either. He just sat there.”

Her face crumpled a bit.

“They never told me what to be. Not once. I was lucky. I know I was.” He looked at his hands. “So I don’t know what yours is like. I can’t say I understand. I don’t.”

“Miles—”

“But I can tell you one thing that’s true. If you want it.”

She looked up at him.

“Your thesis is the best thing I’ve read this year. Not the best student thing. The best thing.” Low, in the stairwell. “On page nine you wrote a paragraph about electrons going along an edge. I put my pen down and looked at the snow for ten minutes. I didn’t want to read the next line yet.”

“Stop it—”

“Nobody made you for that. You made it. Two in the morning, on your bedroom floor, with your corners.”

“How do you know it was the floor—”

“Because you’ve got carpet fluff on every page of the second draft.” He wouldn’t look away. “Your mother can call you anything she likes. She can stand you in any room next to any pearl. I’ve seen what you actually are. It isn’t a jewel.”

“What is it?”

It came out a whisper. He took the question seriously. He always did.

“A physicist.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She cried again. Different, this time. Like something opening that had been shut for years. He held her through all of it. Every time her shoulders shook, something in his chest pulled tight, like a wire between them that someone kept yanking. It hurt. Actually hurt, in his hands. He held on harder.

When she finally lifted her face, it was a complete wreck. He kissed it anyway. Her wet eyelids. One, then the other. The salt on her cheekbone. The corner of her mouth. She made a broken little sound. Then she turned her head and kissed him properly. Hard. Both hands in his collar, like she was holding on to the only fixed point in the building. He kissed her back the same way. It tasted of salt and his tea. When she stopped, she put her forehead against his and stayed there.

“Thank you.” Barely. “For not going away.”

“I was never going away. Not if you’d thrown the tissues at me.” A pause. “I did put my tea on the floor, though. In the corridor.”

She laughed. Wet and shaky. Real.

“You put your tea on the floor? You’ll kick it over!”

“Almost certainly.”

She wiped her face with the back of her hand. She stood up. He stayed on the step, long legs folded, glasses crooked, his collar soaked through.

“I’m not going to Geneva.”

He looked up at her.

“I don’t know how yet.” Her chin came up. Her eyes were red and swollen and completely fierce. “But I’m not going.”

She bent and kissed him once more, quick, on the mouth. Then she went down the stairs. Past the third floor. Past the second. He sat and listened to her footsteps go all the way down, until the fire door at the bottom opened and banged shut.

He went back up. Opened the fire door at the top. Kicked his tea over.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she took the calendar off her bedroom wall. She looked at the gold square at the end. 20 June. Then at where the week after it should be. Where her mother’s engagement would go. There weren’t any squares there. She’d never drawn any. She’d made the calendar in September, when the twentieth of June had looked like the end of everything.

She got a pencil. She drew a line after the gold square. Then another square. Then another. She didn’t know what would go in them. She drew them anyway. A whole new row after the gold one, off the edge of the paper and onto the wall. In the first one, the twenty-first of June, very small, she wrote:

Not a pearl.
